>
> I should have looked in the manual, I guess. :-)

>
> I did a bit more of searching, and read that the negative binomial distribution can also handle zero cases like this, so I decided to try it out before moving to the (in my eyes) more advanced (and maybe not so easy to interpret) zero-inflated model.
>
>
> The model was straight forward to implement, and required only very few modifications to the original code (Go Stan!). I uploaded the model here: https://gist.github.com/demodw/457aaff455b99bd5a36fa8961fb3c8bb. I just put normal(0,5) on the intercept, and normal(0, 2.5) on the coefficients.  When I run the model without any priors on sigma for each regression coefficient, the model converges nicely (R-hat < 1, tree depth ~ 8.5, log-posterior looks unimodal). Step-size is about 0.01 in all chains, so quite low, which may be due to the relatively weak priors (I guess). The coefficients are approximately the same as  if I had run it in 4 separate rstanarm runs. So far so good.
>
>
> However, when I try to add priors on the scale values, I run into trouble. I uploaded the model to https://gist.github.com/demodw/37a7bb1a8e4cb6769f3ee1cf45ad2a25. The intercept is modelled with a normal(0, 2.5) prior on the scale, and the coefficients are modelled with a normal(0, 1) prior on the scale. I would have thought this corresponded approximately to the scenario above, since normal(0, 2.5) has support for values in the range +-5.7, and normal(0, 1) has support for the values in the range +-2.2. The model does converge (R-hat < 1.1, tree-depth ~6.5). Step-size is is about four times at large, at 0.04, in all chains. However there are quite a few divergences. From the inspection of energy and log-posterior, it also seems that it is now multi-model (see attachments). Initially I thought that the model might be unidentified, but I cannot really see why. I have coded male/female as -1, 1. The other categorical variable, Adm, I have forced to have a zero entry.
>
>
> When I inspect each of the coefficients, they all look to behave nicely. They are within the bounds, and look normally distributed. Similar with the scale values, except I start seeing some tails, especially on sigma_A and sigma_B. For these two it seems that Stan tried to explored beyond the bounds of the specified distribution. So, naturally, I tried to increase these a bit. The result was the same: lots of divergences, and Stan once again tried to explore beyond the bonds. I've tried with both double exponential, cauchy, and student_t with 3 and 7 df. Same result. Even increasing the acceptance rate to 0.95 did not change it. Am I missing something? Is there an unidentified component in my model?
>
>
> Cheers,
>
> David

Hi all,

I have experienced similar slowdown using rstan via docker containers in another project so am keen to help figure this out.

Thanks for the example James. I have run your examples natively on a  mac (OS X Yosemite 10.10.5), natively on linux (Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS), and in docker containers (Debian GNU/Linux 8 (jessie)) on both mac and linux. From everything I can see there is a big slowdown exactly as James reported.

Number of CPUs: When i first read James's results I was concerned that perhaps the docker container was only accessing 1 CPU. But that seems not to be the case. The results below show that when I ensure a docker container is using 3 cpus (we're running 3 chains), i get similar elapsed time to James (~800s). When I run results in a docker container using 1 cpu the elapsed time is about 3 times longer (~2243 s) while the time reported by rstan to sample each chain is similar to when using 3 cpus (~700-800s). The attached pictures show evidence of using 1 vs 3 cpu.

Native Mac vs Native Linux: I'm getting similar speeds when running the code on a mac and a linux box running Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS.

In a docker container on Mac or Linux:  I'm getting similar speeds when running the code in the supplied docker container on either a mac or a linux box running Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS.
In both cases the results via docker are running 5-10 times slower in the docker container than when run natively. I verified that the docker containers were accessing all 3 cpus.

Elapsed vs User time: I'm confused as to how to interpret the user vs elapsed time. In all the results I ran, the code had 100% access to the CPUs. > On Nov 30, 2016, at 7:03 PM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Some more fiddling around and I seem to have working model now. hurray. Now I'm just wondering if it can be made computationally better. Right now I am just looping over each data point.
>
> Any advice?

It might be better statistically moving to the non-centered
parameterization (it's location and log scale that get "non-centered").

You can rewrite your loop

    for (n in 1:N) {
      real eta;
      eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
	betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
	betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
	betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
	betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
	betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
	betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
	betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
	logOffset[n];
      // Increment likelihood
      target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
    }

as

 vector[N] eta;
 eta = beta0[Di]
       + betaSex[Di] .* Sex
       ...
       + logOffset;
 Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);

as long as all those variables are vectors.

- Bob

Sometime ago i mentioned the issue of a slowdown in rstan performance when run via docker to some experienced colleagues, Dirk Eddelbuettel and Colin Gillespie. Both wondered whether changing the BLAS library would help. This is all beyond my expertise but I'll mention it FWIW. Apparently optimising the BLAS library can result in a big speed when using R for any machine. But more worrying, Dirk wondered whether there were two layers trying to multithread and use all the cores? This could explain the big slowdown being experienced. He suggested checking what BLAS library stan uses, and what was installed in the docker image. And then try replacing with with Atllas if it's not already the default.

James's docker container is building off rocker/tidyverse <https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/tidyverse/~/dockerfile/> which builds off rocker/rstudio-stable <https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/rstudio-stable/~/dockerfile/> which builds off rocker/r-ver <https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/r-ver/~/dockerfile/> which builds off debian:jessie. The installation of R in construction of rocker/r-ver <https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/r-ver/~/dockerfile/> uses options "--without-blas" which according to these instructions suggests <https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-admin.html#BLAS> it is using R's default BLAS library.

Perhaps one of the stan team can comment on whether this might indeed make any difference and be worth pursuing further?

Let's say I calculate a large matrix for each simulation. I don't want to get that matrix for all simulations - it would be too big. But I want to somehow average out all elements of the matrix for the entire run and just get the mean matrix. Is it possible to do within the Stan framework? Thanks!

On Thursday, December 1, 2016 at 10:13:08 AM UTC-5, Denis Perevalov wrote:
> Let's say I calculate a large matrix for each simulation. I don't want to get that matrix for all simulations - it would be too big. But I want to somehow average out all elements of the matrix for the entire run and just get the mean matrix. Is it possible to do within the Stan framework? Thanks!

In RStan that is possible. Either specify pars = "big_matrix" and include = FALSE in the call to stan() or sampling(), which will not return the whole posterior distribution of the big matrix. But get_posterior_mean() will still return the posterior means of everything including the mean of each cell of the big matrix. If you want the overall mean of the big matrix, you could calculate that in generated quantities and get its posterior distribution.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
Hmm, there are a couple of ways I can thinking of hacking this (or maybe "solving" rather than "hacking" if we can consider these changes as representing a true underlying model):

1.  Continuous-time parameter, continuous-time data:  Allow these weekly effects to start and end midweek.  For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.  With real data, if things actually only start at the beginning of each week, you might still be able to fit this model because the slop and uncertainty would allow a continuous fit.  Sure, it wouldn't be quite correct, but you already have enough noise that you're not always identifying the start and end _weeks_, so would it really be so horrible to allow continuous times?

2.  Continuous-time parameter, discrete-time data:  Again allow a continuous time for the start and end parameters.  But now match them to discrete weekly start and end via an S-curve.  For example, let's label the discrete points as integers.  Then if the continuous start parameter is x, the discrete starting point could be the integer closest to x + epsilon, where epsilon is a distribution such as a logistic or normal with center 0 and scale sigma, and sigma has some value such as 0.5 or 1:  this corresponds to an ordered logit or probit.  The idea is that sigma will be small enough that the start time parameter roughly localizes the actual start time, but large enough that the transition from one integer to the next is smooth, so there's no near-discontinuity that would jar the HMC.  You could implement this model with latent epsilon but I think it would probably work better to use the normal and logistic cdfs.  (In theory these go off to infinity but I'd just truncate to the nearest 3 or 4 discrete possibilities for the likelihood.)  Once you've fit the model, you can then, in the generated quantities block, use simple Bayes calculation to get inference for the epsilons and thus identify the actual starting and end points more precisely.

Of these, I think I prefer #1.  But I'd be happy with either one if it works!

See you
A

> On Nov 29, 2016, at 6:58 PM, Phil Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
>

>
>
> > > What's happening is this: the "start time" and the "duration" are effectively quantized with units of weeks. They are defined as continuous variables, but whether the value of the start time is 2.1 or 2.9 or 2.99 makes no difference: all of these define the start time to be in "week 2". This makes it easy for the system to get trapped in a local likelihood maximum and unable to find the global one.
> >
> > In general, that approach shouldn't work.  The assumption built into
> > Stan's algorithms is that the log density function is continuously
> > differentiable.  By hacking in discrete variables the way you do, you break
> > that property.
>
>
> I'm not surprised, indeed this is sort of what I expected...except that at the Stan meeting I attended a few weeks ago, I thought this was the model the Stan experts said I should fit.
>
> I thought it seemed possible that the prior distributions could provide a sort of tug in one direction or another: even though the predictions are exactly the same for any start times that have the same integer week number, the likelihood will not be the same. But you're right that it will be discontinuous across the boundary, so I guess that is the problem.
>
> Did I misunderstand what Andrew and Michael were suggesting?
>
>
> > The only thing that'll work well in Stan is marginalizing out the
> > discrete parameter.  As we discussed when you're in town, this can be
> > combinatorially prohibitive.  If it is, then you're just out of luck with
> > the model as formulated in Stan.  Andrew or others may have ways to reformulate
> > to get the same effect, but I don't have any ideas.
> >
> >
>
> If I have to try every combination of start time and duration, that would be combinatorially prohibitive. With 100 weeks of data, there are 100 possible start times, and, uh...let's see, duration has to be less than or equal to the number of remaining weeks, so... that's (100*99) + (99*98) + (98*97) + ... different possibilities, which is 1 million. And each time of day could have a different start time and duration, so if I do hours that's 24 million (and in fact it would be more convenient to work with 15-minute data, so that's 100 million)...and this all assumes just one "impulse" per time of day, over a two-year period. A more common real-world case would be 10 or more.  10 would not be 10x as much computation, since we could set a constraint that the next impulse has to be after the first one has ended, but I would still be in the hundreds of millions of combinations. This is not an appealing approach.
>
> However, it seems like there should be a way to greatly reduce the amount of computation because it shouldn't be necessary to test every possible start time and duration:  Although p(y | start time, duration, magnitude ) is not a _continuous_ function of start time and duration, it is monotonic. If I were writing a search algorithm rather than a statistical model, I could find the week that is most different from the average and set the start time at the start of that week and the duration to 1 week. Then try increasing the duration to 2 weeks. Keep increasing the duration until things stop getting better. Then try stepping the start time back one week while increasing the duration one week (so the end time stays the same). Keep doing this until things stop getting better. I'm done. Then, to do another impulse, do the same thing with the residuals from the first one. And so on. Repeat until I'm happy with how well things fit.
>
> Perhaps there are other approaches too.
>
> Hmm. I would love to be able to do all of this in Stan, but perhaps I will need to try some kind of ping pong approach: use one system to come up with the first set of impulse start times and durations, then have Stan fit all of the continuous parameters, then pop back to system 1 to come up with the next impulse times, etc. Ugh.
>
> Thanks for your help, Bob.
>
>
>
>

> On Dec 1, 2016, at 1:23 AM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:

>

> > On Nov 30, 2016, at 7:03 PM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Some more fiddling around and I seem to have working model now. hurray. Now I'm just wondering if it can be made computationally better. Right now I am just looping over each data point.
> >
> > Any advice?
>
> It might be better statistically moving to the non-centered
> parameterization (it's location and log scale that get "non-centered").
>
> Fit didn't really seem to improve, and tree depth increased from 6 to 8, so computation time also went quite a bit up. Truth be told I've never really had luck with the Matt trick for multilevel models.

If you have a lot of data, the centered parameterization will
mix better.   We usually see the tree depth going down and
mixing improving dramatically with only small counts per group.

Though I don't know how much of that is the location
and how much the scale component.

> I attached the modified script for those interested.
>
>
>
> You can rewrite your loop
>
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>       real eta;
>       eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
>         betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
>         betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
>         betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
>         betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
>         betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
>         betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
>         betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
>         logOffset[n];
>       // Increment likelihood
>       target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
>     }
>
> as
>
>  vector[N] eta;
>  eta = beta0[Di]
>        + betaSex[Di] .* Sex
>        ...
>        + logOffset;
>  Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);
>
> as long as all those variables are vectors.
>
>
> Is that actually faster, computationally, or does it just look cleaner?

It'll be faster for two reasons.  First, the scalar vector
products can produce much more compact pieces of the overall
expression graph.  Second, vectorizing the call to neg_binomial_2
will convert a bunch of virtual functions into a single virtual
function call.  How much of a difference it'll make will depend
on the size of N.

Also, Stan doesn't have the same problem as BUGS or R in its
parser, so you can put the operators like "+" on the next line
like you'd see it in other programming languages and in math
typesetting.

- Bob

messages.subject: Phylogenetic meta-analysis: model optimization and WAIC calculation
messages.subject_clean: Phylogenetic meta-analysis: model optimization and WAIC calculation
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am conducting a global meta-analysis on pairwise plant species interactions in order to understand whether invasive species are generally better competitors than native species.

Each data point in the dataset represents an outcome of competition between two different species, with each species being classified according to its biogeographic origin as either native or nonnative (invasive). The two species origins give four combinations of interacting species pairs, all of which are represented in the dataset: native-native, native-nonnative, nonnative-native, and nonnative-nonnative. The overall goal of the analysis is to conclude on whether the intensity of competition between those four groups significantly differs.

In my model, I've been trying to incorporate multiple potential sources of nonindependence among effect sizes (Hedges' d), the main three of which are:
1) the study effect (effect sizes coming from the same experiment/research group are most probably more similar that those from different experiments);
2) sampling nonindependence, which arises when the same control was used to estimate multiple effect sizes;
3) phylogenetic relatedness among competitor species and phylogenetic relatedness among target species (closely related competitors might have similar effects on target species and, similarly, closely related target species may respond in a similar way to competition).

I got the model run, and it returns plausible results. I am not sure, however, how to specify pointwise log-likelihood in Stan that I would need to perform model evaluation and comparison.

I've attached the data, Stan model, and all the R code needed to perform the analysis. I would enormously appreciate any suggestions regarding the model itself (mistakes, ways to optimize it, etc.) and, even more importantly, any help on the model evaluation approach that would work best in this case.

Kind regards,
Marina

messages.body_plain:
> I don't remember ever talking about discrete parameters or associated mixtures.  We were talking about time series with multiple time components identified by priors.  For example,
>
> f(t) = A1 sin(t / T1) + A2 sin(t / T2) + A3 sin(t / T3);
> T1 ~ normal(0, 20 minutes);
> T2 ~ normal(1 hour, 5 minutes);
> T3 ~ normal(1 day, 2 hours);
>
> In particular you were talking about boxcar-like effects that could turn on or off for different periods, which could be modeled with a continuous start time (perhaps guided towards certain times of the day by priors) and a continuous duration (identified into time scales by priors like above).

This example with the sin functions is far enough divorced from my case that I am having trouble mapping it onto my problem. In my problem, there are patterns that recur every 24 hours exactly, starting on some start day and ending on some other day. They are not necessarily continuous functions with period 24 hours, although they can be. For instance, suppose there is exterior lighting that turns on every day at 6pm and turns off every day at 7am. I can already capture that recurring pattern. But suppose, starting November 1 and ending the next March 1, the lighting turns on every day at 5pm instead. Let's say the lighting is 1 kW. As a deviation from the original situation, this shows up as a new spike in the hourly data point at 5 pm. Everything else remains unchanged.

There are different ways of conceptualizing or modeling that case, which looks like a square wave of off-on-off-on (or, if you like, a chain of boxcars) for which the length increases by an hour from November 1 to March 1. (Of course, in the real-world application, this square wave will be superimposed on the many other electric loads in the building). As described in the paragraph above, I picture it as a recurring square wave that doesn't vary in length, plus the one-hour pulse every day from Nov-Mar. But I'm happy to consider other ways of expressing it. However: sometimes there really is something that happens only as a single data point each day, starting on one day and ending on another: Every day from 1am-2am the industrial ovens are turned to full blast to clean them, things like that. So whatever the parameterization, it does have to be able to handle spiky behavior that starts one week and ends another.

My examples above assume a period of 24 hours. There can also be changes with a period of 1 week (e.g. something new happens every Monday at 8 am or whatever). My desired model includes both.

I don't see how the paradigm you are suggesting would allow me to model this. Unlike your example, the periods are not unknowns to be estimated from the data. I know the periods, what I don't know is the start and stop times: when does the boxcar start and how long is it? My current (non-working) model makes the start time and duration continuous variables, but this doesn't fit the application: what does it mean to say that starting (week 4, Tuesday, 3pm) we add 1 kW daily at 5pm? It doesn't mean anything, and therein lies the problem.

See below for why I don't just let every start and stop time be in the mix, with only the magnitudes unknown.

>
> But at no point were we talking about trying to turn the components on or off -- you just assume that they always there and if the data don't need them then they'll be pushed towards zero and have minimum effect on the fit.

The last paragraph (immediately above)  is how I started to implement the impulse model, immediately after our discussion, and I may return to it: I assumed that every day at every hour was the start of a new impulse of unknown duration and magnitude. So, for instance, a new impulse starts on week 3 at 4 pm that applies every day at 4pm until the end of the impulse. This will not work, however, because the duration can only be an integer number of weeks so I run into the same issue of non-differentiability that is plaguing my current implementation. There might also be an issue with selecting priors so as to capture what I want without overfitting, but perhaps I'd be able to resolve that.

Another option, at least conceptually, is to include every start time and duration so that only the magnitudes are unknown: Have an impulse that occurs every day at 3pm in week 1 with a duration of 1 week; another one that occurs every day at 3pm in week 1 with a duration of 2 weeks; and so on for every duration and every week and every time of day. There are some major identifiability problems if I try it this way, but perhaps they could be solved with a judicious choice of priors. The bigger problem is simply the enormous number of parameters, which would be well into the millions for a year-long dataset.

So...sorry for being a dope, but I'm still not getting it.

On Thursday, December 1, 2016 at 10:33:16 AM UTC-8, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hmm, there are a couple of ways I can thinking of hacking this (or maybe "solving" rather than "hacking" if we can consider these changes as representing a true underlying model):
>
> 1.  Continuous-time parameter, continuous-time data:  Allow these weekly effects to start and end midweek.  For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.  With real data, if things actually only start at the beginning of each week, you might still be able to fit this model because the slop and uncertainty would allow a continuous fit.  Sure, it wouldn't be quite correct, but you already have enough noise that you're not always identifying the start and end _weeks_, so would it really be so horrible to allow continuous times?

Yes, I've thought about this, at least in the context of the daily changes. Indeed, the "time of day" effect really should be able to change at any day, and not just change at the start of a week, so it would be good if it can change any day, not just any week. But this doesn't solve the problem. See below for a case that is super easy to see.

Consider the "time of week" effect -- something that happens, say, every Monday at 3 pm. It really does not make any sense to say that the "Mondays at 3pm" effect changed starting on Tuesday at 8:14.  When I say "it doesn't make any sense", what I mean is that my predictions will all be exactly the same whether the "Mondays at 3pm" effect changes on Tuesday at 8:14 or on Friday at 11:45.  So I end up with the discontinous derivatives that are a problem with my current implementation too.

This happens with the "time of day" effect too. Suppose the building gets set, so that starting July 1 the air conditioning comes on at 7am daily instead of 6am. That is going to have no discernible effect outside the range 6am-8am or so.  Whether we say that the change happened on July 1 at 5am or on June 30 at 2pm will have no effect on the prediction and thus will lead to a discontinous likelihood.

>
> 2.  Continuous-time parameter, discrete-time data:  Again allow a continuous time for the start and end parameters.  But now match them to discrete weekly start and end via an S-curve.  For example, let's label the discrete points as integers.  Then if the continuous start parameter is x, the discrete starting point could be the integer closest to x + epsilon, where epsilon is a distribution such as a logistic or normal with center 0 and scale sigma, and sigma has some value such as 0.5 or 1:  this corresponds to an ordered logit or probit.  The idea is that sigma will be small enough that the start time parameter roughly localizes the actual start time, but large enough that the transition from one integer to the next is smooth, so there's no near-discontinuity that would jar the HMC.  You could implement this model with latent epsilon but I think it would probably work better to use the normal and logistic cdfs.  (In theory these go off to infinity but I'd just truncate to the nearest 3 or 4 discrete possibilities for the likelihood.)  Once you've fit the model, you can then, in the generated quantities block, use simple Bayes calculation to get inference for the epsilons and thus identify the actual starting and end points more precisely.

Hmm...you're thinking of sort of tricking the solver by working at the limits of its numerical precision? If its step size can never go below 1e-12, we can make it so 1e-12 corresponds to a change of a whole integer? This seems incredibly kliudgy but would be kind of fun if it works. Can it possibly work, though? I would say that if the answer is "yes" then you guys should make discrete models "legal" in Stan.

My gut feeling is that this will not work. Bob, what do you think?

Phil

You'll have to model a mixture of duration times (1 unit of time, 2 units of time, 3 units of time...) for each possible effect.  Because the effects are independent you can do the marginalizations one at a time for a complexity of around n_effects * n_time_units. The only way this is going to be feasible is if you add more structure to the model (i.e. not just a collection of effects but a few AC effects with specific structure that differentiates them from other effects, etc).

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, December 1, 2016 at 5:57:40 PM UTC-8, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I don't see why a mixture would be needed.  Why not just model it all directly?
>

Because Stan won't let you evaluate duration = 1, duration = 2, duration =3, ... directly.   The only way you can do it is to have a mixture of duration=1, duration=2, duration=3, ..., and estimate the mixture coefficients.  Ditto for the start days or start weeks.

With 24 hours per day, 50 or 100 weeks, 5 or 7 days per week (I can probably ignore weekends and just work with weekdays), and all possible durations from 1 week to N weeks, and allowing at least a few impulses for any given time of day...it's just way too much if I try to do a giant mixture model. Which is really too bad because in most cases I'm interested in, some small number of modes are going to account for the lion's share of the likelihood and I would be happy to completely ignore the others.  If someting turns on every day at 7pm from November through March, the mode that has it turning on at 7pm from August through May is going to have essentially 0 weight.

I think I'm just SOL. Perhaps my best bet is, as I mentioned before, some sort of ping pong model: Fit a Stan model with no impulses; examine the residuals (outside Stan) to come up with candidate impulse start times and durations for each time of day; now fit a model that includes those (with fixed values for the start times and durations); rinse; repeat.

I encourage the Stan team to consider extending the language to allow me to do all of this within Stan. I mean, obviously that isn't going to happen in time for me to use it for this specific problem, I'm not expecting that. But if I have to play ping pong, I'd rather do it all within one language, and to have access to the Stan data structures, rather than have Stan finish and output a bunch of stuff on which I have to write R functions (or Python or whatever) to extract the data I need. Perhaps this is a totally stupid suggestion, you guys are doing a great job with the language and clearly know your business so if you've thought about this and concluded it is untenable then I assume you're right.  But if it _is_ possible to extend the language to allow this, count me as one vote saying it's a good idea.

messages.subject: Re: Phylogenetic meta-analysis: model optimization and WAIC calculation
messages.subject_clean: Phylogenetic meta-analysis: model optimization and WAIC calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

WAIC is a method to approximate predictive performance, and thus you need to define which prediction task is interesting for you. Instead of WAIC it is easier to think about that by considering cross-validation (leave-one-out cross-validation being asymptotically equivalent with WAIC, but having generally better finite sample performance). If you consider cross-validation, you need to think at which level you want to make the predictions. Could you tell whether you would be interested in predictions for new (or left-out)
 - single observations (for same studies, sampling groups etc.)
 - studies
 - sampling groups
 - biogeogr origin groups
or
 - species?
(If I did understood correctly your model, then I found these different ways to group the data).

Easiest and most robust way to do the predictive performance estimate, would then be to use k-fold-CV by leaving out one or several "things" at the desired level (observation, study, sampling group, biogeogr origin group, species).

A computationally faster way is to use leave-one-thing-out with PSIS-LOO approximation.

You could also easily compute log likelihood terms required by PSIS-LOO for sampling groups by adding following to the generated quantities block

for (i in 1:K){
    log_lik[i] = multi_normal_lpdf(segment(d, pos, L[i]) | segment(theta, pos, L[i]), block (V_d[i], 1, 1, L[i], L[i]));

but then it depends how large L[i]'s are whether importance sampling approach works for this.
Luckily loo package will give you warnings if this doesn't produce a well behaving approximation (note that is PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails even more badly).

Thus to continue you need to first think what you want to predict.

Aki

On Friday, December 2, 2016 at 1:29:04 AM UTC+2, Marina Golivets wrote:
> Dear All,
>
> I am conducting a global meta-analysis on pairwise plant species interactions in order to understand whether invasive species are generally better competitors than native species.

> Each data point in the dataset represents an outcome of competition between two different species, with each species being classified according to its biogeographic origin as either native or nonnative (invasive). The two species origins give four combinations of interacting species pairs, all of which are represented in the dataset: native-native, native-nonnative, nonnative-native, and nonnative-nonnative. The overall goal of the analysis is to conclude on whether the intensity of competition between those four groups significantly differs.
>
> In my model, I've been trying to incorporate multiple potential sources of nonindependence among effect sizes (Hedges' d), the main three of which are:
> 1) the study effect (effect sizes coming from the same experiment/research group are most probably more similar that those from different experiments);
> 2) sampling nonindependence, which arises when the same control was used to estimate multiple effect sizes;
> 3) phylogenetic relatedness among competitor species and phylogenetic relatedness among target species (closely related competitors might have similar effects on target species and, similarly, closely related target species may respond in a similar way to competition).
>
> I got the model run, and it returns plausible results. I am not sure, however, how to specify pointwise log-likelihood in Stan that I would need to perform model evaluation and comparison.
>
> I've attached the data, Stan model, and all the R code needed to perform the analysis. I would enormously appreciate any suggestions regarding the model itself (mistakes, ways to optimize it, etc.) and, even more importantly, any help on the model evaluation approach that would work best in this case.
>
> Kind regards,
> Marina

Hi again!

I now realize I posted my questions slightly prematurely! After digging more into the Stan manual (I truly recommend this, it is super!!) I realized that the vectorization was not the solution but reparameterization was! I had already done some reparameterizations in other parts of my code but I hadn't still managed to do any reparameterization to the multi_normal. On pages 234-235 I found (and finaly understood) a thorough description of how to reparameterize the multi_normal such that the multi_normal probability function was not needed but could be replaced by a standard normal and some fancy transformations in the transformed parameter block.

Following these descriptions resulted in no more divergent transitions, and I could very well use matrix algebra to form Mu, i.e. all problems went away!
SInce the description can be easily found in the manual (Modeling Language User's Guide and Reference Manual, Version 2.12.0 <https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/download/v2.12.0/stan-reference-2.12.0.pdf> ) I refrain from posting my final code here. If anyone happens to find themselves having similar problems as the above I will be happy to answer questions (within the limits of my rudimentary knowledge about these issues...)-

Thanks to the authors of the Stan manual. Outstanding work! And thanks also to the authors of Stan!

Sincerely,
Martin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi stan users,
>
> I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.

Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.

Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)

I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).

> The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
>
>
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> }
>
> However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
>
> But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
>
> row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
>
> keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
>
> for(n in 1:N){
>         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
>       }
>
> But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
>
> My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
> "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?

NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.

In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.

For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
1. Mu = X*Beta;
    use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
    loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);

2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
    loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)

3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)

My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.

Daniel

On Friday, December 2, 2016 at 9:01:34 AM UTC+2, Stefano wrote:
> usually the variance (standard deviation ^2) is modeled as random variable with scaled_inv_chi_square. Can you confirm this general knowledge?

For variance parameter in a normal model scaled_inv_chi_square is a conjugate prior, which is useful for Gibbs sampling or partial analytic marginalisation, but HMC/NUTS can handle non-conjugate priors as easily as conugate priors, so there is no need to restrict the prior shape. Instead choose the prior based on what you know.  Nowdays it's rare to see scaled_inv_chi_square prior used in Stan models. See  also the discussion of priors at Stan prior choice wiki https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

Aki

> On Thursday, December 1, 2016 at 5:57:40 PM UTC-8, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I don't see why a mixture would be needed.  Why not just model it all directly?

> Because Stan won't let you evaluate duration = 1, duration = 2, duration =3, ... directly.   The only way you can do it is to have a mixture of duration=1, duration=2, duration=3, ..., and estimate the mixture coefficients.  Ditto for the start days or start weeks.
>
> With 24 hours per day, 50 or 100 weeks, 5 or 7 days per week (I can probably ignore weekends and just work with weekdays), and all possible durations from 1 week to N weeks, and allowing at least a few impulses for any given time of day...it's just way too much if I try to do a giant mixture model. Which is really too bad because in most cases I'm interested in, some small number of modes are going to account for the lion's share of the likelihood and I would be happy to completely ignore the others.  If someting turns on every day at 7pm from November through March, the mode that has it turning on at 7pm from August through May is going to have essentially 0 weight.
>
> I think I'm just SOL. Perhaps my best bet is, as I mentioned before, some sort of ping pong model: Fit a Stan model with no impulses; examine the residuals (outside Stan) to come up with candidate impulse start times and durations for each time of day; now fit a model that includes those (with fixed values for the start times and durations); rinse; repeat.
>
> I encourage the Stan team to consider extending the language to allow me to do all of this within Stan. I mean, obviously that isn't going to happen in time for me to use it for this specific problem, I'm not expecting that. But if I have to play ping pong, I'd rather do it all within one language, and to have access to the Stan data structures, rather than have Stan finish and output a bunch of stuff on which I have to write R functions (or Python or whatever) to extract the data I need. Perhaps this is a totally stupid suggestion, you guys are doing a great job with the language and clearly know your business so if you've thought about this and concluded it is untenable then I assume you're right.  But if it _is_ possible to extend the language to allow this, count me as one vote saying it's a good idea.

I'm not sure what it is you want Stan (RStan?) to implement.
What you're trying to do sounds very particular to your specific
model.  We don't want to try to take over R's job on the data
munging side.  For example, I'm not sure what we'd provide
to "examine the residuals" that wouldn't be very model specific.
RStanArm can provide a lot of this kind of functionality because
it constrains the model classes and thus knows what everything
is.

- Bob

> On Dec 2, 2016, at 4:46 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi stan users,
>
> I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
>
> The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
>
>
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> }
>
> However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
>
> But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
>
> row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
>
> keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
>
> for(n in 1:N){
>         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
>       }
>
> But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
>
> My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
> "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
>
> I'd really appreciate any input on this

> Sincerely,

messages.body_plain:
Multiplying by 0 or 1 is much less efficient in Stan than
doing a select.  That is, if

  int<lower=0, upper=1> cond;
  real a;

rather than writing

  cond * a

it's better to write

  cond ? a : 0

or even better yet, to just skip all the calculations where the
zero would propagate.  So if you're adding in an intercept, you'd
just have something like:

  if (cond) predictor = predictor + a;

The reason is that all the arithmetic operations get stored in the
expression graph we travers to propagate the chain rule for derivatives.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Marc Scott (a colleague of Vince Dories's) asked me to post this to the
list for him:

I have read some stan threads about dealing with label switching in mixture models, and I'm not asking you to help me with the label switching problem.  Let's assume I've written code (and I have) that can find the correct permutation of labels for the parms of interest.  My problem is in reassigning the results to a stan fit object.

In the function fixLabels, I extract: stanFit@sim$samples[[i]]  for each chain i.
I then construct those variable names, like mu[1], mu[2] etc, and reference them well enough to permute a full copy of the ...@sim$samples list.

I then reassign those samples to a copy of the fit object in the global env (lines start ###***###):

fit_stanMix <- stan(model_code = stanMix,fit=NULL, model_name = "Mix", data = simdat, iter = 4000, chains = 3, sample_file = 'Mix.csv', verbose = TRUE)

fit_stanReMix <- fixLabels(fit_stanMix,pars=c("theta","mu","sigma","prob_comp"),2)

print(fit_stanMix,pars=c("theta","mu","sigma"))
###***###
fit_stanMix2 <- fit_stanMix
for (i in 1:3) {
   fit_stanMix2@sim$samples[[i]] <- fit_stanReMix[[i]]
}
print(fit_stanMix2,pars=c("theta","mu","sigma"))

I've checked, and the reassignments WORKED.  The means have moved into the right place so they are under the same name in each chain. Ie, mu[1] has the same mean, no matter what chain.  Label switching solved!

The QUESTION IS: why do my traceplots() LOOK FINE, but the second print, above, or the stan_rhat call (not shown) FAIL(S) to take into consideration the new assignment I just did, that clearly worked, but....

I didn't just switch the NAMES of the sims, I actually assigned the values so the ordering of parms is exactly the same in each chain.

WHAT STAN OBJECT COMPONENT DID I LEAVE OUT?

Thank you, Aki!

Unfortunately, effect sizes within sampling groups might be coming from different biogeographic origin groups.

Here is a short explanation why it is the case:
Each sampling group is a collection of effect sizes that were calculated using a single control. In this study, a control was the biomass of a target species when grown in monoculture, and then a treatment was the biomass of the same target species when grown in a mixture with a competitor. Sampling dependencies arose from the experiments where species-specific effects of multiple competitor species (among which there could be both native and non-native species) were tested on the same target species.

Marina

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Why is rstan so much slower in a docker container
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,
I finally managed to find some time to develop some simpler examples without the `remake` workflow and other stuff.

Basically I set up a repository with 4 models (3 of my own + the 8schools example) to test.

Example 1: 8schools
8schools is a simple example taken directly from the stan repository. In total the model estimates 10 parameters.

Example 2: recruits
recruits is a simple count model that also extracts for categorical generated quantity parameters. In total the model estimates 5 parameters + 32 plot random effects.

Example 3: shrub density
density is another count model but with many more parameters & random effects. In total this model has 209 parameters (200 of which are random effect parameters). This model also contains range of generated quantities

Example 4: shrub density minus generated quantities.
is the same as example 3 except with no generated quantities.

You can see the actual models by going to: https://github.com/jscamac/mwe_stan_docker
That link also provides instructions on how these models can be run in a docker container using an image I've already prebuilt (for details see the Dockerfile in the repository).
But the basics:
On docker container:

R version 3.3.2 (2016-10-31)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Debian GNU/Linux 8 (jessie)

On host/local machine

R version 3.3.2 (2016-10-31)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0 (64-bit)

Running under: OS X 10.11.6 (El Capitan)

Both are running rstan 2.12.1.

Below are the time results I got from running these models both locally on my iMac  (4 GHz i7, 16 GB RAM, OSX = 10.11.6) and within the docker container on the same machine.

Main thing to notice is that the chain times for ALL models are substantially faster locally then on the docker container (see attached). Even in the 8 school example. Like Daniel Falster, I found all models completed substantially faster on the local machine. So the system.time estimates (as seen under TOTAL) seem a little odd. As such I'd probably focus more on stan's chain times - as you can see for pretty much all models, it takes 10x as long within the docker container.

Hi James,

The work you put in for the table is on the right path, but isn't enough to distinguish causes. We're trying to find an order of magnitude difference.

I think I remembered Bob outlining a few things that could have differences in a docker container vs local. Here are some that I can think of:
- cpu runtime
- parallel not implemented correctly
- I/O

If you want to see if it's the first or the second, please rerun with 1 core only. It looks like when you run in parallel, time doesn't report the subprocesses.

For the I/O, one way to do that is with a comparison to CmdStan.

Daniel

Stan already has von_mises_lpdf(), so you don't really need to have your own function. Indeed, I believe von_mises_lpdf() accepts vectors for its arguments. To implement your 3-parameter model, you'd just be doing "amp*von_mises_lpdf(y|offset,kappa)"

Dalhousie University

On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 6:14 AM, Solabs <onat...@gmail.com> wrote:

> dear all,
>
> I built a simple model and tested it with a set of known values. I thought I could share the results here to get some feedback and hopefully get it done better and faster.
>
> The model tries to fit a circular Gaussian, also known as von Mises function to a set of data points. Don't get confused, this is not a circular probability function, it is just a circular Gaussian curve with 3 parameters, the precision kappa, the difference between top and bottom, amp, and the offset of the curve i.e. the position on the y-axis where the minimum of the curve is located.
>
> The data organized as clusters, so that each of the M clusters contain T such vM profiles. Thus each cluster has an hyperparameter, which dictates a prior on the profiles it contains.
>
> von Mises function is defined in the functions{} block... wrt performance, could one vectorize this operation, or wouldn't it matter any way?
>
> between line 52-60, where I define the hyperparameters. should these lines be included in the for loop block?
>
> I took the pain and generated some artificial data to compare the fitted parameters to their true values. I used 125 clusters that resulted by combining the following values... For each profile I added some random normal noise independently.
>
> amp   =  [-5 -2.5 0 2.5 5];
> offset  =  [-5 -2.5 0 2.5 5];
> kappa =  [-4.6   -2.6  -0.7   1.3    3.2];
>
> The figure depicts this relationship between fitted cluster parameters and ground truth. The second row shows the joint error matrix after marginalizing for the 3rd parameter.
>
> I see that the offset and amplitude parameters are nicely fit and the values are close to the data  The kappa parameter is another story, there are lots of points all away from the identity line. But the joint error matrix shows that these are originating mostly from the case where the amplitude parameter is 0, which makes the kappa value undetermined. Otherwise, I am a bit surprised about the sigma_noise parameter which is always undershot by the fitting procedure even though it has a rather non-informative prior (line 56).
>
> cheers,
> s.
>
>
>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-WTN8RpFc0F8/WEU7TL4_9qI/AAAAAAAADOo/FoSzRWCOdhwTOsAHBcc0AyFYNAisuZoOwCLcB/s1600/ModelTesting.png>
>
>
>
>
>
> > functions {
> >         #Function to fit to dependent variables. This is a vonMises function scaled to span [0 1],
> >         #centered on 0 degree.
> >         #amp is the difference between peak and thorough
> >         #offset is the height of the minimum value.
> >         #kappa is the precision parameter.
> >         #no free parameter for the location of the peak, it is always at 0 degrees.
> >         real vonMises(real x, real amp, real kappa, real offset) {
> >                 #how to vectorize this?, cos does only take real values not real[].
> >                 real y;
> >                 y <- amp*((exp(kappa*cos(x))-exp(-kappa))/(exp(kappa)-exp(-kappa)))+offset;
> >                 return y;
> >         }
> > }
> > data {
> >         #the data consists of T columns of X data points, which are to be modelled using the vM function
> >         #Columns originates M different groups and within each group there T profiles.
> >         #Each participant is present in each group:
> >         #Nth profile in each group comes from the same participant, but this is ignored here.
> >
> >         int<lower=0>                     X;              #number of independent variables.
> >         vector[X]                        x;              #independent variables in degrees.
> >         int<lower=0>                     T;              #total number of profiles.
> >         real                             y[X,T];         #dependent variable, each column is one vMises profile.
> >         int<lower=0>                     M;              #number of groups.
> >         int                              m[T];           #indicator variable for origin of y (specifies the recording modality).
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >         #group-level parameters:
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_y[M];     #noise variance for each group
> >         real                             mu_amp[M];      #average amplitude for the group
> >         real                             mu_offset[M];   #average offset for the group
> >         real<lower=0,upper=400>          mu_kappa[M];    #average precision for the group, values bigger than 400 leads to NaN output from vonMises function above.
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_amp[M];   #variance for amplitude for group
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_offset[M];#variance for offset for the group
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_kappa[M]; #variance for kappa
> >         #profile level parameters
> >         real                             amp[T];         #amplitude for single profiles
> >         real                             offset[T];      #offset    for single profiles
> >         real<lower=0,upper=400>          kappa[T];       #precision for single profiles
> >
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > }
> >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Daniel for input!
Even if you hadn't read my additional post I still found useful information in your reply.
I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).

And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).

Thanks!

Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:

> Hi Martin,
>

> On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi stan users,
> >
> > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
>
> Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
>
> Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
>
> I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
>
>
> > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> >
> >
> > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> >
> > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> >
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > }
> >
> > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> >
> > Mu=X*Beta;
> >

>
>

A

messages.body_plain:
> On Nov 24, 2016, at 12:42 PM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>

> I agree that there is a tradeoff between expressivity and efficiency (which is, of course, a special aspect of the general tradeoff between competence and performance).

I think Chomsky's introduction of that distinction ruined linguistics
in the 1960s so badly that it's never recovered.

>
> I also agree that the nature of MCMC computations tips the scales very heavily in favor of performance. (and, yes, I understand that a general-purpose Lisp-like list isn't efficient (linear access time...)). In my case, the scale has just been tipped a bit too far...
>
> But a vector-of-vectors *can* be accessed efficiently : it "just" needs a *different* accessor, that offsets its index. *That* should be implemented.

Two dimensional arrays in Stan are vectors of vectors.
You get each "row" access, but no overall memory locality.

Matrices in Stan store just the values and use the offsets,
but are stored column major.  So traversing by row isn't
efficient in terms of memory locality.

We just introduced a choose(n, m) function to avoid all
the duplication of people writing n * (n + 1) / 2.

I'm afraid I didn't understand exactly what you were proposing in the way of a
function or data structure for Stan.  Some kind of general tensor
structure or triangular matrix structure?  We'll probably get around
to both eventually, but I'll probably take on sparse matrices and then
general ragged arrays first.

And yes, you can just normalize gamma(alpha[i], 1) draws to get a Dirichlet:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution#Gamma_distribution

- Bob

>
> As for implementing it myself : Heavens ! My performance in C++ is abysmal.
>
> For my problem : I think that, in current Stan, I can neglect that M[1,1]==1 constant create auxilliary functions translating (row-column) adresses in M to linear adresses in a vector and back, and declare a vector of parameters :
> vector<min=0,max=1>[n*(n+1)/2] p_raw;
> and making
>  p[suitable_adresses]<-p_raw[same_adresses)/sum(p_raw[same_adresses]).
> That should induce Stan to take care of the jacobians. Finding the prior distribution on p_raw giving the "right" Dirichlet prior to p is probably somewhere in the literature, but, in my case, I can also go with a
> p_raw~uniform(0,1)
> without being far from the truth... which spares me to add anything to the log-posterior for these priors. Yay !
> Only problem : force initialization to non-zero values, to avoid sum(p_raw[<suitable_adresses])==0, which would cause a division by 0 exception...
>
> What do you think ?
>
> --
> Emmanuel Charpentier
>
> Le mercredi 23 novembre 2016 01:23:59 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
>
> > On Nov 22, 2016, at 6:29 PM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Bob,
> >
> > Le mardi 22 novembre 2016 à 16:44 -0500, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> >> I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
> >> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.
> >
> > Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)
> >
> > Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
> > always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
> > approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
> > competition.
> >
> >> Sadly, we don't
> >> have a clean way to code that.
> >
> > The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
> > the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
> > "weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).
> >
> > That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by feature of C++.
>
> If you define an array in C++ (or in C), it's rectangular.
>
> If you use the Eigen matrix library in C++, the matrices
> and vectors are dense.  They have a sparse matrix library,
> but it's not as complete and it's *much* slower.  The obsession
> computer scientists have with rectangular structures is that
> it allows us to control memory locality and blocking in order
> to write these efficient matrix operations.
>
> If you use the vector class in the standard C++ library,
> you do get ragged structures, but you don't get efficient,
> low-memory structures with guaranteed memory locality.
>
> So it's all a tradeoff, as usual.
>
> > The
> > obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
> > somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
> > represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
> > are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
> > structures.
>
> I only play a statistician on this list.
>
> As you may have noticed in my last message, I said I'd be
> working on adding sparse and ragged structures.  They're
> also much harder to work with on the code side, which is why
> I can't bang them out in a weekend.
>
> >> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
> >> are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
> >> create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
> >> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
> >> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
> >> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
> >> can be folded into a function).
> >
> > That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...
> >
> >>
> >> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
> >> and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
> >> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
> >> simplexes.
> >
> > A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
> > or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
> > Python list) would be a good start.
>
> Not going to happen on my watch.
>
> > After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
> > pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to...
>
> No!  It's not efficient at all.  It might seem that way compared
> to R or python, but it's terrible from a CPU perspective.
> Specifically, it destroys memory locality, introducing "pointer chasing",
> which can take an order of magnitude longer than an arithmetic operation
> even on a machine with fast memory.  Wherever possible, optimizing
> compilers will unfold this chase statically at compile time (inlining,
> etc.), but if you make it dynamic, you're hosed.  And making it
> really dynamic in terms of type is what makes R and Python so slow
> in their interpreted forms.
>
> It also loses type safety because a pointer is just a pointer to
> memory.
>
> > You know the
> > drill.
>
> Sadly, I do.
>
> > And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
> > with exactly one data structure to do all of this.
>
> And even less efficient.
>
> > (And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
> > Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
> > *that*).
>
> Memory allocation isn't the issue (it's an issue, but that's not why
> pointers are avoided in modern C++ libraries like Boost and Eigen---it's
> the fact that they require pointer-chasing at run time---it's the same
> reason templates are preferred over OO).
>
> We're managing dynamic memory  in C++ through operator new abstractions
> for reverse-mode autodiff and RAII patterns for other memory (following
> both the std::vector and Eigen::Matrix pattern).
>
> And we take code contributions and are happy to welcome new contributors!
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
In general, we can't map a circular statistic to R
in a way that preserves continuity.  I've been meaning to
try using our unit_vector parameterization for points on
a circle, which overaparameterizes and constrains, but
does have locality of the right kind.

You can't learn much from point estimates in Bayesian analysis;
you want to measure coverage of intervals to see if the parameters
are being recovered properly.  In general, there can be biases
if you build a hierarchical model and the data aren't generated
from such a model.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] model averaging in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] model averaging in Stan
messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 1, 2016, at 5:35 PM, Bryan Galvin <bcga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey everyone,
>
> I have a similar issue to what is described here:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Bayesian$20model$20averaging$20without$20reversible-jump$20MCMC$20on$20highly-dimensional$20models%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/ixBFDRJj8Y0/Zag10wQlBQAJ
>
> where I have several hierarchical regression models with different parameterizations and I'd like to combine them to make predictions.

We generally recommend model expansion rather than model averaging.
Just build one big model with all the predictors.

Or you can build a mixture model at the object level rather than
trying to fit and then mix.  And we'd recommend regularization.

Historically, model averaging was just a stop-gap measure because
the full joint model would be too expensive to fit.

More below.

> I'm first attempting to follow Andrew's weighted model approach described in that thread (before maybe looking into mixture modeling) and am unsure if my implementation is correct:
>
> data{
>   int<lower=0>  N;              //number of observations
>   int<lower=0>  K;              //number of predictors
>   matrix[N,K]     x;               //matrix of predictions
>   vector[N]        y;               //response variable
> }
>
> parameters{
>   simplex[K]    lambda;      //weights for each predictor
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>   real<lower=0> squared_error;
>   squared_error = dot_self(y - x*lambda);
> }
>
> model{
>   target += -squared_error;
> }
>
>
> Here I'm trying to find the ideal weights for each model by minimizing the sum of squared prediction errors. So from this I have a few questions:
>
> 1) am I on the right track with this implementation?

You could just write

 y ~ normal(x * lambda, 1 / sqrt(2));

and avoid having to define the error yourself.  It'll be a little
less inefficient (I'd suggest a scale of 1 rather than 1 / sqrt(2),
which you get from your version).

> 2) should I be using Stan's optimization methods here instead of sampling?

If you want the maximum likelihood fit, that's what you need to do.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi, To determine whether the slowdown James and I have experienced is specific to stan or more generally because of using docker, I benchmarked R running natively vs R running inside docker. (I get similar results using the rocker/tidyverse docker container or james's jscamac/rstan_docker_test container.)

In summary, running R inside the rocker/tidyverse container results took 1.28 times longer than running natively. This is a slowdown but nothing like the 10x slowdown we're seeing in the stan sampling.

I used the package benchmarkme to run a standardized set of tests https://github.com/csgillespie/benchmarkme
In docker, individual tasks take from 0.92-2.5 times the time take when run natively. Summed across all tests docker takes 1.28 times running natively.

Code for running the tests is below. Rds files with my results are attached.

To start docker machine: docker run -v ${PWD}:/root -it rocker/tidyverse R

# Running tests in docker
install.packages("benchmarkme")
library(benchmarkme)
benchmarkme::get_ram()
res = benchmark_std()
saveRDS(res, "/root/docker-6GB.rds")

# Running tests natively
install.packages("benchmarkme")
library(benchmarkme)
benchmarkme::get_ram()
res = benchmark_std()
saveRDS(res, "native.rds")

# Comparing results
library(tidyverse)
res1 <-  readRDS("native.rds") %>%
  mutate(grp= "native")
res2 <-  readRDS("docker-6GB.rds") %>%
  mutate(grp= "docker")
results <- bind_rows(res1, res2)

# plot docker v native
ggplot(results, aes(test, user)) +
  geom_point(aes(col=grp)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "User (sec)")

# ratio of docker to native by task
results %>% group_by(grp, test) %>% summarise(mn=mean(user)) %>% arrange(test) %>% ungroup() %>%
  group_by(test) %>%
    summarise(native = mn[grp=="native"], docker = mn[grp=="docker"], ratio = mn[grp=="docker"]/mn[grp=="native"])

# ratio of docker to native summed over all tasks
results %>% group_by(grp) %>% summarise(mn=sum(user)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    summarise(native = mn[grp=="native"], docker = mn[grp=="docker"], ratio = mn[grp=="docker"]/mn[grp=="native"])

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, December 5, 2016 at 9:02:26 PM UTC-5, Daniel Emaasit wrote:
> How can I define a hidden state z as a parameter in Stan considering that its Categorical? After an exhausting search within the mailing list, I saw some responses suggesting to define z as real in the parameters-block, then converting it to discrete in the model-block. I did that in my code below.

That doesn't work well because it mess up the gradient information in the original variable, which is essential for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. You have to marginalize out the discrete categorical variables.

> How can I resolve the following error that I get when I run the code? (Test dataset is attached)
> [1] "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:"
> [2] "Exception thrown at line 41: beta_log: Random variable[3] is 7.3254, but must be less than or equal to 1"
> [3] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"
> [4] "but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."
> [5] "Rejecting initial value:"
> [6] "  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value."

Declare omega with an upper bound of 1, as in

vector<lower=0,upper=1>[S] omega;

Ben

Hi James,

That output illuminates a lot! And it opens up a lot more questions.

How does Ex 1 work? On docker, it's ~0.5 sec per chain and total time is 17 sec. On local, it's ~0.05 sec per chain (that's an order of magnitude) and the total time is ~27 sec. What's going on? How many chains are you running? If that's because you've enabled parallelization through RStan, turn that off (don't do this: options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores()) -- I don't know how to turn it off once it's on).

Regarding those benchmarks you ran: how many times did you run them? There's a lot of variation run-to-run. Locally, I see something like a 2x difference on small runs... even when no active processes are running. Just because. I don't know what the variation is going to be through a docker container. You'll want to know how much variation there is when you're running the same bits (make sure seeds are the same, everything is the same).

I was telling Bob earlier, I wish I knew more about docker. If I did, I would probably run through these things out of curiousity.

Daniel

Hi Daniel,
It isn't running parallel processors. I made sure of that. It is running 4 chains using rstan's default settings (i.e. a single processor). This means the chains run sequentially (i.e. one chain at a time).
I have run a single chain example and the same 10-fold difference doesn't change.

I think the bulk of the total time (i.e. system.time() ) is captured by the compiling of the model rather then the run itself. I'm less worried about the compiling times and more worried about the sampling times (i.e. chain times).
Also I have set the same seed for all models (12345).

I'm not sure what benchmark runs you are referring too? The tables are the time results for each chain (total of 4 chains) for each model. Plus the TOTAL which refers to R's system.time() return.

J

Great. That's good to know. For future timing, can you separate the compile time from the run time?

And... are you getting similar n_effs? (We've already been bitten by that across different compilers.) I just want to make sure we're comparing apples to apples as much as we can.

Speaking of... what versions of compilers are you using? Sorry for being so pedantic, but these things matter if you want to time.

And can you verify that this is with optimization O3 on both? If the total time (compile + runtime) is shorter for example 1 on docker, that's fishy. Maybe the compiler options aren't actually set properly.

> I think the bulk of the total time (i.e. system.time() ) is captured by the compiling of the model rather then the run itself. I'm less worried about the compiling times and more worried about the sampling times (i.e. chain times).

That's fine, but when there's a difference where the compile time is faster in the docker image, that should have thrown a red flag.

> Also I have set the same seed for all models (12345).

I don't think this will hold, but can you see if the draws are identical? If not, then you'll have to compare time / n_eff, not total time (or time / iterations).

> I'm not sure what benchmark runs you are referring too? The tables are the time results for each chain (total of 4 chains) for each model. Plus the TOTAL which refers to R's system.time() return.
