messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Fitting a Gaussian Curve
messages.body_plain:
thx Bob for the conceptual remarks, made me thing about my analysis.

On Monday, December 5, 2016 at 10:02:30 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> In general, we can't map a circular statistic to R
> in a way that preserves continuity.  I've been meaning to
> try using our unit_vector parameterization for points on
> a circle, which overaparameterizes and constrains, but
> does have locality of the right kind.
>
> You can't learn much from point estimates in Bayesian analysis;
> you want to measure coverage of intervals to see if the parameters
> are being recovered properly.  In general, there can be biases
> if you build a hierarchical model and the data aren't generated
> from such a model.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Dec 5, 2016, at 11:59 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Oh, and you'll want to restrict the range of the offset parameter, else you'll get multiple modes as -pi is the same as +pi
> >
> >
> > --
> > Mike Lawrence
> > Graduate Student
> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > Dalhousie University
> >
> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> >
> > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:55 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Stan already has von_mises_lpdf(), so you don't really need to have your own function. Indeed, I believe von_mises_lpdf() accepts vectors for its arguments. To implement your 3-parameter model, you'd just be doing "amp*von_mises_lpdf(y|offset,kappa)"
> >
> >
> > --
> > Mike Lawrence
> > Graduate Student
> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > Dalhousie University
> >
> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> >
> > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 6:14 AM, Solabs <onat...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > dear all,
> >
> > I built a simple model and tested it with a set of known values. I thought I could share the results here to get some feedback and hopefully get it done better and faster.
> >
> > The model tries to fit a circular Gaussian, also known as von Mises function to a set of data points. Don't get confused, this is not a circular probability function, it is just a circular Gaussian curve with 3 parameters, the precision kappa, the difference between top and bottom, amp, and the offset of the curve i.e. the position on the y-axis where the minimum of the curve is located.
> >
> > The data organized as clusters, so that each of the M clusters contain T such vM profiles. Thus each cluster has an hyperparameter, which dictates a prior on the profiles it contains.
> >
> > von Mises function is defined in the functions{} block... wrt performance, could one vectorize this operation, or wouldn't it matter any way?
> >
> > between line 52-60, where I define the hyperparameters. should these lines be included in the for loop block?
> >
> > I took the pain and generated some artificial data to compare the fitted parameters to their true values. I used 125 clusters that resulted by combining the following values... For each profile I added some random normal noise independently.
> >
> > amp   =  [-5 -2.5 0 2.5 5];
> > offset  =  [-5 -2.5 0 2.5 5];
> > kappa =  [-4.6   -2.6  -0.7   1.3    3.2];
> >
> > The figure depicts this relationship between fitted cluster parameters and ground truth. The second row shows the joint error matrix after marginalizing for the 3rd parameter.
> >
> > I see that the offset and amplitude parameters are nicely fit and the values are close to the data  The kappa parameter is another story, there are lots of points all away from the identity line. But the joint error matrix shows that these are originating mostly from the case where the amplitude parameter is 0, which makes the kappa value undetermined. Otherwise, I am a bit surprised about the sigma_noise parameter which is always undershot by the fitting procedure even though it has a rather non-informative prior (line 56).
> >
> > cheers,
> > s.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > functions {
> >         #Function to fit to dependent variables. This is a vonMises function scaled to span [0 1],
> >         #centered on 0 degree.
> >         #amp is the difference between peak and thorough
> >         #offset is the height of the minimum value.
> >         #kappa is the precision parameter.
> >         #no free parameter for the location of the peak, it is always at 0 degrees.
> >         real vonMises(real x, real amp, real kappa, real offset) {
> >                 #how to vectorize this?, cos does only take real values not real[].
> >                 real y;
> >                 y <- amp*((exp(kappa*cos(x))-exp(-kappa))/(exp(kappa)-exp(-kappa)))+offset;
> >                 return y;
> >         }
> > }
> > data {
> >         #the data consists of T columns of X data points, which are to be modelled using the vM function
> >         #Columns originates M different groups and within each group there T profiles.
> >         #Each participant is present in each group:
> >         #Nth profile in each group comes from the same participant, but this is ignored here.
> >
> >         int<lower=0>                     X;              #number of independent variables.
> >         vector[X]                        x;              #independent variables in degrees.
> >         int<lower=0>                     T;              #total number of profiles.
> >         real                             y[X,T];         #dependent variable, each column is one vMises profile.
> >         int<lower=0>                     M;              #number of groups.
> >         int                              m[T];           #indicator variable for origin of y (specifies the recording modality).
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >         #group-level parameters:
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_y[M];     #noise variance for each group
> >         real                             mu_amp[M];      #average amplitude for the group
> >         real                             mu_offset[M];   #average offset for the group
> >         real<lower=0,upper=400>          mu_kappa[M];    #average precision for the group, values bigger than 400 leads to NaN output from vonMises function above.
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_amp[M];   #variance for amplitude for group
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_offset[M];#variance for offset for the group
> >         real<lower=0>                    sigma_kappa[M]; #variance for kappa
> >         #profile level parameters
> >         real                             amp[T];         #amplitude for single profiles
> >         real                             offset[T];      #offset    for single profiles
> >         real<lower=0,upper=400>          kappa[T];       #precision for single profiles
> >
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >
> >                 #group level (does this need to be inside the for loop?)
> >                 sigma_kappa   ~ cauchy(0,1);#what alternative are there for these parameters?
> >                 sigma_amp     ~ cauchy(0,1);
> >                 sigma_offset  ~ cauchy(0,1);
> >                 sigma_y       ~ cauchy(0,10);
> >
> >                 mu_kappa      ~ lognormal(0,1.5);
> >                 mu_amp        ~ cauchy(0,10);
> >                 mu_offset     ~ cauchy(0,10);
> >
> >                 for (i in 1:T) {#run over profiles
> >                         #parameters of single profile are distributed according to group-level parameters.
> >                         #could this be vectorized?
> >                         offset[i]           ~ normal(mu_offset[m[i]]         , sigma_offset[m[i]]);
> >                         kappa[i]            ~ lognormal( log(mu_kappa[m[i]]) , sigma_kappa[m[i]]);
> >                         amp[i]              ~ normal(mu_amp[m[i]]            , sigma_amp[m[i]]);
> >
> >                         for (xi in 1:X){#run over the dependent variable
> >                                 y[xi,i] ~ normal(  vonMises(x[xi],amp[i],kappa[i],offset[i]) , sigma_y[m[i]] );
> >         }}}
> >
> >

On Tue, Dec 6, 2016 at 5:08 PM, Jeff Alstott <jeffa...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Are you using pystan? I believe it works fine in RStan.
> I am using pystan.

Thanks for reporting back. For future reference, it helps to let us know up front that you're on pystan (or rstan or cmdstan).

The I/O is written separately for each of the interfaces, so errors in one interface may not translate to another interface.

> >
> > When you say "crash," what do you mean? Does it take down whatever you were running in? Or does it just quit?
> I upon running the model for sampling we get a runtime error, with the message I showed before:
> RuntimeError: int variable contained non-int values; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=gap_lengths; base type=int
>
> Changing gap_lengths to an array of reals removes this message.
>
> In either case I'm sending an empty list from Python. If I send an empty array, with type 'int', then we don't get this error. So it does seem to be in the plumbing from Python to Stan.

That seems like the correct behavior. Remember that Stan is a strongly typed language. An array of reals is not an array of ints. It seems like an empty array in Python is created with a floating point type by default, so it's interpreted as an 0-length array of Stan type "real." I'm sure with clever enough I/O, someone could write better I/O in PyStan so empty arrays could be interpreted as both int arrays and real arrays, but the current behavior seems right for now.

Daniel

>
>
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> > On Dec 6, 2016, at 3:05 PM, Jeff Alstott <jeffa...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

It looks like there's an issue where RStan is pulling alpha from the global environment, which is a function, not the value you set.

> ?alpha
Help on topic ‘alpha’ was found in the following packages:
  Package               Library
  scales                /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.3/Resources/library

or even:

I don't know enough about how RStan grabs things out of the global environment to tell if this can be dealt with automatically, but the current workaround is to pass data into the Stan call.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Denis,

We compute everything on the log scale for numeric stability.

The reason why we don't add things to the language for convenience is really a practical one. It's a maintenance burden. Rather than having the Stan language support another 30+ functions, you can easily write exp(foo_lpdf(...)) and be done with it. If Stan exposed it, then it's on Stan to indicate when it underflows to 0 or overflows to 1 and we'd have a ton more work to do. If it were free to do it, we would just implement it.

On Wed, Dec 7, 2016 at 12:07 PM, Denis Perevalov <deni...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I see in manual that there are only _lpdf functions, like normal_lpdf, student_t_lpdf etc.. Why don't we have _pdf functions too?
>
> I need pdf in some of my calculations, so every time I have to expontiate lpdf or I would have to write my custom pdf function, even for the most common distributions.

Yes, just do that. Althought... you're probably writing your function wrong. Just computing things on the log scale.

>
> Also, it would be nice to have a Variance-Gamma distribution
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance-gamma_distribution
> It should be straightforward to implement since all special functions that are used for it are available in Stan.

Great! Go ahead and write a custom lpdf function in your program. I think that absolute value in there might introduce a discontinuity, so it might not be something that should go in Stan in general. And I forget if the modified Bessel function of the second kind is exposed in the Stan language. If it's not, it's probably because we can't get reasonable gradients out of it. For Stan's algorithms, gradients are required, so it's more than just being able to compute the log joint probability distribution function. You need to be able to compute the gradients also.

Good luck with the Variance-Gamma distribution! Let us know you're able to get a working version with a function.

Daniel

With some caveats.  First, you need four physical CPUs --- a lot of
people will only have two these days on a notebook.  And you need
enough memory, though that's usually not a problem.

Also, it does use the four CPUs, which means they're not available
for other tasks, which can be problematic if the job's going to
run for some time.  And on some machines, even running two
number crunching processes full bore will cause enough memory or
disk contention to make everything else sluggish.

So basically, your performance is going to vary with hardware.
Having said that, investing in a decent i7 4-core machine is
easily justified if you do a lot of number crunching and can
afford it.

This is one of the reasons we need a Stan-in-the-cloud solution
for people!

messages.body_plain:
Why do you want to do this?  If you're building something like
a regression with different predictors, then how much a predictor
adds to the mix depends on the other predictors you use and what
the prior is.  There are some really neat illustrations of this in
the Hastie et al. machine learning book when they look at path
regressions (you can find it in the same diagrams in their elastic
net paper, too).

We tend to compare models by their calibration (do they get
the right posterior coverage in held out or cross-validation
tests) and their sharpeness (do they make tight predictions in
the sense of the posterior predictive intervals being narrow).
We can also evaluate more traditionally just on held-out data
likelihood.

There are a bajillion traditional methods for doing this, such
as ANOVA, many of which have Bayesian analogues.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

An example of the problem where I want _pdf is as follows.

Suppose I have a time series of daily returns. I have a model that predicts a distribution of returns. So each sample(simulation) predicts its own probability of returns - not a number but a distribution. Usually I use a normal pdf. So, for every day I have lots of return pdfs after I train my Bayesian model on a training sample. Now I want to compute a metric of how my model performed on a testing sample. Each day I observe only single return. Overall lpdf for every j-th day will be

lpdf_j = log(1/N * sum_i=1^N  pdf_i(r_j)), where the sum is over simulations.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 7, 2016, at 3:41 PM, Denis Perevalov <deni...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> An example of the problem where I want _pdf is as follows.
>
> Suppose I have a time series of daily returns. I have a model that predicts a distribution of returns. So each sample(simulation) predicts its own probability of returns - not a number but a distribution. Usually I use a normal pdf. So, for every day I have lots of return pdfs after I train my Bayesian model on a training sample. Now I want to compute a metric of how my model performed on a testing sample. Each day I observe only single return. Overall lpdf for every j-th day will be
>
> lpdf_j = log(1/N * sum_i=1^N  pdf_i(r_j)), where the sum is over simulations.

Great.  That's easy.  You can program that much much more stably
as:

  vector[N] lp;
  for (n in 1:N) lp[n] = foo_lpdf( ...n... );
  lpdf_j = log_sum_exp(lp) - log(N);

where you just assign the lpdf term to lp.  log_sum_exp does
sums on the linear scale of inputs on the log scale and
returns a result on the log scale, all while maintaining maximal
arithmetic precision (not to mention avoiding underflow and overflow).

> With regard to Variance-Gamma. I can implement it in the Stan language, no problem. If it works fine and needs to be committed to Stan repository does it need to be in a C++ implementation?

Implementing a distribution for Stan itself is much more work
because we want them to be vectorized (template expressions)
compute return types (template metaprogram) and drop constant terms
(template traits).  And we need it not just for reverse-mode autodiff
but also for forward mode (requiring additional template expressions).
And we require extenstive testing using our density testing framework.
You can see how that goes for existing distributions in the code.
It's in the stan-dev/math repo.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: How is standard error in elpd calculated in LOO package?
messages.subject_clean: How is standard error in elpd calculated in LOO package?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben, SE(elpd) in the loo package is computed as sqrt(N * var(pointwise_elpd)).  So, for example, the following

x <- loo(ll) # ll is pointwise log-likelihood matrix
print(x)
se_elpd1 <- x$se_elpd_loo # the SE reported by print

pointwise_elpd <- x$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
se_elpd2 <- sqrt(ncol(ll) * var(pointwise_elpd))

should result in equal values for se_elpd1 and se_elpd2.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

> GMO does not assume multivariate normality but it does use a normal approximation for the distribution of the local variables conditional on the hyperparameters.

I don't understand. The estimated standard errors of phi are based on the observed Fisher information. Is there a way that the observed Fisher information yields appropriate standard error estimates without the posterior distribution of phi | y being multivariate normal?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gmo as possible solution?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] gmo as possible solution?
messages.body_plain:
I think of the main goal of GMO as being to get the point estimate of phi, so then the shape of p(phi|y) is not such a big deal.  But if we want posterior draws from phi (which, I agree, we do), I was thinking of the normal approx as a starting point, which could be improved via importance sampling.  This can work in various realistic settings where the dimensionality of phi is low.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reply Bob. The sample is currently at around 7000 samples in 24 hours so nothing patience can't solve. Good to know that this wasn't (entirely) a problem with my code or stan. The "lines" are my J (group) variables. The covariance matrices are only 6 x 6.

Is there a was to increase the resolution on what sample stan is running during the sampling as opposed to it being broken down into 10 steps (1/10000, 1000/10000, 2000/10000 etc.)?

Thanks for the correction on the Cholesky factors. Admittedly I don't know a huge amount about them and copied this part out of the manual.

Could you give me a one sentence tip on where the coding can be improved? Always keen for development.

I agree this may not be the best model for fitting the data, however we're trying to recreate the results from the aforementioned paper to demonstrate the usefulness of HMC when we can't assume conjugacy. Unfortunately, a lot that is published in our field assumes conjugacy so that a Gibbs sampler can be used, even though often it seems inappropriate to do so (normal error when it is clearly skewed etc.).

Thanks for your time,

Lachlan

messages.subject: Copula Marshall Olkin, Multivariate Student-t
messages.subject_clean: Copula Marshall Olkin, Multivariate Student-t
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've had convergence problems with the multivariate student-t distribution, so I came along and found this
beauti

https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/15449-copula-generation-and-estimation/content/mvcoprnd.m?requestedDomain=www.mathworks.com

which lead me to think about Copulas in STAN.

1.
Let's consider the gumbel copula, since some Frank, Joe,...  require discrete distributions.

     case 'gumbel'
        % uses Marshall-Olkin's method
        if theta < 1
            error('archrnd:BadGumbelParameter', ...
                  'THETA must be greater than or equal to 1 for the Gumbel copula.');
        end
        if theta == 1
            y = rand(m,n); %independence
        else
            %uses positive, scaled by (cos(pi/2/theta))^theta, stable distribution
            V = rand(m,1)*pi-pi/2;
            W = -log(rand(m,1));
            T = V + pi/2;
            gamma = sin(T/theta).^(1/theta).*cos(V).^(-1).*((cos(V-T/theta))./W).^(1-1/theta);
            y = exp( - (-log(rand(m,n))).^(1/theta)./(gamma*ones(1,n))  );
        end

Considering the 'else' branch:

This is easy to implement in STAN. Note m is the sample size. Thus we would only need
to define two uniform variables for V, W and n parameters, normal(0,1) distributed
and take its CDF, since rand(m,n) is in [0,1].

2.
Multivariate Student-t

        corrtest(theta); %test if R is a correlation matrix.
        s = chi2rnd(nu,m,1);
        y = tcdf(randn(m,n)*chol(theta).*( sqrt(nu./s)*ones(1,n) ),nu);

This is a 'MATT'-trick decomposition the multivariate student-t distribution to normal(0, 1)
ones.

3. Numerical solutions 'fixed-Talbot'

Would a implementation of numerical algorithm in STAN like the fixed talbot
to overcome the restrictions of not only discrete parameterizations, but also
allow other than Archimedean copulas?

----

Does somebody have experiences with this already? Comments are
welcome.

Thanks so much,
Andre

Would any of you be willing to help convert my stan model to one that can be used with gmo, both for your testing and my benefit?
It's a model that relies heavily on mixture models, so it seems like a prime candidate for this sort of procedure.
The issue is that it's got several mixtures. It's a measurement model (think CFA, 2PL, GRM), but each individual's (i) response on an item (j) can either be produced from a "non-DIF" item model (item j's parameters equal across groups) or from a "DIF" item model (item j's parameters differ across groups). Moreover though, if their response is generated from a DIF item model, it will estimate which latent group the individual belongs to.
The likelihood is something like:

for a CFA.
So there are two 'layers' of mixtures that cross.
There is a mixture model per-item, and within one of the mixture components for each item is a latent group model. Eek. Works decently in NUTS, miserably in vb and optimizing.
mu, lambda, theta, and sigma vectors are all treated as unknown. Each individual's pi vector is estimated using [multinomial] logistic regression, or could just be estimated from an intercept-only model.
Priors are placed to make lambdas positive, and lambdas are ordered across latent groups for one item (to reduce label switching).

I'd love to give gmo a task like this, but I'm not sure what separates the parameters from hyperparameters in this case.

On Wednesday, December 7, 2016 at 9:49:23 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Suppose I have a stanfit object called "fit" and 3000 simulation draws (which I can get using extract(fit)).  I want the gradient for each of these simulation draws.  I'm confused trying to figure out how to do this using grad_log_prob.  It seems like I have to extract the simulations, pull them out one at a time, then put them back into lists.  There must be an easier way, no?

No, due to the fact that the compiled Stan function can only input a vector of (unconstrained) parameters.

> Also it seems that grad_log_prob gives me the gradient on the unconstrained space.  How to I get the gradients on the original (constrained) space?

There is an adjust_transform argument that is TRUE by default which indicates that the gradient calculation should be with respect to the constrained parameters. So, all together it would be

pars <- as.matrix(posterior)
skel <- get_inits(posterior)[[1]]
grad <- t(apply(pars, MARGIN = 1, FUN = function(theta) {
  grad_log_prob(posterior, upars = unconstrain_pars(posterior, relist(theta, skel)))
}))
colnames(grad) <- colnames(pars)

Ben

Delta j is the probability of the second component to the mixture . That is, the probability that an item needs separate parameter estimates between groups.

Imagine your data are generated as such: you have a 10 item survey with 9 response options on each item. You sample from two populations, unbeknownst to you, who do not respond to items 3 and 4 in the same way. Given equal latent ability, those in group 1 have a different expected value than those in 2 on items 3 and 4. So there exist two populations for whom the item parameters of 3 and 4 are different.

This model attempts to estimate 1) the probability of each item having meaningfully different parameters between groups 2) the probability of each person belonging to each group that differs on those items 3) the latent abilities of those individuals and 4) the item parameters for all items.

So Delta j is the probability of the item having separate item parameters between groups, pi is the probability of each person belonging to each latent group, theta is latent ability for each person, lambda is the factor loading for the item j and mu is the intercept for item j.

> I agree this may not be the best model for fitting the data, however we're trying to recreate the results from the aforementioned paper to demonstrate the usefulness of HMC when we can't assume conjugacy. even when everything's conjugate.  So I hope they're
being careful about monitoring that at least.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trying to program a linear interpolation (or something smoother would be even better)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] trying to program a linear interpolation (or something smoother would be even better)
messages.body_plain:
There's not a good way to do these in Stan.  So yes,
it'd make sense to build them in.  The log densities should
be continuously differentiable up to gradients anyway.

You can't use ceil() that way because it returns a real value.

You have to hack it in a loop or if-then-else chain.

We could build it in.  The reason we don't want to do this
in general is that it lets people build log densities that
aren't continuously differentiable.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] truncation parameter
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] truncation parameter
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Michael for your reply,Sorry I didn't see it earlier -- I thought email notifications were on, but apparently not.

Firstly, sorry about the plots that were point estimates, I just didn't have plots at the time that were better representatives of the uncertainty distributions (I do now).

I have a few questions in reply. Firstly, I at least think I understand what you say about generative models. That was my approach to it. I guess switching xtrue and x_meas would have been more explicit in terms of the generative model approach, but I figured it didn't matter anyhow since the normal distribution is symmetric. Just in case this really was the thing that was driving the solution in the wrong direction, I've re-run swapping these two. The solutions are unchanged as far as I can tell, which is what I would expect.

I know using uniform priors with bounds is discouraged, but I thought it would be a reasonable place to start, and surely it shouldn't screw things up too much? I'll re-run again with the priors you suggest to make sure, but I wouldn't think putting extra weight on the wrong solution will fix the problem.

Just to be clear, the model I ran this time was:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
    vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
    vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0,upper=10> xmin;
    vector<lower=xmin,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
}

model {
    xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
    for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
}

So here are some indicative results from my run:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-oppl5Fc8oSc/WEkAHzUwI4I/AAAAAAAABSs/9uCMZfJsrq82ckBsVGeiBV9DAUvZ2vEoACLcB/s1600/N1_m6.0_s1010_sys_n10_w1000_i3000_DENSITYPLOT.jpg>

Here the dark red region indicates the results from every iteration after warmup, and the bright red is the inner 68% region. Clearly, the upper end of the distribution is not pulled back to where it should be. This is the same behaviour I was seeing before, just now its a bit more robust. I ran several realisations, using different random seeds each time to produce the sample, and plot the marginalised posteriors of the parameters:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-PzzDP9iMffo/WEj-6CxvrTI/AAAAAAAABSg/sKLShwB200AD4bPs4IsVvIDzzKBsmYJ4QCKgB/s1600/collective_Fiducial_triangle.jpg>

As you can see, all random samples lead to biased results in the same direction for mu and sigma.

Oddly, this only occurs when the uncertainty is a function of the independent variable. If I produce my samples in exactly the same way, but then add a random gaussian number to each of them to bring them up to the same uncertainty (the maximum in the sample), then the bias disappears (though the resulting uncertainties on parameters are a bit larger). Any ideas on why this would be?

Thanks heaps for your help once again,

Steven

On Tuesday, 11 October 2016 09:15:45 UTC+8, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Firstly, looking at point estimates is rarely if never helpful.
> Bayes is about uncertainty, which means when you judge
> a model you want to look at _intervals_, not points.  The
> question is wether, say, the 5-95% credible interval captures
> the true value.
>
> Secondly, neither of your models are correct.  Please read
> the section of the manual on truncation and censoring.  To
> build these models correctly you have think _generatively_
> and match how you simulated the data.  The latent x is
> generated from a truanted normal, and then the measured
> x is generated from the latent x.  Also, don’t use bounds
> and uniform priors.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
>   vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
>   vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real mu;
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>   real xmin;
>   vector<lower=xmin>[N] xtrue;
> }
>
> model {
>   mu ~ normal(0, 10);
>   sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>   xmin ~ normal(0, 10);
>
>   // First model the latent x
>   for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma)T[xmin,];
>
>   // Then model the observation, note the swap
>   x_meas ~ normal(xtrue, uncertainty);
>
> }
>
> By thinking generatively you’ll also find that you want to model
> the observation variability and not assume that you know it
> absolutely.  Even for a population based model like you mention
> you have to consider that those populations are themselves
> measured with uncertainty.
>
> On Oct 10, 2016, at 8:06 PM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> >
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have asked this question before, but with a complicated model so it was hard to see the actual problem. I have done a bit more work on it and realised that the same problem occurs in much simpler models, so I'm hoping someone can help me :)
> >
> > Let say I produce a set of samples by the following code (I'm using pystan, but this shouldn't matter...):
> >
> > ### Parameters
> > xmin = 5     # Truncation location of data
> > mu = 4       # Mean of data
> > scale = 2.0  # Standard deviation of data
> >
> > ### Produce samples (final size ~5000)
> > xint = np.random.normal(loc=mu,scale=scale,size=15000)
> > xint = xint[xint>xmin]
> >
> > ### Add some measurement uncertainty
> > n = 2 + np.random.poisson(10**((xint-mu-0.5)))
> > sd = 2*np.clip(1 - 0.43*np.log10(n), 0.02, np.inf)
> > xobs = xint + np.random.normal(scale=_sd)
> >
> > The addition of the uncertainty is a bit strange but corresponds in some rough way to how I add uncertainty to my real problem, where each variate represents a (dark matter) halo mass, and the halo mass is correlated with the number of galaxies within it, and the number of galaxies yields the measurement uncertainty. Basically you can think of it as adding large uncertainty to low-valued variates, and much less to high-valued variates. In any case, the final distribution looks like
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>
> >
> > Of course, there is some probability mass outside the shown range for the uncertain case (stuff that got scattered down). Also, the reason for the turnover in the intrinsic curve is just because it's a KDE. It really peaks at 5 or very close to it.
> >
> > Anyway, to me the obvious way to code the Stan for parameter estimation is:
> >
> > data {
> >     int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
> >     vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >     real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
> >     real<lower=0> sigma;
> >     real<lower=0,upper=10> xmin;
> >     vector<lower=xmin,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >     xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
> >     for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
> > }
> >
> > The interesting part is that xtrue has a  lower bound which is a parameter. When I run this through Stan (I ran 700 warmup and 2000 iterations for 4 chains), the first thing I notice is that it has a hard time converging -- each chain seems to settle in a different spot. But none of these spots are very close to the solution. In fact, they are all biased to high mu and low sigma. The median values for all chains are:
> >
> > {u'lp__': -3491.0188530263313,
> >  u'mu': 6.33030908325631,
> >  u'sigma': 1.1798037697816155,
> >  u'xmin': 4.9482856755250273,
> >  u'xtrue': 6.5643129692386513}
> >
> > The thing is, the iteration with highest likelihood has much higher likelihood than the "true" answer does. If "gaussmode" is the highest-likelihood iteration, then
> >
> > print gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars({'mu':mu,"sigma":scale,"xmin":xmin,"xtrue":xint})) - gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars(gaussmode))
> >
> > gives  -2518.74677702.
> >
> > However, another way to formulate the model might be the following:
> >
> > data {
> >     int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
> >     vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >     real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
> >     real<lower=0> sigma;
> >     vector<lower=0,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >     real xmin;
> >     xmin <- min(xtrue);
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >     xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
> >     for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
> > }
> >
> > This time, xtrue is left free, and xmin is chosen as the minimum of xtrue. This means that there is not a heavy jacobian adjustment on xtrue (since in the previous model, most of xtrue should be close to xmin, the jacobian adjustment becomes large and negative). Using this model, and doing exactly the same calculation as above (i.e. the log_prob at the truth minus the log_prob at the mode of the other model) gives a positive number, i.e. the truth is more likely.
> >
> > Of course, just because it is more likely doesn't mean that that is where the probability density is. So, I then ran the same length chains with the "no mmin" model. This model ran a lot slower than the first (not sure why?). Again, each chain settles in a different place, so I guess I'd have to run longer to get convergence (or maybe it will never converge?), but here is the Stan summary:
> >
> > Inference for Stan model: anon_model_2d2e212313b2a3b52815285bebd934ce.
> > 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=700; thin=1;
> > post-warmup draws per chain=1300, total post-warmup draws=5200.
> >
> >               mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
> > mu            5.79    0.18    0.4    4.8   5.54   5.88   6.09   6.31    5.0   2.38
> > sigma         1.44    0.09   0.17    1.2   1.32   1.41   1.57   1.86    4.0   2.52
> >
> > xmin          4.81    0.04   0.08   4.67   4.74   4.82   4.88   4.92    4.0    2.5
> > lp__        3167.5   57.93 129.53 2935.1 3058.7 3181.9 3255.7 3414.5    5.0   2.07
> >
> >
> > This is a little closer to the truth than the first model in all but xmin. Still not very good though. The thing is, the mean likelihood is higher than the likelihood at the truth.
> >
> > The last thing to see is the density plot of xtrue for each model. To plot, I just chose the highest likelihood iteration, but I don't think this choice affects the qualitative judgment of the outcome:
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>
> >
> > It seems like the second model does "better". I was wondering if there is any reason it *should* do better, or in fact if it should be different at all from the first model?
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Steven

messages.subject: quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.subject_clean: quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stans,

I have n posterior distributions computed independently and from different sources for what I believe to be the same quantity of interest θ, that is f1(θ), f2(θ), ..., fn(θ).
Each fk(θ) is obtained by MCMC and smoothed with a KDE; but for this question let's assume that the fk(θ) are simply given and I cannot recompute them.

I would like to combine the information from these posteriors in a single posterior by multiplying together the fk(θ)
(let's assume that the prior contribution for each fk(θ) is absent or negligible so that there is no trouble with that).

Before combining the fk(θ), it seems to be a sane thing to check whether these posteriors are "compatible" in the first place.
Intuitively, I would plot the fk(θ) and check that they somewhat overlap (e.g., the 95% CI overlap).
If they don't, I may have to revise my assumption that the posteriors are actually measuring the same thing.

Is there a (somewhat) established statistical way of doing that & quantifying "compatibility" in this sense, besides the noble ancient technique of visual inspection?
(I am asking since I can think of many ways of quantifying this; I wonder if there is a standard.)

Thanks,
Luigi

I tried to code the original Bugs program in Stan as directly as possible (as above). Everything in the transformed variables block is there to accommodate constraints in Stan that work differently from those in Bugs. Are you computing both with Stan so you know you have the
same model?

Bayesian estimates are posterior means, which can be arbitrarily
far away from the posterior mode, which is what you get from
the MLE.   Often, asymptotically with more data, they'll converge
to the same value.

Why do you think that's a problem?  What you want is not something
close to the MLE, but something that's well-calibrated to return
the parameters in the posterior intervals.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] optimizing analysis through vectorization of the multi_normal probability function
messages.body_plain:
Daniel,
Sorry for late reply.
I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!

Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.

A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post.
I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
(N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior

and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):

 a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
> Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
 b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
>   Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
 c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
>  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
 d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),
>  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R~LKJ(1); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)

The "effect" of reparameterization differs somewhat between these versions.

Note also that I set adapt_delta to different values in the two model versions...

Anyhow, this is what I did and can report (I work in R using rstan):
For each stanfit I extracted the summary and took the mean n_eff over all parameters (mean(summary(stanfit)$summary[,'n_eff'])).
I also used get_elapsed_time() on the stanfit and calculated mean timing of the "sample" part over the chains (colMeans(get_elapsed_time(stanfit))[,'sample']).

I then simply divided n_eff with time.

These are the results for the original multi-normal version (note separate values for models with different priors for Sigma):

Prior        n_eff/time

IW              38.7
SIW            3.90
SSIW          12.9
SSLKJ        0.537

And these are the results for the reparameterized version:

Prior        n_eff/time

IW              38.4
SIW            36.3
SSIW          34.0
SSLKJ        67.6

I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.

/Martin

> Since you're looking at it, can you report the n_eff / time for the before and after models?
>
> On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:08 PM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks Daniel for input!

> > I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
> > Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).
> >
> > And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > > Hi Martin,
> > >
> > > On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi stan users,
> > > >
> > > > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
> > >
> > > Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
> > >
> > > Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
> > >
> > > I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
> > >
> > >
> > > > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> > > >
> > > > for (n in 1:N) {
> > > >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > >
> > > > But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
> > > >
> > > > row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > >
> > > > keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
> > > >
> > > > for(n in 1:N){
> > > >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> > > >
> > > > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
> > >
> > >
> > > NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
> > >
> > > In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> > > Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
> > >
> > > For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> > > 1. Mu = X*Beta;
> > >     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
> > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
> > >
> > > 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
> > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
> > >
> > > 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
> > >
> > > My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > > P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > >
> > > > I'd really appreciate any input on this
> > > >
> > > > Sincerely,
> > > > Martin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
There is no statistically rigorous way of combining samples like this,
regardless of whether they look “compatible” or not.  You can combine
independent likelihood components this way, but not posteriors as at
the very least the prior correlates all of the components.  This means
that the total posterior does _not_ factor into independent components,
at least unless your posterior is exactly Gaussian.

There have been many papers trying to approximate this process when
the posterior is approximately Gaussian, but they all end up quite fragile
as even small perturbations away from a Gaussian distribution can skew
the results.

Unless you can fit everything jointly, we can’t offer any advice other than
“try it and see if it’s good enough for you”.

messages.body_plain:
This is not correct.

The Jacobian adjustment is for a 1-1 transformation which always
yields a square Jacobian.  For many-to-one or one-to-many
transformations you have to first construct a 1-1 transformation
with auxiliary parameters and then marginalize out the auxiliary
parameters from the resulting joint distribution.  For example,
if you had pi(x, y) and wanted the density for r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
then you could compute

pi(r) = \int d(theta) pi(r, theta) = \int d(theta) pi( x(r, theta), y(r, theta) ) | J (r, theta) |

Additionally, computing J and then calling log_determinant will be
viciously inefficient.  You almost always want to (and can) figure
out the log Jacobian determinant analytically.

Hi Michael,

thanks for the answer, but the question was really about a compatibility statistic.
Please forget for now about combining the posteriors (or, more correctly, likelihoods -- I did say to ignore the prior :)).

My question is more basic -- I have these say two posteriors coming from two experiments (e.g., measurements of supposedly the same quantity of interest).
Intuitively, if they are extremely narrow, Gaussian-like and separated by say 20 SDs, I have to conclude that the sampling procedure is wrong, or the model is wrong (e.g., massively misspecified), or the two experiments are not measuring the same quantity.

What I'll do next is up to me -- for example, if I find that they are compatible, I can rerun the analysis on the joint dataset.
If the posteriors are "suspiciously" incompatible, I might go and re-check my assumptions.

So, nothing beyond visual inspection?

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 8, 2016, at 2:12 PM, Bistoon <bistoon....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> OK. By below function, one can generate the Beta Power (BP) distribution in R:
>
> rBP = function(n, par) qbeta(runif(n),par[1],par[2])^(1/par[3])/par[4]
>
> Let me ask another question. If I generate n = 1000 observation from the BP, I expect that the BP will be a good fit (by using UMVUE, MRE, MLE, Bayes and etc.). Am I wrong?

"Bayes" isn't a specific estimation procedure.  There are many ways
to define estimates with a Bayesian model.  The usual way
to do it is as a posterior mean, as that minimizes expected
square error (posterior median minimizes expected absolute error).
This contrasts with the posterior mode you get with a MAP (or max
penalized likelihood) estimate.  For a beta(a, b) distribution,
the posterior mode is (a - 1) / (a + b - 2) and the posterior mean
is a / (a + b).  So if a/(a + b) remains constant and a and b
grow, they converge to the same place, but with less data, there's
no guarantee they'll even be close.  Other skewed distributions
have similar problems.  The MLE doesn't always exist, but the
Bayesian posterior mean will exist as long as the posterior has
finite variance.

How did you code that density in Stan?  It looks like the normalization
might depend on the extra parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
We use split R-hat to test whether two sets of draws from a
posterior are from the same distribution.  This assumes they
have the same number of parameters.

What we'd usually recommend is that if you have shared parameters theta
and two sets of data, y1 and y2, then the full joint model is

  p(y1, y2, theta) = p(y1 | theta) * p(y2 | theta) * p(theta)

That's all koshwer.  But it's combinining likelihoods for different
groups of data, not combining posteriors.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).

That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
lots of quantity of interests to compare.

- Bob

> On Dec 8, 2016, at 11:21 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Daniel,
> Sorry for late reply.
> I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!
>
> Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
> I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.
>
> A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post.
> I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
> (N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
> e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior
> and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):
>
>
>  a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
> Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
>  b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
>   Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
>  c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
>  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
>  d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),

And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).

> Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> Hi Martin,
>
> On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi stan users,
>
> I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
>
> Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
>
> Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
>
> I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
>
>
> The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
>
>
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> }
>
> However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
>
> But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
>
> row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
>
> keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
>
> for(n in 1:N){
>         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
>       }
>
> But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
>
> My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
>
> Mu=X*Beta;
> "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
>
> Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
>
>
> NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
>
> In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
>
> For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> 1. Mu = X*Beta;
>     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
>     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
>
> 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
>     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
>
> 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
>
> My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
> P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
>
>
>
>
> I'd really appreciate any input on this
>
> Sincerely,
> Martin

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
Right, combine the likelihoods and then fit jointly.

All of our tools for comparing distributions, for example Rhat of
samples from the distributions, assume that the distributions are
all the same.  In this case that would imply the same data and
the same parameters in _every_ model being considered.

But if that’s the case then you wouldn’t need to combine the
separate inferences at.  I’m being cagey because I’m 90% that
what you want to do isn’t really a valid statistical procedure and
hence you’ll have to resort to approximations and hacks and
deal with the consequences yourself.

On Dec 8, 2016, at 2:59 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> We use split R-hat to test whether two sets of draws from a
> posterior are from the same distribution.  This assumes they
> have the same number of parameters.
>
> What we'd usually recommend is that if you have shared parameters theta
> and two sets of data, y1 and y2, then the full joint model is
>
>  p(y1, y2, theta) = p(y1 | theta) * p(y2 | theta) * p(theta)
>
> That's all koshwer.  But it's combinining likelihoods for different
> groups of data, not combining posteriors.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Dec 8, 2016, at 1:22 PM, Luigi Acerbi <luigi....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Michael,
>>
>> thanks for the answer, but the question was really about a compatibility statistic.
>> Please forget for now about combining the posteriors (or, more correctly, likelihoods -- I did say to ignore the prior :)).
>>
>> My question is more basic -- I have these say two posteriors coming from two experiments (e.g., measurements of supposedly the same quantity of interest).
>> Intuitively, if they are extremely narrow, Gaussian-like and separated by say 20 SDs, I have to conclude that the sampling procedure is wrong, or the model is wrong (e.g., massively misspecified), or the two experiments are not measuring the same quantity.
>> So, I was looking for some empirical statistic to measure this compatibility (similar in spirit to e.g. the Rhat statistic for chain convergence).
>>
>> What I'll do next is up to me -- for example, if I find that they are compatible, I can rerun the analysis on the joint dataset.
>> If the posteriors are "suspiciously" incompatible, I might go and re-check my assumptions.
>>
>> So, nothing beyond visual inspection?
>>
>> Thanks,
>> Luigi
>>
>>
>> On Thursday, 8 December 2016 12:23:59 UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> There is no statistically rigorous way of combining samples like this,
>> regardless of whether they look “compatible” or not.  You can combine
>> independent likelihood components this way, but not posteriors as at
>> the very least the prior correlates all of the components.  This means
>> that the total posterior does _not_ factor into independent components,
>> at least unless your posterior is exactly Gaussian.
>>
>> There have been many papers trying to approximate this process when
>> the posterior is approximately Gaussian, but they all end up quite fragile
>> as even small perturbations away from a Gaussian distribution can skew
>> the results.
>>
>> Unless you can fit everything jointly, we can’t offer any advice other than
>> “try it and see if it’s good enough for you”.

>>> (I am asking since I can think of many ways of quantifying this; I wonder if there is a standard.)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior choice
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Prior choice
messages.body_plain:
Parameters need to be chosen based on what you know about
the parameters.  So just seeing your parameter declarations
isn't enough to make concrete recommendations.  Also,
I'd skip doc that just duplicates what the code says.  It'll
get out of synch and just confuse people.

Usually, we don't recommend those interval-constrained priors
unless there's something physical constraining values into
those intervals.  Instead, we prefer softer constraints that
concentrates prior probability mass in the intervals where you
think it should be.

Usually Stan doesn't require hand-done initialization, so
I'd try it without providing hand-tuned initialization to begin.

- Bob

Thanks again.

I appreciate what's the correct way of combining priors and likelihoods, and there are issues with the multiplicity of priors if you have posteriors from multiple sources -- that's why I said to assume that the prior is flat or negligible (so that you are effectively multiplying likelihoods). What I wrote is correct under the specified assumptions, although I understand why it may have raised flags.
Anyhow, forget about combining these distributions -- honestly, the question was much simpler.

I just want to check whether these "posteriors under a flat prior" are compatible.
If they are compatible, I might do the kosher thing.
But first I want to check whether I should instead consider other models in which for example y1 and y2 are actually measuring different things.

And yes, I know that the truly kosher thing to test whether these posteriors are measuring the same thing would be to do some joint fits & model comparison in which theta is either the same for y1 and y2, or there are two distinct parameters theta1 and theta2 for respectively y1 and y2, and then I could do some model selection, or build a complete model and do inference within it (RJMCMC), or perhaps have another parameter that interpolates between these scenarios (unique theta vs. distinct thetas). All possible and statistically sound ways of dealing with this problem -- and expensive in my case.

To be honest, I don't think it's incorrect to use a heuristic check before embarking in an expensive analysis, but perhaps we see it differently here.
(I am not a statistician, just a former theoretical physicist turned to computational neuroscience -- I like to hack.)

> We use split R-hat to test whether two sets of draws from a
> posterior are from the same distribution.  This assumes they
> have the same number of parameters.

Saying that two sets of draws are drawn from the same distribution is much stronger than what I want to check for.
The posteriors I have might very well be different even if they are about the same quantity, since they come from different data (actually, there is really no reason why they should be the same).

The indirect conclusion from this discussion seems to be that there is no such (possibly heuristic) "compatibility statistic"...

Thanks!
Luigi

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] quantifying compatibility of independent posterior distributions
messages.body_plain:
> What do you mean by "compatible"?

Compatibility is how likely are two or more measurements to be about the same quantity of interest.

In Bayesian terms:
- H0 is that p(theta1|y1) and p(theta2|y2) represent posteriors about the same variable theta == theta1 = theta2.
- H1 is that theta1 and theta2 are distinct (physically, or because something went wrong in the measurement, or for whatever reason).
A fully Bayesian approach would compute the posterior ratio p(H0 | y1, y2) / p(H1| y1, y2) and then do something with it. The problem is that the full Bayesian approach is expensive.

The heuristic I have in mind is probably something along classical hypothesis testing.
The idea is that, for example, if p(theta1|y1) and p(theta2|y2) have near-zero overlap (and I am confident about the sampling procedure), I probably (barring weird priors or other caveats) don't even need to run the joint fit and model selection to say that we are in scenario H1 (theta1 and theta2 are different).

> It depends on the false positive and false negative rate of your heuristic
> and how important the problem is.

Good point, I agree -- that's what I am planning to investigate with some toy examples.

> > The indirect conclusion from this discussion seems to be that there is no such (possibly heuristic) "compatibility statistic"...
>
> Do they have the same parameters?  You can do something like
> measure KL divergence.  Or check interval coverage.  But it's
> not clear what you want to do from these messages.

Yep, I am working out something based on coverage.

Thanks,
Luigi

PS: Actually, it looks like I can be (approximately) Bayesian in answering the original question H0 vs H1, so I'll go along that way.

Yea that could be it. For some groups I only have small counts, but for most groups the counts are quite high.

>
>
> > I attached the modified script for those interested.
> >
> >
> >
> > You can rewrite your loop
> >
> >    for (n in 1:N) {
> >      real eta;
> >      eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
> >        betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
> >        betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
> >        betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
> >        betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
> >        betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
> >        betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
> >        betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
> >        logOffset[n];
> >      // Increment likelihood
> >      target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
> >    }
> >
> > as
> >
> > vector[N] eta;
> > eta = beta0[Di]
> >       + betaSex[Di] .* Sex
> >       ...
> >       + logOffset;
> > Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);
> >
> > as long as all those variables are vectors.
> >
> >
> > Is that actually faster, computationally, or does it just look cleaner?
>
> It'll be faster for two reasons.  First, the scalar vector
> products can produce much more compact pieces of the overall
> expression graph.  Second, vectorizing the call to neg_binomial_2
> will convert a bunch of virtual functions into a single virtual
> function call.  How much of a difference it'll make will depend
> on the size of N.
>
> Also, Stan doesn't have the same problem as BUGS or R in its
> parser, so you can put the operators like "+" on the next line
> like you'd see it in other programming languages and in math
> typesetting.
>

Cool, thanks, that’s good to know!

On another note, I tried to change to a poisson likelihood instead of the negative binomial. I had some problems with the posterior predictive values of the NB being systematically lower. When I did the fit with ADVI the number of iterations needed for convergence increased from 350 to 1750. I tried multiple restarts just to see if it was due to initialisation, but it was the same. Is that kind of model just especially difficult for ADVI, compared to a NB? When I did the fit with HMC it worked quite well, and the runtime was even faster than ADVI.

Cheers,
David
