messages.body_plain:
Bob,
Thanks for the link. I'll take a closer look.

I know you don't recommend the Wishart and that conjugacy is a non-issue in Stan. I wanted to try all these versions of prior for Sigma/Rho to see how they affected my results. Some literature on "joint modelling of species"
use the inverse-Wishart as it is and don't seem to worry about for example the relationship between variances and correlations in the prior and I wanted to see how important it was for my results.
It did affect posteriors of correlations and variances, generally in the expected way, but had only minor effects on the inferences of my study.
I will look more into information about the LKJ prior to see its characteristics and potential limitations.
I've for example seen somewhere that LKJ(1) might shrink correlation matrices towards the identity when dimensions are high (above 10).
I do see some shrinkage when using LKJ as compared to using IW in the "separation strategy" and that this seem to be larger for covariance/correlation matrixes of higher dimension (i.e. there are differences when using 15, 10 or 5 species in the modelling).
LKJ(eta<1) might apparently mitigate this but then I've seen claims that the LKJ sampler might be less stable and I haven't as yet experimented with it myself.
I am supposed to draw some ecological inferences from my analyses too and maybe not delve too far into statistics...ecology is after all my subject,  statistics is supposed to be one of my tools.

Thanks for  all input given by all of you.

/Martin

Den torsdag 8 december 2016 kl. 21:20:36 UTC+1 skrev Bob Carpenter:
> We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
> convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
> on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:
>
> http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/
>
> The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
> Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
> which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
> governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).
>
> That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
> lots of quantity of interests to compare.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Dec 8, 2016, at 11:21 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Daniel,
> > Sorry for late reply.
> > I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!
> >
> > Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
> > I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.
> >
> > A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post.
> > I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
> > (N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
> > e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior
> > and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):
> >
> >
> >  a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
> > Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
> >  b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
> >   Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
> >  c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
> >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> >  d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),
> >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R~LKJ(1); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> >
> >
> > The "effect" of reparameterization differs somewhat between these versions.
> >
> > Note also that I set adapt_delta to different values in the two model versions...
> >
> > Anyhow, this is what I did and can report (I work in R using rstan):
> > For each stanfit I extracted the summary and took the mean n_eff over all parameters (mean(summary(stanfit)$summary[,'n_eff'])).
> > I also used get_elapsed_time() on the stanfit and calculated mean timing of the "sample" part over the chains (colMeans(get_elapsed_time(stanfit))[,'sample']).
> >
> > I then simply divided n_eff with time.
> >
> > These are the results for the original multi-normal version (note separate values for models with different priors for Sigma):
> >
> > Prior        n_eff/time
> >
> > IW              38.7
> > SIW            3.90
> > SSIW          12.9
> > SSLKJ        0.537
> >
> > And these are the results for the reparameterized version:
> >
> > Prior        n_eff/time
> >
> > IW              38.4
> > SIW            36.3
> > SSIW          34.0
> > SSLKJ        67.6
> >
> > I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
> > And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
> > I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.
> >
> > /Martin
> >
> >
> > Den måndag 5 december 2016 kl. 18:12:15 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > Since you're looking at it, can you report the n_eff / time for the before and after models?
> >
> > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:08 PM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks Daniel for input!
> > Even if you hadn't read my additional post I still found useful information in your reply.
> > I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
> > Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).
> >
> > And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > Hi Martin,
> >
> > On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi stan users,
> >
> > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
> >
> > Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
> >
> > Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
> >
> > I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
> >
> >
> > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> >
> >
> > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> >
> > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> >
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > }
> >
> > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> >
> > Mu=X*Beta;
> >
> > But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
> >
> > row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> >
> > keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
> >
> > for(n in 1:N){
> >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> >       }
> >
> > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> >
> > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> >
> > Mu=X*Beta;
> > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> >
> > Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
> >
> >
> > NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
> >
> > In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> > Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
> >
> > For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> > 1. Mu = X*Beta;
> >     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
> >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
> >
> > 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
> >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
> >
> > 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
> >
> > My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
> >
> >
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> > P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I'd really appreciate any input on this
> >
> > Sincerely,
> > Martin

>
> On Thursday, December 8, 2016 at 4:11:08 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > The Jacobian is a matrix of partial derivatives of the form
> >
> > J_{ij} = f_{i} / x_{j}.
> >
> > If f is a function that maps N inputs to M outputs then it
> > is a N x M matrix.  If M = 1 then it reduces to a vector,
> > perhaps that is of what you are thinking?
> >
> > It is also evident from the definition that the Jacobian
> > matrix is _not_ symmetric.

> > On Dec 8, 2016, at 4:03 PM, Vishv Jeet <vishv...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> >
> > >
> > > Hi Krzysztof,
> > >
> > > Can you explain the Jacobian components? I don't understand why Jacobian is a matrix in the first place, shouldn't it be a vector? Also Jacobian components should be symmetric in x and y. The J[2, 1] and J[2, 2] seem to care more about x then y.
> > >
> > > regards,
> > > vishy
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, October 20, 2015 at 4:43:28 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > > I recently did a brief intro to Stan and I tried to come up with an example of
> > > > a model that needs a Jacobian adjustment due to a transformation and can
> > > > be explained in fairly intuitive terms.  The density I used was one with a normally
> > > > distributed radius parameter and a uniformly distributed angle parameter.  The first
> > > > Stan model was:
> > > >
> > > > data {
> > > >   real r_mu;
> > > >   real r_sd;
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > parameters {
> > > >   real x;
> > > >   real y;
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model {
> > > >   real r;
> > > >   r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
> > > >   r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > This version of the model, when looking at the samples of r_mu, estimates something like
> > > > 8.5 instead of the 8 used to simulate the data.  With the Jacobian adjustment the model was:
> > > >
> > > > model {
> > > >   real r;
> > > >   matrix[2,2] J;
> > > >   real lad_J;
> > > >   r <- sqrt(x^2+y^2);
> > > >   r ~ normal(r_mu, r_sd);
> > > >
> > > >   # Sigh, this model needs more maths:
> > > >   J[1,1] <- x/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
> > > >   J[1,2] <- y/sqrt(x^2+y^2);
> > > >   J[2,1] <- (x^2*(x^2+y^2)^(-3.0/2.0) - (x^2+y^2)^(-1.0/2.0)) / sqrt(1-(x^2)/(x^2+y^2));

> > > >

messages.body_plain:
> To be honest, I don't think it's incorrect to use a heuristic check before embarking in an expensive analysis, but perhaps we see it differently here.
> (I am not a statistician, just a former theoretical physicist turned to computational neuroscience -- I like to hack.)

I am a former experimental particle physicist turned statistician.  I’ve seen
all the excuses for hacks, but 1 - epsilon of the time they have poor
practical consequences.  When you’re having trouble trying to well-pose
your problem, like trying to define “compatibility” rigorously, it’s usually
a sign that you’re trying to do something ill-posed within probability theory.

If you want robust approximations that will be accurate in practice then
you need to start with a well-posed approach and _then_ start adding
principled approximation whose consequences you can understand.
Again, I’m not speaking out of any speculative zealousness but mounds
of empirical evidence.  Take of that what you will, but consider it a friendly
foreboding.

When making such comparisons you have to be very careful with
your evaluations.  Different priors choices can affect not only sampling
speed and posterior inferences, but also the ability to fit the model
accurately at all.  Wishart and Inverse-Wishart not only imply odd
distributions for the correlations but they induce nasty posteriors that
frustrate accurate fitting, leading to the kinds of problems you see
here.

So before comparing speed/efficiency or posteriors, you have to
validate that you’re getting a reasonable value.  This requires all
of the tricks — running multiple chains and checking Rhat,
checking all of the HMC diagnostics like divergences and
the E-BFMI, and fitting simulated data and confirming that you
can recover the true values.  If you can’t do all of these then
the model can’t be fit with your sampler, and you can’t even
move onto the next step.

Lots of comparisons have been compromised by neglected
this step, which is especially important when Gibbs samplers are
involved!

> > > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > >

> > >
> > > for(n in 1:N){
> > >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> > >       }
> > >
> > > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> > >
> > > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> > >
> > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"

> > >

>
> > To be honest, I don't think it's incorrect to use a heuristic check before embarking in an expensive analysis, but perhaps we see it differently here.
> > (I am not a statistician, just a former theoretical physicist turned to computational neuroscience -- I like to hack.)
>
> I am a former experimental particle physicist turned statistician.  I’ve seen
> all the excuses for hacks, but 1 - epsilon of the time they have poor
> practical consequences.  When you’re having trouble trying to well-pose
> your problem, like trying to define “compatibility” rigorously, it’s usually
> a sign that you’re trying to do something ill-posed within probability theory.
>
>
> If you want robust approximations that will be accurate in practice then
> you need to start with a well-posed approach and _then_ start adding
> principled approximation whose consequences you can understand.
> Again, I’m not speaking out of any speculative zealousness but mounds
> of empirical evidence.  Take of that what you will, but consider it a friendly
> foreboding.

messages.body_plain:
Vishv, let me elaborate again.

In order to perform a change of variables on a probability density
you need a 1-to-1 transformation.  Given the parameters x and a
density pi(x), the density for y = f(x) is given by

pi(y) = pi(f^{-1}(x)) | J_f(y) |

Because f is 1-to-1 (same number of inputs as outputs) the Jacobian
will always be square and the Jacobian determinant will be well-
defined.

In your case, (x, y) -> z is _not_ a 1-to-1 and so does not admit
a change of variables formula.  Instead you have do induce a 1-to-1
transformation by padding the output and then marginalizing.  So,
for example, you could do (x, y) -> (z, theta) then

pi(z) = \int d(theta) pi(z, theta).

Or you could do (x, y) -> (z, x) with

pi(z) = \int dx pi(z, x),

etc.  Lots of potential ways, but each yields the same marginal
density.  The art is figuring out a clever way that facilities analytical
calculations.

> On Dec 8, 2016, at 8:18 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

>
> target += log_sum_exp(log1m(pi) + normal_lpdf(alpha | beta, .01) , log(pi) + normal_lpdf(alpha | beta, 1);
>
> Is there a simple way of doing the above, but doing so on a unit scale? Intuitively, I thought I could do ... normal_lpdf(alpha*100 | beta, 1), but it leads to a very different estimate altogether for reasons I don't understand.

Because it's not the same density.  Just write out the log density
up to a propirtion:  look at the kernel:

  0.5 * ((alpha * 100 - mu) / 1)^2 != 0.5 * ((alpha - mu) / .01)^2

We typically recommend the Cauchy distribution if you want to concentrate
most of the mass around a point but allow for long tails.  It's got
better continuity and differentiability properties than this kind of
mixture.

- Bob

>

> Now to my problem:
>
> I am implementing fully conditional imputation of amongst
>
> others ordinal variables. I validated the model (code
>
> below) with simulated data, but now it turns out that
>
> fitting is very slow when using HMC for real data.
>
> When using a subset of my data -2500 cases, 4 variables,
>
> two of which are ordinal, with 4 and 6 levels, respectively-
>
> fewer than 100 iterations are done after 12h (with
>
> adapt_delta=.8, on a PC with a 3.4 ghz processor and 8gb RAM).

>
> The same data and model can be fit in around a minute
>
> using variational Bayes, but then vb is “experimental”.
>
>
> My questions:
>
> 1) Does anybody see a way to speed up the model?

I can help with speedig up the computations.  You want to look
at other things going on to see if there's some way to parameterize
it better.

Overall, our ordered logistic isn't the fastest thing in the world,
especially if you can't vectorize it.

The biggest saving you can get in Stan speed is saving any intermediate
computations you do in order to reuse them.  For that, you have to
comb over your program and find things in loops that don't depend on
the loop index and pull them out.  And try to vectorize as much as possible.
So if you have a bunch of ordered logistics with the same cutpoints, save
up their arguments if you can and make one call (not sure this is possible).

And don't store things in lp_dv that are 0 and then put them
into other expressions.  Just push the branching logic down and
only create and multiplyw hen needed.

For clarity, you don't ever want to compare to 0 or 1 in a conditional.
Instead, convert

missings[n,1] == 0 ? Dx[n,1] : idv1

into

  missings[n, 1] ? idv1 : Dx[n, 1];

You can probably do things like this:

  ta = alpha[k] + iDx2[j]*betas[k,1] + xi[n,1]*betas[k,2] + xi[n,2]*betas[k,3];

with matrix algebra, which might be faster.

>
> I assume the speed-bottle neck is marginalizing out multiple
>
> (here 2) ordinal variables.
>
>
>
> 2) Is there a reasonable approach to determine that vb
>
> results can be trusted?

Not that we know of other than comparing them to HMC or other
reference output.

> I am thinking of (a) simulating data with the same
>
> characteristics as my real data and validate vb by
>
> comparing true and imputed data and/or

You want to do this with interval posterior coverage,
not with point estimation.  We do know that by construction
VB tends to underestimate uncertainty (the construction is
the direction of KL divergence being minimized).

> (b) taking multiple
>
> (very) small subsets of my real data and checking that
>
> for those hmc and vb give the same results.

Same results here means same posterior, not just posterior means.

> On Dec 9, 2016, at 5:05 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
>

> Bob,
> Thanks for the link. I'll take a closer look.
>
> I know you don't recommend the Wishart and that conjugacy is a non-issue in Stan. I wanted to try all these versions of prior for Sigma/Rho to see how they affected my results. Some literature on "joint modelling of species"
> use the inverse-Wishart as it is and don't seem to worry about for example the relationship between variances and correlations in the prior and I wanted to see how important it was for my results.
> It did affect posteriors of correlations and variances, generally in the expected way, but had only minor effects on the inferences of my study.
> I will look more into information about the LKJ prior to see its characteristics and potential limitations.

> I've for example seen somewhere that LKJ(1) might shrink correlation matrices towards the identity when dimensions are high (above 10). LKJ(eta<1) might mitigate this but then I've seen claims that the LKJ sampler might be less stable.

> I do see some shrinkage when using LKJ as compared to using IW in the "separation strategy" and that this seem to be larger for covariance/correlation matrixes of higher dimension (i.e. there are differences when using 15, 10 or 5 species in the modelling).
> LKJ(eta<1) might apparently mitigate this but then I've seen claims that the LKJ sampler might be less stable and I haven't as yet experimented with it myself.
> I am supposed to draw some ecological inferences from my analyses too and maybe not delve too far into statistics...ecology is after all my subject,  statistics is supposed to be one of my tools.
>
> Thanks for  all input given by all of you.
>
> /Martin
>
>
> Den torsdag 8 december 2016 kl. 21:20:36 UTC+1 skrev Bob Carpenter:
> We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
> convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
> on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:
>
> http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/
>
> The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
> Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
> which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
> governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).
>
> That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
> lots of quantity of interests to compare.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Dec 8, 2016, at 11:21 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Daniel,
> > Sorry for late reply.
> > I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!
> >
> > Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
> > I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.
> >
> > A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post.
> > I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
> > (N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
> > e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior
> > and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):
> >
> >
> >  a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
> > Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
> >  b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
> >   Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
> >  c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
> >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> >  d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),
> >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R~LKJ(1); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> >
> >
> > The "effect" of reparameterization differs somewhat between these versions.
> >
> > Note also that I set adapt_delta to different values in the two model versions...
> >
> > Anyhow, this is what I did and can report (I work in R using rstan):
> > For each stanfit I extracted the summary and took the mean n_eff over all parameters (mean(summary(stanfit)$summary[,'n_eff'])).
> > I also used get_elapsed_time() on the stanfit and calculated mean timing of the "sample" part over the chains (colMeans(get_elapsed_time(stanfit))[,'sample']).
> >
> > I then simply divided n_eff with time.
> >
> > These are the results for the original multi-normal version (note separate values for models with different priors for Sigma):
> >
> > Prior        n_eff/time
> >
> > IW              38.7
> > SIW            3.90
> > SSIW          12.9
> > SSLKJ        0.537
> >
> > And these are the results for the reparameterized version:
> >
> > Prior        n_eff/time
> >
> > IW              38.4
> > SIW            36.3
> > SSIW          34.0
> > SSLKJ        67.6
> >
> > I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
> > And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
> > I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.
> >
> > /Martin

> > Den måndag 5 december 2016 kl. 18:12:15 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > Since you're looking at it, can you report the n_eff / time for the before and after models?
> >
> > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:08 PM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks Daniel for input!
> > Even if you hadn't read my additional post I still found useful information in your reply.
> > I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
> > Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).
> >
> > And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > Hi Martin,
> >
> > On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi stan users,
> >
> > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
> >
> > Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
> >
> > Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
> >
> > I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
> >
> >
> > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> >
> >
> > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> >
> > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> >
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > }
> >
> > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> >
> > Mu=X*Beta;
> >
> > But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
> >
> > row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> >
> > keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
> >
> > for(n in 1:N){
> >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> >       }
> >
> > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> >
> > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> >
> > Mu=X*Beta;
> > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> >
> > Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
> >
> >
> > NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
> >
> > In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> > Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
> >
> > For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> > 1. Mu = X*Beta;
> >     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
> >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
> >
> > 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
> >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
> >
> > 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
> >
> > My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
> >
> >
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> > P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I'd really appreciate any input on this
> >
> > Sincerely,
> > Martin
> >

Every line with "~" in the model block in a Stan program is adding a term to the log-posterior density.  No sampling is done.

> On Dec 9, 2016, at 4:38 PM, Luis O'Shea <los...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I have what I suspect is a very basic question about what a sampling statement really means in Stan.
>
> For example, consider the following simple model (which is very similar to the first example in the "Regression Models - Linear Regression" section of the Stan reference:
>
> // Save in OneFactorCrossSectional.stan
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;
>   vector[N] r;
>   vector[N] sigma;
>   real sigma_g;
> }
> parameters {
>   real g;
> }
> model {
>   r ~ normal(g, sigma); // (1)
>   g ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
> }
>
> which we can run from R as follows:
>
> library(rstan)
>
> data <- data.frame(
>   r     = c(0.2, 0.4),
>   sigma = c(1,   2),
>   g     = 1)
>
> # Linear model ####
> print(summary(lm(r ~ g + 0, data = data, weights = 1/data$sigma ^ 2)))
>
> # STAN model ####
> sigma_g <- 10
> one.fac.fit <- stan('OneFactorCrossSectional.stan',
>                     data = list(N = nrow(data),
>                                 r = data$r,
>                                 sigma = data$sigma,
>                                 sigma_g = sigma_g))
>
> My question is about equation (1) in the Stan file: r ~ normal(g, sigma). My issue is that the LHS, "r", is a constant, so it seems odd to sample from it! I believe an equivalent version of this sampling statement is to replace (1) with (2), below:
>
> 0 ~ normal(g - r, sigma); // (2)
>
> This appears to produce the same results as (1), but now we are expressing the distribution of 0, which seems even stranger (to me). The most natural way to write this (but bear in mind that I'm new to Stan) is as
>
> g - r ~ normal(0, sigma); // (3)
>
> Which also seems to produce the same results. Are these all equivalent? Why can we state what the distribution of a constant is?
>
> One of my problems arising from these doubts, is what happens when things are a little more complicated. For example, suppose our model is that r is equal to g^2 (g squared) plus an error. Then the above examples suggest two ways to model it.  First we can follow the Stan reference, accept the peculiarity of stating what the distribution of a constant is, and write something like:
>
> 0 ~ normal(g*g - r, sigma); // (4)
>
> This parses and compiles without warning, although sampling from the model generates many divergent transitions. An alternative approach, which seems more natural to me, is to write
>
> g*g - r ~ normal(0, sigma); // (5)
>
> This, of couse, generates a warning reminding us to add a term to the log prob. Is (4) equivalent to (5) plus a suitable increment to the log prob?
>

Basic questions like this are all covered in gory detail in
the manual.  In short,

  y ~ foo(theta);

gets translated as roughly

  target += foo_lpdf(y | theta);

where foo_lpdf is the density (or mass function it'll be _lpmf).

The answers to all of your questions derive from the
definition of foo_lpdf and what the variables are.  See below.

- Bob

Yes, in terms of their effect on the target log density.

>> One of my problems arising from these doubts, is what happens when things are a little more complicated. For example, suppose our model is that r is equal to g^2 (g squared) plus an error. Then the above examples suggest two ways to model it.  First we can follow the Stan reference, accept the peculiarity of stating what the distribution of a constant is, and write something like:

These produce the same reuslt in terms of what gets added to
the target density, but conceptually these are very different.

If you're trying to use the second one to put a distribution on
transformed parmaeters, then you need the Jacobian adjustment.
If they're used as priors, you don't.

messages.body_plain:
In my implementation, which I have posted, duration is a continuous parameter (so is start time and end time).   This is your #1. This is already the way I do it. I'm not sure how many different ways I can say it.

Let me try it this way: Your solution #1 does not work.

As for #2...as I understand it, in order for this to work we need a function so steep that the smallest "continuous" change, at computer's precision, corresponds to an integer change in the parameter. Right?

If, instead, I'm going to have to find some delicately balanced model to trick Stan into fitting a type of model it's designed not to be able to fit, I sort of don't see the point.

Stan is hard to trick --- most of the attempts to do discrete parameters
other than marginalization will either just not work or they'll be very
slow to mix (the line between these isn't sharp).

We tried to build it to fit the largest class of continuous parameter
models that could be reliably fit.  I don't think that includes the
models you're talking about because the discrete component is combinatorially
prohibitive to marginalize.

We might extend that goal to discrete parameters that can't be marginalized,
but that may just be a fool's errand as many of these systems are bound
to be truly intractable (in the sense of no polynomial algorithms) or
at best NP-complete (tractable unbounded parallel algorithms but no known
untractable algorithms and a very very strong suspicion none exist).

Let us know if you find something to fit this model as you conceive it.
You might want to look at PyMC3, which lets you write down a model with
mixed discrete and continuous parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
P

Yes, I understand your general concern.  I think the way Bob or Michael might put it is that purely discrete problems are essentially uncomputable because of the combinatorial explosion. So this leaves you with a few options:

1.  Set up the problem exactly as you did, accept the combinatorial explosion, and aim to get a reasonable solution, or some set of reasonable solutions.  This is an approximate-Bayes problem, and it represents an important general class of approximate-Bayes problems, and it's the sort of thing that Stan _should_ be able to do, but Stan can't yet do it.  So far with Stan we've focused on full Bayes, with approx algorithms as an afterthought.  But the machine learning world is the opposite:  they're mainly focused on approximate algorithms.  Those sorts of programs can require a bit of tuning, but this can be worth it if you can get good solutions.  Currently the machine learning programs seem to be focused on specific models.  It would be an interesting thing for someone to build out Stan to be able to attack this sort of problem.

2.  Back to my solution #1, which does not work.  Does it fail even if you simulate fake data with continuous parameters?  (As I wrote, "For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.")  I guess I'm still missing something here.  Yes, I understand that you are coding all these as continuous, but it also sounds like you're creating your data in such a way that the underlying parameters are discrete.  If you could have things start at 8:14pm on Tuesday, then wouldn't you be able to recover such things?

3.  In my solution #2, I'm assuming a function that's not so steep, that would allow the model to be fit but at the price of a bit of blurring of the inferences.  Such blurring is undesirable but it was my impression that you were already having a bit of blurring, a bit of difficulty identifying start and stop in the presence of noise.  So I was thinking that a little more blurring might not be so bad.

4.  As Bob wrote in his reply, you can't really trick Stan into fitting a discrete model that it can't fit.  My suggestions were more in the direction of making the problem easier, basically by blurring out the discrete modes.  I agree that, to the extent the real world is discrete, this is not an optimal approach, but it can work.  Imagine a spherical cow etc.

5.  Yet another approach is to keep the model discrete but to recognize that it has structure.  It's not a purely discrete problem because the weeks are ordered.  This would point toward some sort of custom solution to the problem, developing an algorithm that finds a good solution.  But that's a pain in the ass.  Pre-Stan, we wrote custom solutions all the time but now we prefer not to.

6.  Finally, maybe you can have it all (or most of it all) but first blurring the problem (following my ideas 1 and 2, which are items 2 and 3 in the above list) and then, if you want to work toward a discrete solution, using random draws from the continous-model posterior as starting points.

A

> As for #2...as I understand it, in order for this to work we need a function so steep that the smallest "continuous" change, at computer's precision, corresponds to an integer change in the parameter. Right?
>
> That does seem like it might give the behavior I want, if it works at all. But then why not make this part of the language? It seems just incredibly kluldgy and fragile and machine-dependent and lots of other bad things.
>
> I guess I should try it. I have to say, I'm pretty demoralized. It might be possible to trick Stan into fitting this model, but a lot of the appeal was the ability to write a model that expresses what I think is actually happening, and then fit it. If, instead, I'm going to have to find some delicately balanced model to trick Stan into fitting a type of model it's designed not to be able to fit, I sort of don't see the point.
>
>
>
>
>

Hmm, there are a couple of ways I can thinking of hacking this (or maybe "solving" rather than "hacking" if we can consider these changes as representing a true underlying model):

1.  Continuous-time parameter, continuous-time data:  Allow these weekly effects to start and end midweek.  For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.  With real data, if things actually only start at the beginning of each week, you might still be able to fit this model because the slop and uncertainty would allow a continuous fit.  Sure, it wouldn't be quite correct, but you already have enough noise that you're not always identifying the start and end _weeks_, so would it really be so horrible to allow continuous times?

2.  Continuous-time parameter, discrete-time data:  Again allow a continuous time for the start and end parameters.  But now match them to discrete weekly start and end via an S-curve.  For example, let's label the discrete points as integers.  Then if the continuous start parameter is x, the discrete starting point could be the integer closest to x + epsilon, where epsilon is a distribution such as a logistic or normal with center 0 and scale sigma, and sigma has some value such as 0.5 or 1:  this corresponds to an ordered logit or probit.  The idea is that sigma will be small enough that the start time parameter roughly localizes the actual start time, but large enough that the transition from one integer to the next is smooth, so there's no near-discontinuity that would jar the HMC.  You could implement this model with latent epsilon but I think it would probably work better to use the normal and logistic cdfs.  (In theory these go off to infinity but I'd just truncate to the nearest 3 or 4 discrete possibilities for the likelihood.)  Once you've fit the model, you can then, in the generated quantities block, use simple Bayes calculation to get inference for the epsilons and thus identify the actual starting and end points more precisely.

Of these, I think I prefer #1.  But I'd be happy with either one if it works!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob
thanks for taking the time to reply.

The application I have in mind is one of causal inference with bayesian networks in biological data. Programs like bnlearns and others try to learn bayesian networks that explains the observed data. An example is to try to learn the connection between genes from observed gene expression.

Because of uncertainty in learning the structure, it is common to learn multiple Bayesian networks and see what patterns are constant. One way to accomplish this is by bootstrapping the data.

Once we have the different networks one important step is to try to figure out what perturbations (or interventions) have the largest effect on a specific outcomes. For example, if I knockdown a gene (make it have zero value. This can be accomplish in practice with certain drugs) what is the effect on some other gene of importance (a gene that is known to be associated to disease progresssion for example). Once we have the different networks we can alter the networks to simulate this type of knowdown and then sample from the network and see what happens to the gene of interest.

Anyway, I'm trying to figure out how to use Stan can help improve some of the process. Specifically, I'm trying to understand how I could rank perturbations in terms of the largest effect accounting for uncertainty and magnitude as well as the fact that we can get different estimated effects from the different networks.

thanks
Fred

On Wed, Dec 7, 2016 at 3:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Why do you want to do this?  If you're building something like
> a regression with different predictors, then how much a predictor
> adds to the mix depends on the other predictors you use and what
> the prior is.  There are some really neat illustrations of this in
> the Hastie et al. machine learning book when they look at path
> regressions (you can find it in the same diagrams in their elastic
> net paper, too).
>
> We tend to compare models by their calibration (do they get
> the right posterior coverage in held out or cross-validation
> tests) and their sharpeness (do they make tight predictions in
> the sense of the posterior predictive intervals being narrow).
> We can also evaluate more traditionally just on held-out data
> likelihood.
>
> There are a bajillion traditional methods for doing this, such
> as ANOVA, many of which have Bayesian analogues.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 30, 2016, at 5:34 PM, FKG <fgr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Everyone,
> > I have a question regarding the proper way to rank variables in terms of their effect on an outcome. Any papers, books, or ideas are welcome.
> >
> > Suppose I construct a collection of bayesian models that explain an outcome. These are created by some feature selection algorithm like stepaic or glmnet with bootstraping or some other procedure. So now I have a series of stan models from which I can predict samples. By sampling from this emsemble I can get the posterior of the outcome.
> >
> >  I would like to get an idea of the importance of each of the variables involved, by perturbing  each of them (by setting them to small or large values) and sample from the outcome under each condition (and for each model), and then calculate a "treatment" effect. Some perturbations may have a large effect on the outcome but with a large variance while others may have a smaller effect but with less variance.
> >
> >  What is the proper way to rank the effect of each perturbation on the outcome? I'm concerned about applying some standard statistical test because I can sample any number of samples from the model so any tiny difference in effect would be significant with enough samples.
> >
> >  thanks
> > FKG

The goal of the model was to test another parameterization I've seen in paper. They purposefully have one prior with a spiked dsitribution and another that isn't. The idea is to choose between the priors.

Specifically, it either allows two parameters to be essentially equivalent (spiked prior) or to be different (non-spiked prior).

I couldn't find an easy way of speeding it up because ultimately the posterior will have a spike somewhere, so I think I'm giving up on it. Ran a little longer than my current method and provided less accurate inferences.

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 9, 2016, at 7:08 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> P
>
> Yes, I understand your general concern.  I think the way Bob or Michael might put it is that purely discrete problems are essentially uncomputable because of the combinatorial explosion. So this leaves you with a few options:
>
> 1.  Set up the problem exactly as you did, accept the combinatorial explosion, and aim to get a reasonable solution, or some set of reasonable solutions.  This is an approximate-Bayes problem, and it represents an important general class of approximate-Bayes problems, and it's the sort of thing that Stan _should_ be able to do, but Stan can't yet do it.  So far with Stan we've focused on full Bayes, with approx algorithms as an afterthought.  But the machine learning world is the opposite:  they're mainly focused on approximate algorithms.  Those sorts of programs can require a bit of tuning, but this can be worth it if you can get good solutions.  Currently the machine learning programs seem to be focused on specific models.  It would be an interesting thing for someone to build out Stan to be able to attack this sort of problem.

I understand about the combinatorial explosion, but this is still a slightly unsatisfying situation. When a human looks at a time series that, starting on the 9th week, shows a 2-hour spike every Tuesday afternoon for the next 8 weeks, it’s easy to see what is happening. A computer can analyze chess moves a zillion times faster than me, so how come it’s paralyzed by the combinatorial explosion in this case and I’m not?  The answer, of course, is I’m not laboriously working through every single possibility. But why not?

Or think about some sort of modified traveling salesman problem, where I have some sort of noisy information on the total distance the salesman drove — maybe I know how much gas he used in his car. Let’s say he visits the 20 biggest cities in the U.S. and my estimate is that he drove 10% farther than the shortest possible route, plus or minus 8%, but no shorter than the shortest possible route of course.  99.99999% of possible routes are going to be a lot longer than that and will have probability very close to zero.  Is exhaustively exploring all of the routes really the best we can do? Clearly not.

I understand Stan is built for a certain kind of model, and is just not the right tools for these kinds of jobs. But, as with your “R sucks” blog post, the fact that Stan is great at what it does seems to amplify my frustration when it won’t do this other thing I want it to do.

In this case, in the continuous world Stan doesn’t force me to exhaustively sample all of continuous parameter space (something that can’t be done anyway, obviously!); by design, it spends most of its time in the high-probability regions of parameter space, and nearly none of its time where the probability is very very low. I would like to have the same capability in discrete space: hop around between discrete states, and spend most of its time where the probability is high. Indeed, if one of the tricks you suggested actually works (which I doubt) you could do this already in Stan: create a function that maps tiny “continuous” steps onto discrete state changes, and let Stan do its thing.

>
> 2.  Back to my solution #1, which does not work.  Does it fail even if you simulate fake data with continuous parameters?  (As I wrote, "For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.")  I guess I'm still missing something here.  Yes, I understand that you are coding all these as continuous, but it also sounds like you're creating your data in such a way that the underlying parameters are discrete.  If you could have things start at 8:14pm on Tuesday, then wouldn't you be able to recover such things?

Good question…I was thinking about this yesterday while exercising — it really is true that mulling things over while “not working” can be the best way to work —  and I think this approach will work, just not as I implemented it.  As with some of those morphing issues we never quite worked out, there might be a way to make this work as a fully continuous problem. After all, the actual electric load in the building really is a continuous function of time, even though it only gets measured every 15 minutes.

This is going to be somewhat complicated, though, or at least I think so….Complicated to conceptualize and program, not necessarily to fit.  The issue is that there really are these discrete events, some of which recur daily and some weekly, and some only for limited duration, and they can overlap.  But yeah, I can  have weekly-recurring event 1 start at some time t1_0 and end at t1_1, and so on for other events, and since those times won’t match up to the meter times I’ll just do some interpolation at the ends… it all sounds workable, although I will have to be careful in order to define a fully specified model.

For now I will do a toy problem and see if I can get it to work. I’m optimistic. Thanks for your help.

P

> A
>
> > On Dec 9, 2016, at 7:56 PM, Phil Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > In my implementation, which I have posted, duration is a continuous parameter (so is start time and end time).   This is your #1. This is already the way I do it. I'm not sure how many different ways I can say it.
> >
> > Let me try it this way: Your solution #1 does not work.
> >
> > As for #2...as I understand it, in order for this to work we need a function so steep that the smallest "continuous" change, at computer's precision, corresponds to an integer change in the parameter. Right?
> >
> > That does seem like it might give the behavior I want, if it works at all. But then why not make this part of the language? It seems just incredibly kluldgy and fragile and machine-dependent and lots of other bad things.
> >
> > I guess I should try it. I have to say, I'm pretty demoralized. It might be possible to trick Stan into fitting this model, but a lot of the appeal was the ability to write a model that expresses what I think is actually happening, and then fit it. If, instead, I'm going to have to find some delicately balanced model to trick Stan into fitting a type of model it's designed not to be able to fit, I sort of don't see the point.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> Hmm, there are a couple of ways I can thinking of hacking this (or maybe "solving" rather than "hacking" if we can consider these changes as representing a true underlying model):
>
> 1.  Continuous-time parameter, continuous-time data:  Allow these weekly effects to start and end midweek.  For example, suppose that the "start time" is 2.39, which corresponds, say, to 8:14pm on Tuesday.  Then the change would start at that time.  With fake data, you could actually do this by picking the start time from some distribution and then starting things at whatever continuous time comes out.  With real data, if things actually only start at the beginning of each week, you might still be able to fit this model because the slop and uncertainty would allow a continuous fit.  Sure, it wouldn't be quite correct, but you already have enough noise that you're not always identifying the start and end _weeks_, so would it really be so horrible to allow continuous times?
>
> 2.  Continuous-time parameter, discrete-time data:  Again allow a continuous time for the start and end parameters.  But now match them to discrete weekly start and end via an S-curve.  For example, let's label the discrete points as integers.  Then if the continuous start parameter is x, the discrete starting point could be the integer closest to x + epsilon, where epsilon is a distribution such as a logistic or normal with center 0 and scale sigma, and sigma has some value such as 0.5 or 1:  this corresponds to an ordered logit or probit.  The idea is that sigma will be small enough that the start time parameter roughly localizes the actual start time, but large enough that the transition from one integer to the next is smooth, so there's no near-discontinuity that would jar the HMC.  You could implement this model with latent epsilon but I think it would probably work better to use the normal and logistic cdfs.  (In theory these go off to infinity but I'd just truncate to the nearest 3 or 4 discrete possibilities for the likelihood.)  Once you've fit the model, you can then, in the generated quantities block, use simple Bayes calculation to get inference for the epsilons and thus identify the actual starting and end points more precisely.
>
> Of these, I think I prefer #1.  But I'd be happy with either one if it works!

messages.subject: Possible to implement Gibbs Sampler with Metropolis Step in STAN?
messages.subject_clean: Possible to implement Gibbs Sampler with Metropolis Step in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm working on a causal inference problem that is similar to the problem solved in Hirano, Imbens, Rubin and Zhou (2000) "Estimating the Effect of Flu Shots in a Random Encouragement Design" (which is also discussed in Chapter 25 of the Imbens and Rubin "Causal Inference" book). Basically, the problem is to get a posterior for the complier average causal effect (CACE) using data from a randomized experiment with two way non-compliance.

This would be very easy to implement in STAN if I could observe the complete data likelihood, where I know the compliance status of the experimental units (whether they always take treatment regardless of assignment, never take treatment regardless of assignment, or whether they take the treatment to which they were randomly assigned).

The usual way to do this would be to set up a gibbs sampler where I draw the latent variables of interest conditional on some covariates and my parameter vector, then draw the missing potential outcomes conditional on some covariates, the latent variable and my parameter vector, and then update my parameter vector with an annoying metropolis step.

I would prefer not to write customized MCMC code for this, mostly to avoid the pain of exploring tuning parameters for the metropolis step.

Is there a way to leverage STAN for these types of problems? Basically, using it for the metropolis step somehow? Or can I scrap the gibbs sampler approach and deal with latent variables in some other fashion in STAN?

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks!

If the latent parameters are continuous, this is straightforward
in Stan (not "STAN" --- it's not an acronym).   See the missing data
chapter of the manual.

If they are binary or small categorical, they can be marginalized out,
which is more work.  See the latent discrete parameter chapter of the manual.

If they're counts, it's pretty much impossible to do in Stan without
approximating the model somehow.

- Bob

messages.subject: Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.subject_clean: Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):

dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,

where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.

There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).

It's a lot like this:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE

apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.

If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.

We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK). Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363), which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem. So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood. But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).

What can I do to diagnose the problem?

I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters. For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:

    a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)

i agree with all of what andrew said. the current state of the code is usable; algorithm hyper parameters will need to be tweaked for it to work well in practice.

one challenge in GMO is how to scale it to high-dimensional parameters. we’d like to avoid explicit calculations of the importance weights while still remaining an exact MML algorithm (otherwise we’d just do variational EM). i have some ideas to get at this that are not in the current code base.

best,
dustin

messages.body_plain:
In a simulation study, I would like run the same stan models on different data sets at the same time. I am the rstan interface, and SLURM (Linux) to generate the batch job. Unfortunately, this results in the following errors:

checkForRemoteErrors(val): 7 nodes produced errors; first error: unable to load shared object '/tmp/RtmpisFRKa/file3966e77c594.so':
  /tmp/RtmpisFRKa/file3966e77c594.so: file too short

and

In writeBin(dso@.CXXDSOMISC$dso_bin, libLFile) :
  problem writing to connection

Is there an elegant way to prevent this issue? I see two possible workarounds, but I hope there is a better way: (a) copy my original .stan script to a task-specific script, so each task effectively has its own stan script and it's own .so, hopefully circumventing clashes OR (b) load the model using auto_write=FALSE. Downside is that I have wait for the compilation to occur every time I run my script. Both are rather ugly.

It is probably difficult for you to replicate this issue, because it requires to have the same environment. Still, I hope that your deeper understanding of the inner works can lead to a suggestion. What is suspect is happening, is that the simultaneous tasks try to write to the same .so file, while another one is trying to use it at the same time.

Thanks in advance,
Stijn.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] gmo as possible solution?
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, one of the challenges in getting the GMO paper finished is that there are so many different scenarios.  One set of problems is the INLA-type situation in which the dimensionality of the hyperparameters if fairly low, and in that case iterative importance sampling could help.  But I also agree with Dustin that if we're gonna do iterative importance sampling, we'd probably be better off doing something variational.

To put it another way, GMO is a version of ADVI, and marginal posterior mode is a version of variational inference, but in either case the key step is the partitioning of parameter space into local parameters (which get averaged over) and hyperparameters (which get optimized).

Once we get GMO working for real in its prototype version (i.e., demonstrating that we can use the GMO algorithm to get good answers for real problems much faster than NUTS), then we can talk about expanding the Stan language so Stan can do GMO internally.  I don't think this will be much of a technical challenge, but I don't think it makes sense to ask this of the Stan development team until we have a algorithm that we're convinced is working.  Which I hope we will have in the near future...
A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] abs and fabs
messages.body_plain:
I can take another look at that.  We've followed the easy path
of mirroring the C++ design.  To remind everyone of the issue,
in C++, fabs() has a single signature (actually it includes parallel
versions for float and long double, but this is the only relevant one)

  double fabs(double);

whereas abs() has two signatures

  double abs(double);
  int abs(int);

When you combine this with the way promotion from integers to
real (floating point) numbers works in C++ and in Stan, what you
get is this:

  abs(int) : int
  abs(real) : real

  fabs(int) : real
  fabs(real) : real

The result type is different for integer arguments.  All the functions
we have vectorized (like log and exp and sqrt) behave like fabs --- they
always return real values, even if the argument is an integer.

We could deprecate fabs() and either

  * forego vectorizing abs(), or

  * we could implement a one-off non-standard vectorization for abs
    that would return integers when given integer arguments

What we can't do is just decide to have abs return real values for
integer inputs---that'd mess up programs.

- Bob

Bob,

I defer to you on this.  If fabs is the way to go, it's the way to go, and then we just need something in the manual explaining why.  I agree that it would be weird to have both abs and fabs if they do different things.  I also think vectorization is important for user-friendliness.  Indeed, in my opinion, the user-friendliness of vectorization outweighs the un-user-friendliness of abs.

The larger issue, I think, is that the integer/real distinction causes problems all over the place in Stan.  It's unavoidable, perhaps, but still annoying.  The example that keeps coming up is when I switch from linear regression to logistic.  With linear I have vector[N] y; and with logistic I have int y[N].  It's becoming less of a problem for me because I've been trying to consistently use the "long" format for regression data, but when I had data such as y[i,j] and was using to_vector(), it was kind of annoying.

A

I think we can give you the behavior you want without
confusing the relation between Stan and C++.  I don't
think Stan programmers are going to need the fabs version
that applies to an integer and returns a real value.

It's just more work to vectorize abs because it doesn't
have the right signature.

We'll still be able to keep fabs() in the math library.

I can prioritize getting this change in.  I reopened
the issue:

I agree that it would be weird to have both abs and fabs if they do different things.  I also think vectorization is important for user-friendliness.  Indeed, in my opinion, the user-friendliness of vectorization outweighs the un-user-friendliness of abs.
>
> The larger issue, I think, is that the integer/real distinction causes problems all over the place in Stan.  It's unavoidable, perhaps, but still annoying.  The example that keeps coming up is when I switch from linear regression to logistic.  With linear I have vector[N] y; and with logistic I have int y[N].  It's becoming less of a problem for me because I've been trying to consistently use the "long" format for regression data, but when I had data such as y[i,j] and was using to_vector(), it was kind of annoying.

>> On Dec 11, 2016, at 8:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> I can take another look at that.  We've followed the easy path

>> in C++, fabs() has a single signature (actually it includes parallel
>> versions for float and long double, but this is the only relevant one)
>>
>> double fabs(double);
>>
>> whereas abs() has two signatures
>>
>> double abs(double);
>> int abs(int);
>>
>> When you combine this with the way promotion from integers to
>> real (floating point) numbers works in C++ and in Stan, what you
>> get is this:
>>
>> abs(int) : int
>> abs(real) : real
>>
>> fabs(int) : real
>> fabs(real) : real
>>
>> The result type is different for integer arguments.  All the functions
>> we have vectorized (like log and exp and sqrt) behave like fabs --- they
>> always return real values, even if the argument is an integer.
>>
>> We could deprecate fabs() and either
>>
>> * forego vectorizing abs(), or
>>
>> * we could implement a one-off non-standard vectorization for abs
>>   that would return integers when given integer arguments
>>
>> What we can't do is just decide to have abs return real values for
>> integer inputs---that'd mess up programs.

messages.subject: RStan fails to install on debian testing
messages.subject_clean: RStan fails to install on debian testing
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I spend Sunday trying to install rstan following the instuctions listed on the page:
https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Installing-RStan-on-Mac-or-Linux

and it failed to compile no rstan but its dependencies. Digging into the problem I found the solution.
The solution is simple: install not the lastest version of libssl-dev (1.1.0c-2),  but version 1.0 by the usual command

sudo apt-get install libssl1.0

The lastest version of libssl changed the definitions in its headers of some structures and the package PKI, needed by rstan, does not compile under libssl-1.1.0 but it compiles without a problem with libssl-1.0.

I hope that this information can reach other people trying to install rstan in debian testing or any system that install the latest version of libssl.

An advice in the page  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Installing-RStan-on-Mac-or-Linux  would certainly helps.

All my best and thanks for accepting me in the group!!

Luciano

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your quick repsonse Bob!

I have a 2 short follow up questions:

1) Is it possible that no vectorized version of the ordered_logistic_ ...
    functions is available?
2) I implemented matrix multiplication, but this is a bit tricky because
    some of my variables are discrete and others are continuous.
For example, this line:
eta = alpha[k] + iDx1[j]*betas[k,1] + iDx2[j]*betas[k,2] + xi[n,2]*betas[k,3];
became this
eta = alpha[k] + append_col(to_row_vector(iDx[,j]),xi[n,3]) * betas[,k];

Now I am not sure if the new version would be faster or slower, because
of the usage of append_col and to_row_vector.

Best - Guido

On Friday, December 9, 2016 at 10:32:13 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Dec 9, 2016, at 4:20 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > As it cannot be said often enough:
> >
> > Thanks to the Stan-team for the time and effort
> >
> > they invest to make this a great list!!
> >
> >
> > Now to my problem:
> >
> > I am implementing fully conditional imputation of amongst
> >
> > others ordinal variables. I validated the model (code
> >
> > below) with simulated data, but now it turns out that
> >
> > fitting is very slow when using HMC for real data.
> >
> > When using a subset of my data -2500 cases, 4 variables,
> >
> > two of which are ordinal, with 4 and 6 levels, respectively-
> >
> > fewer than 100 iterations are done after 12h (with
> >
> > adapt_delta=.8, on a PC with a 3.4 ghz processor and 8gb RAM).
>
> >
> > The same data and model can be fit in around a minute
> >
> > using variational Bayes, but then vb is “experimental”.
> >
> >
> > My questions:
> >
> > 1) Does anybody see a way to speed up the model?
>
> I can help with speedig up the computations.  You want to look
> at other things going on to see if there's some way to parameterize
> it better.
>
> Overall, our ordered logistic isn't the fastest thing in the world,
> especially if you can't vectorize it.
>
> The biggest saving you can get in Stan speed is saving any intermediate
> computations you do in order to reuse them.  For that, you have to
> comb over your program and find things in loops that don't depend on
> the loop index and pull them out.  And try to vectorize as much as possible.
> So if you have a bunch of ordered logistics with the same cutpoints, save
> up their arguments if you can and make one call (not sure this is possible).
>
> And don't store things in lp_dv that are 0 and then put them
> into other expressions.  Just push the branching logic down and
> only create and multiplyw hen needed.
>
> For clarity, you don't ever want to compare to 0 or 1 in a conditional.
> Instead, convert
>
> missings[n,1] == 0 ? Dx[n,1] : idv1
>
> into
>
>   missings[n, 1] ? idv1 : Dx[n, 1];
>
> You can probably do things like this:
>
>   ta = alpha[k] + iDx2[j]*betas[k,1] + xi[n,1]*betas[k,2] + xi[n,2]*betas[k,3];
>
> with matrix algebra, which might be faster.

I suspect the answer is 'no' to the above, but thought I'd ask in case anyone has any bright ideas.

Best,

Ben
