messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matthew,

Thanks for being thorough. There are definitely missing pieces in the description like why the stochastic differential equation looks the way it does. (I don't know these models, so this might be obvious to people that do work on these models, bit definitely not to me.)

Some simpler questions to start with:
Did you simulate the data from that process?
What was the last version of this model that was fitting reliably?

Long questions like these are hard to answer. Maybe ask your question more plainly and you'll get more help? I'll try the best I can. More below.

On Dec 11, 2016, at 10:30 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):
>
> dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,
>
> where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.
>
> There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).

Use softmax and run with identical seeds. Make sure results are identical. (if you're thinking it's a gradient issue, well, you should check that it's not a function value issue first.)

>
> It's a lot like this:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE
>
> apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.
>
> If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.

The traceplots look bad. Can you show the results of fixed eta? Can you make one eta a parameter and see if that works?

Because chains end up in different places doesn't quite mean that it's multimodal. It could also mean that the posterior is improper and chains aren't actually converging. From the traceplots, it didn't look like chains were actually stuck in modes.

>
> We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK).

?
If you've got something to tell you that, could you enlighten me? I have intuition when things aren't identified, but I have a very hard time telling when it will be. The geometry of the unconstrained space isn't just defined by the Stan program. It's actually the joint lpdf, which depends on data. And I stay away from claims like that when it's clear that something is not correct.

> Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363),

I didn't dig through the paper, but did you implement that model?

> which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem.
> So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood.

Or it's a non identifiability through the non linear transformation.

One thing to check: how are the values of lp__ for the different chains? If they're all roughly the same values, thats clearly a non identifiability: different values of parameters are resulting in the same joint lpdf on the unconstrained space. Quick check: traceplot the lp__.

Now, if you think it's really the gradients, there is a test gradient mode built in just for this purpose. Check the doc on your interface of choice.

> But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).

Jacobian warnings are a function of the Stan program and don't have anything to do with runtime diagnosis.

Plotting lp__ against eta and not seeing that... what did you see? Sounds like you spotted non identifiability,but maybe didn't know what it looked like?

>
> What can I do to diagnose the problem?

My suggestions:
- always start simpler. Find a model that fits and then build up from there. If you jump to where things aren't working, the space of things that could have gone wrong is too large.
- don't assume anything is right. I wouldn't buy that the whole model is specified correctly. I'd start there. How do you know the function value is right? Have you plugged in values and evaluated the lp__ coming out?
- were there divergences or problems with tree depth? If so, fix those first.
- put more informative priors or more info / structure in the model. And think generatively while you're at it. When you put down priors, draw from them when you simulate data.
- what does your posterior predictive check look like? If you simulate fake data and it looks just like the real data, that also signals a non identifiability. If the fake data looks nothing like real data, then something else is wrong.

>
> I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters.

I missed the other parameters. It sounds like you're describing a non identified model. Check lp__ first and see what you get.

> For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:
>
>     a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)
>     B <- matrix(c(-0.04184048, 0.06290105, 0.01222532, -0.03466200), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
>     x0 <- c(-0.7, 0.9)
>     Sigma <- matrix(c(0.01, -0.005, -0.005, 0.03), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
>     eta <- c(-0.69, -0.40)
>
> and we generated 1001 equally-spaced observations, each with n = 1000 in the multinomials.

Hope that helps.

Daniel

> On Dec 12, 2016, at 9:53 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

Not yet.  It's on our to-do list.  The framework we
set up to vectorize everyhting else doesn't work for
non-scalar parameters, so we need to figure out how to
generalize.

> 2) I implemented matrix multiplication, but this is a bit tricky because
>     some of my variables are discrete and others are continuous.
> For example, this line:
> eta = alpha[k] + iDx1[j]*betas[k,1] + iDx2[j]*betas[k,2] + xi[n,2]*betas[k,3];
> became this
> eta = alpha[k] + append_col(to_row_vector(iDx[,j]),xi[n,3]) * betas[,k];
>
> Now I am not sure if the new version would be faster or slower, because
> of the usage of append_col and to_row_vector.

The append_col and to_row_vector just copy.  The bottleneck is
almost always in the size of the autodiff graph, so usually it's
a win to aggregate operations.  The original line was eta[j], right?
And I didn't follow why the k changed places in betas.  But in general,
it's usually worth appending and reshaping if you can use matrix
operations.  Sometimes you can redeclare variables so that the reshaping
is easy.

- Bob

messages.subject: Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
messages.subject_clean: Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I was playing with rgl and thought others might appreciate this figure I generated for explaining what an HMC sampler is more or less doing.
I actually generated it for a class paper because the prof is not familiar with Bayesian inference, posterior distributions, MCMC, or HMC.

I more or less explain it as "imagine flipping this upside down and rolling a ball around in it and recording the coordinates in space every so many seconds.
The samples were from stan, of course, using NUTS. Though the image isn't on the log-scale, I still tell the students (or the prof) to flip it upside down and imagine randomly flicking a marble in some direction and recording the positions.
This made sense to many of my undergraduates, and they better understood what I meant by a marginal distribution too. The inner line is the first 10 non-warmup steps.

The figure is below, but one can view a webGL version of it (that you can rotate and such) in the attached index.html.

messages.body_plain:
Not sure what you're looking for.  We fit these all the time,
including lots of hierarchical models.  The hierarchical model
can usually be done two ways---directly on whatever constrained
scale you have with priors that match the constraints or on
an unconstrained scale with transforms to the constrained scale.

- Bob

In addition I would love to hear comments on PBPK (physiologically based PK) population models but any comments on traditional compartmental PK population models would be a good starting point.
>
> Thanks,
> Linas

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow imputation of ordered variables with HMC, variational bayes?
messages.body_plain:
OK, then I am looking forward to vectorization for non-scalar parameters.

I also had already changed the model to use vectorization wherever possible,
and to compute the marginalization operatons only for rows with missing
discrete data. This made things noticeably faster.

eta was always just eta and k changed its place in betas because i
changed the dimensions of betas.

about eta:
right now eta is intialized as a single real value and calculated within
the loop for the marginalization.  e.g.

// loop throug all possible combinations of discrete variable values

for (j in 1:n_lps[n]) {
        real eta;

       ...

        eta = alpha[k] + append_col(to_row_vector(iDx[,j]),xi[n,3]) * betas[,k];

        lps[j] = lp_dv[j] + normal_lpdf(xi[n,4] | eta, sigmas[2]);
}

Instead, I could again use matrices to calculate
all etas outside the loop:
real etas[n_lps[n]];
matrix[n_lps[n],K-1] tmp_x;
tmp_x = append_col(append_col(iDx1,IDX2), rep_vector(xi[n,4],[n_lps[n])
etas = alpha[k] + tmp_x *  betas[,k];

for (j in 1:n_lps[n]) {

  ....
  lps[j] = lp_dv[j] + normal_lpdf(xi[n,4] | etas[j], sigmas[2]);
}

would this be faster?
I do not understand well what goes into the construction of the autodiff graph.
Is there a section in the manual that explains this, so that I can figure
out myself what changes to the model most likely impove speed?

Guido

On Tuesday, December 13, 2016 at 8:46:03 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Dec 12, 2016, at 9:53 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks for your quick repsonse Bob!
> >
> > I have a 2 short follow up questions:
> >
> > 1) Is it possible that no vectorized version of the ordered_logistic_ ...
> >     functions is available?
>
> Not yet.  It's on our to-do list.  The framework we
> set up to vectorize everyhting else doesn't work for
> non-scalar parameters, so we need to figure out how to
> generalize.
>
> > 2) I implemented matrix multiplication, but this is a bit tricky because
> >     some of my variables are discrete and others are continuous.
> > For example, this line:
> > eta = alpha[k] + iDx1[j]*betas[k,1] + iDx2[j]*betas[k,2] + xi[n,2]*betas[k,3];
> > became this
> > eta = alpha[k] + append_col(to_row_vector(iDx[,j]),xi[n,3]) * betas[,k];
> >
> > Now I am not sure if the new version would be faster or slower, because
> > of the usage of append_col and to_row_vector.
>
> The append_col and to_row_vector just copy.  The bottleneck is
> almost always in the size of the autodiff graph, so usually it's
> a win to aggregate operations.  The original line was eta[j], right?
> And I didn't follow why the k changed places in betas.  But in general,
> it's usually worth appending and reshaping if you can use matrix
> operations.  Sometimes you can redeclare variables so that the reshaping
> is easy.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Guido,

On Wed, Dec 14, 2016 at 9:28 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you Daniel,
> I had hoped for a shorter way to learn this,
> but let me see if I can take a short cut :-).

Ha... there isn't really a short cut here.

At some point, you either have to spend the time to understand autodiff if you're serious about trying to optimize runtime. Or just follow along with best practices and stop trying to squeeze out maximal performance. (Honestly, I'd suggest the second option any day.)

>
> Figure 1 in the paper shows an expression graph.
> Is it correct to say that if I have column and row
> vectors x and b of length 3, then if I write anywhere
> in the model (or transformed parameters) block
> eta = x[1]*b[1] + x[2]*b[2] + x[3]*b[3];
> this results in 11 automatic differentiation variables,
> and an expression tree with 3 levels, whereas
> eta = x * b;
> results in only 3 automatic differentiation variables
> and an expression tree of 2 levels?

No. It's much more complicated than that. And this is why Stan is fast. It depends whether eta, x, and b are parameters or data. Your original Stan program was too many posts before, so I don't remember what they are.

There's a large section in the paper about how we actually implement the C++ so that we cut out lots of the expression graph. So... no, you're not right here.

If you were to write the expressions in C++ directly without using built in functions, then yes, you're right. (in the second expression, eta = x * b, you'd have to write eta = stan::math::multiply(x, b), but yes).

Daniel

> > > > > Now I am not sure if the new version would be faster or slower, because
> > > > > of the usage of append_col and to_row_vector.
> > > >
> > > > The append_col and to_row_vector just copy.  The bottleneck is
> > > > almost always in the size of the autodiff graph, so usually it's
> > > > a win to aggregate operations.  The original line was eta[j], right?

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Michael for input!

Den fredag 9 december 2016 kl. 15:02:57 UTC+1 skrev Michael Betancourt:
> When making such comparisons you have to be very careful with
> your evaluations.  Different priors choices can affect not only sampling
> speed and posterior inferences, but also the ability to fit the model
> accurately at all.  Wishart and Inverse-Wishart not only imply odd
> distributions for the correlations but they induce nasty posteriors that
> frustrate accurate fitting, leading to the kinds of problems you see
> here.

Well most of my problems went away once I managed to reparameterize the multinormal.

>
> So before comparing speed/efficiency or posteriors, you have to
> validate that you’re getting a reasonable value.  This requires all
> of the tricks — running multiple chains and checking Rhat,
> checking all of the HMC diagnostics like divergences and
> the E-BFMI, and fitting simulated data and confirming that you
> can recover the true values.  If you can’t do all of these then
> the model can’t be fit with your sampler, and you can’t even
> move onto the next step.

Yes I understand this. When I say that the problems went away I generally base this on diagnostics as the ones you mention above.
I admit I haven't gone through all of them yet (and I don't consider myself finished with my analyses either). For example I haven't simulated similar data nor checked E-BFMI.
As regards simulations, I understand they are really an important way to check the model is able to estimate what I want it to estimate. I'm not very good at simulation (I'm learning though) and one thing I find problematic is to make sure I simulate the important potential pathologies of the real dataset. Of course, if my model cannot recover the true parameters of a simulated dataset I know it is not a good model. But if it can, I still can't be sure that it can estimate properly the parameters in the model run on real data since there migth be pathologies in there which I haven't been able to simulate.
But I have run many (5) chains and got good (excellent!) Rhat values, I get generally very similar results when comparing the different priors (IW, SIW etc.) and in cases they differ they do it in ways corresponding to what should be expected considering the characteristics of the priors. The results do also not differ when I compare runs using different numbers of species included (e.g. 15, 10, or 5 species). And for the situation where I've been able to fit the same (as far as I understand...) model in both JAGS and Stan I also get the same result. These things should indicate I'm not totally off in my analyses, shouldn't they?

I will try to perform simulations as well as posterior predictive checks. And I will check the E-BFMI. For the latter, the problem is that I haven't found out how to get it/calculate it... I've googled it (naturaly, since I didn't know what it was) but mostly found links to stan sites (dev mostly) with long discussions on whether it should be included in default warnings/output from stanfits. I also looked for in the manual but didn't find it. Maybe I missed something but it seems it is no longer part of the default output from stanfits. Any hints are greatly appreciated (as are layman explanations of what it is/measures).

Once again, thanks for input. I try to assimilate it although perhaps slowly...

>
> Lots of comparisons have been compromised by neglected
> this step, which is especially important when Gibbs samplers are
> involved!

> > LKJ(eta<1) might apparently mitigate this but then I've seen claims that the LKJ sampler might be less stable and I haven't as yet experimented with it myself.
> > I am supposed to draw some ecological inferences from my analyses too and maybe not delve too far into statistics...ecology is after all my subject,  statistics is supposed to be one of my tools.
> >

> >
> > /Martin
> >
> >
> > Den torsdag 8 december 2016 kl. 21:20:36 UTC+1 skrev Bob Carpenter:
> > > We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
> > > convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
> > > on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:
> > >
> > > http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

> > > which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
> > > governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).
> > >
> > > That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
> > > lots of quantity of interests to compare.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Dec 8, 2016, at 11:21 AM, martin.s...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Daniel,
> > > > Sorry for late reply.
> > > > I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!
> > > >
> > > > Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
> > > > I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.
> > > >
> > > > A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post.
> > > > I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
> > > > (N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
> > > > e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior
> > > > and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >  a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
> > > > Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
> > > >  b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
> > > >   Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
> > > >  c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
> > > >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> > > >  d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),
> > > >  Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R~LKJ(1); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The "effect" of reparameterization differs somewhat between these versions.
> > > >
> > > > Note also that I set adapt_delta to different values in the two model versions...
> > > >
> > > > Anyhow, this is what I did and can report (I work in R using rstan):
> > > > For each stanfit I extracted the summary and took the mean n_eff over all parameters (mean(summary(stanfit)$summary[,'n_eff'])).
> > > > I also used get_elapsed_time() on the stanfit and calculated mean timing of the "sample" part over the chains (colMeans(get_elapsed_time(stanfit))[,'sample']).
> > > >
> > > > I then simply divided n_eff with time.
> > > >
> > > > These are the results for the original multi-normal version (note separate values for models with different priors for Sigma):
> > > >
> > > > Prior        n_eff/time
> > > >
> > > > IW              38.7
> > > > SIW            3.90
> > > > SSIW          12.9
> > > > SSLKJ        0.537
> > > >
> > > > And these are the results for the reparameterized version:
> > > >
> > > > Prior        n_eff/time
> > > >
> > > > IW              38.4
> > > > SIW            36.3
> > > > SSIW          34.0
> > > > SSLKJ        67.6
> > > >
> > > > I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
> > > > And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
> > > > I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.
> > > >
> > > > /Martin
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Den måndag 5 december 2016 kl. 18:12:15 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > > > Since you're looking at it, can you report the n_eff / time for the before and after models?
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:08 PM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thanks Daniel for input!
> > > > Even if you hadn't read my additional post I still found useful information in your reply.
> > > > I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
> > > > Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).
> > > >
> > > > And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).
> > > >
> > > > Thanks!
> > > >
> > > > Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > > > Hi Martin,
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi stan users,
> > > >
> > > > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
> > > >
> > > > Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
> > > >
> > > > Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
> > > >
> > > > I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> > > >
> > > > for (n in 1:N) {
> > > >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > >
> > > > But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
> > > >
> > > > row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > >
> > > > keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
> > > >
> > > > for(n in 1:N){
> > > >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> > > >
> > > > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
> > > >
> > > > In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> > > > Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
> > > >
> > > > For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> > > > 1. Mu = X*Beta;
> > > >     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
> > > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
> > > >
> > > > 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
> > > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
> > > >
> > > > 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
> > > >
> > > > My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Daniel
> > > >
> > > > P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I'd really appreciate any input on this
> > > >
> > > > Sincerely,
> > > > Martin

> > > > SSLKJ        67.6
> > > >
> > > > I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
> > > > And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
> > > > I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.
> > > >
> > > > /Martin
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Den måndag 5 december 2016 kl. 18:12:15 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > > > Since you're looking at it, can you report the n_eff / time for the before and after models?
> > > >
> > > > On Mon, Dec 5, 2016 at 12:08 PM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thanks Daniel for input!
> > > > Even if you hadn't read my additional post I still found useful information in your reply.
> > > > I agree, optimizing (code or other wise) is not the same thing as reparameterizing.
> > > > Even though I try to write as efficient code as possible my aim was to make the model fit better (sorry if I was not able to expressed myself clearly). And my thinking was that both vectorizing and reparameterization should primarily help stan perform better in the calculations (not necessarily doing thing faster).
> > > >
> > > > And you were quite right in that reparameterization (especially of the multi-normal) did the trick as concerns divergent transitions but also when it comes to practically all other diagnostics (mixing, autocorrelation/number of effective samples etc.).
> > > >
> > > > Thanks!
> > > >
> > > > Den fredag 2 december 2016 kl. 18:23:14 UTC+1 skrev Daniel Lee:
> > > > Hi Martin,
> > > >
> > > > On Fri, Dec 2, 2016 at 4:46 AM, <martin.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi stan users,
> > > >
> > > > I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.
> > > >
> > > > Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization.
> > > >
> > > > Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)
> > > >
> > > > I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:
> > > >
> > > > for (n in 1:N) {
> > > >         loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > >
> > > > But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:
> > > >
> > > > row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > > row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
> > > >
> > > > keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):
> > > >
> > > > for(n in 1:N){
> > > >         Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > > But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?
> > > >
> > > > My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:
> > > >
> > > > Mu=X*Beta;
> > > > "some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
> > > > loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);
> > > >
> > > > Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.
> > > >
> > > > In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
> > > > Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.
> > > >
> > > > For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
> > > > 1. Mu = X*Beta;
> > > >     use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
> > > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);
> > > >
> > > > 2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
> > > >     loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)
> > > >
> > > > 3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)
> > > >
> > > > My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Daniel
> > > >
> > > > P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I'd really appreciate any input on this
> > > >
> > > > Sincerely,
> > > > Martin
> > > >

messages.body_plain:
You want to look at the noise in the model itself.

For instance, in the soil carbon models, respirated carbon,
which is positive constrained, tends to have lognormal measurement
noise (noise is proportional to measurement rather than being
a constant scale additive term).

There's not a huge difference in efficiency between declaring
a positive value and giving it a lognormal distribution and
declaring an unconstrained value, giving it a normal distribution,
and then exp() transforming it to positive.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yes, we're moving to passing everything in as double values
and doing matrix derivatives.  Not entirely there yet, though.

And it's why we've added some specialized matrix functions like
triangular self-multiply transpose.

- Bob

> On Dec 13, 2016, at 10:09 PM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> optimization of my GP Stan code with replacing the matrix multiplication
> by a triangular matrix multiplication, gave a great speed up, 2x and more.
>
> I'm happy, but consequently does this not also imply that there is room

>         lps[j] = lp_dv[j] + normal_lpdf(xi[n,4] | eta, sigmas[2]);
> }

> Instead, I could again use matrices to calculate
> all etas outside the loop:
> real etas[n_lps[n]];
> matrix[n_lps[n],K-1] tmp_x;
> tmp_x = append_col(append_col(iDx1,IDX2), rep_vector(xi[n,4],[n_lps[n])
> etas = alpha[k] + tmp_x *  betas[,k];
> for (j in 1:n_lps[n]) {
>   ....
>   lps[j] = lp_dv[j] + normal_lpdf(xi[n,4] | etas[j], sigmas[2]);
> }
>
> would this be faster?

Yes.

> I do not understand well what goes into the construction of the autodiff graph.
> Is there a section in the manual that explains this, so that I can figure
> out myself what changes to the model most likely impove speed?

Only hints.   The short story is that when the log density is
evaluated, the expression graph is saved.  This stores a data
structure for the result and arguments of every mathematical
operation (evaluation order gives you a nice topologically sorted
stack and proof the graph is directed and acyclic).

The graph is then used to calculate derivatives by passing
the chain rule through it backwards from teh result (hence
the "reversse" in our reverse-mode autodiff).

The derivative passing usually consumes well over 90% of the
compute time in all of Stan's algorithms.

Derivative passing is very slow as it involves walking the
stack of subexpressions and calling a virtual function for
each one.  Memory locality is difficult to achieve for anything
other than matrix operations.

The smaller the expression graph is, the faster Stan is.

Almost all of the optimization tips we provide have the sole aim
of making the expression graph smaller.

Every time you execute an operation, it goes on the expression
graph.  So the best thing you can do is save intermediate
results and reuse them.  It automatically translates into
efficient dynamic programming on the back end (the stack and
its topological sort show it works).

Vectorized probability functions address both points.  It
creates a single result node, so fewer virtual function calls,
and it automatically saves the results of intermediate
computations, for more efficiency.  For example, when we
do y ~ normal(mu, sigma); for vector y and scalars mu and sigma,
we only need to evaluate log(sigma) once, which is hugely
expensive compared to simple arithmetic.

Matrix operations do the same thing.  With scalar * vector,
you can collaps all the individual scalar updates to a single
update, saving virtual function calls and space again.  Matrix
times matrix is even more cost saving.

This is all just computational efficiency.  Reparameterization,
tighter priors, etc., address statistical efficiency, which can
be even more important for overall speed.

The manual chapter on efficiency and optimization addresses
both of these kinds of optimization.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Better yet, here's what we do and what we recommend everyone
else do:

1.  code the model as straightforwardly as possible

2.  generate fake data

3.  make sure the program properly codes the model

4.  run the program on real data

5.  *If* the model is too slow, optimize *one step at a time*
    and for each step, go back to (3).

The optimizations can be of either the statistical or the
computational variety.  Slow iterations can be due to
computational statistical problems with parameterization (requiring
too many iterations) or due to slow code (each log density and
derivative evaluation being too slow).

We'd like to do a better job of helping people figure out how to
do the statistical optimization.  It's usually more important and
also more variable based on the model.  And it's harder to diagnose
because you need to look within iterations and at posterior
draws.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.body_plain:
Thank you. That was very helpful. We've established that it is an identifiability problem after all (obvious in retrospect). Traceplots of lp__ were indeed roughly the same for chains with very different values for eta. Once we knew where to look, it was easy to show that adding eta makes the model not identifiable (it was working fine before we added that). It's possible to show that for any set of parameters (a, B, x_0, Sigma, eta), there is another set (a + B * eta, B, x_0 - eta, Sigma, 0) with the same likelihood (and it's nothing to do with the nonlinear transformation, just a translation of the latent process).

On Tuesday, December 13, 2016 at 7:24:56 AM UTC, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Hi Matthew,
>
> Thanks for being thorough. There are definitely missing pieces in the description like why the stochastic differential equation looks the way it does. (I don't know these models, so this might be obvious to people that do work on these models, bit definitely not to me.)
>
> Some simpler questions to start with:
> Did you simulate the data from that process?
> What was the last version of this model that was fitting reliably?
>
> Long questions like these are hard to answer. Maybe ask your question more plainly and you'll get more help? I'll try the best I can. More below.
>
> On Dec 11, 2016, at 10:30 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):
> >
> > dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,
> >
> > where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.
> >
> > There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).
>
> Use softmax and run with identical seeds. Make sure results are identical. (if you're thinking it's a gradient issue, well, you should check that it's not a function value issue first.)
>
> >
> > It's a lot like this:
> >
> > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE
> >
> > apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.
> >
> > If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.
>
> The traceplots look bad. Can you show the results of fixed eta? Can you make one eta a parameter and see if that works?
>
> Because chains end up in different places doesn't quite mean that it's multimodal. It could also mean that the posterior is improper and chains aren't actually converging. From the traceplots, it didn't look like chains were actually stuck in modes.
>
> >
> > We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK).
>
> ?
> If you've got something to tell you that, could you enlighten me? I have intuition when things aren't identified, but I have a very hard time telling when it will be. The geometry of the unconstrained space isn't just defined by the Stan program. It's actually the joint lpdf, which depends on data. And I stay away from claims like that when it's clear that something is not correct.
>
> > Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363),
>
> I didn't dig through the paper, but did you implement that model?
>
> > which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem.
> > So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood.
>
> Or it's a non identifiability through the non linear transformation.
>
> One thing to check: how are the values of lp__ for the different chains? If they're all roughly the same values, thats clearly a non identifiability: different values of parameters are resulting in the same joint lpdf on the unconstrained space. Quick check: traceplot the lp__.
>
> Now, if you think it's really the gradients, there is a test gradient mode built in just for this purpose. Check the doc on your interface of choice.
>
>
> > But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).
>
> Jacobian warnings are a function of the Stan program and don't have anything to do with runtime diagnosis.
>
> Plotting lp__ against eta and not seeing that... what did you see? Sounds like you spotted non identifiability,but maybe didn't know what it looked like?
>
> >
> > What can I do to diagnose the problem?
>
> My suggestions:
> - always start simpler. Find a model that fits and then build up from there. If you jump to where things aren't working, the space of things that could have gone wrong is too large.
> - don't assume anything is right. I wouldn't buy that the whole model is specified correctly. I'd start there. How do you know the function value is right? Have you plugged in values and evaluated the lp__ coming out?
> - were there divergences or problems with tree depth? If so, fix those first.
> - put more informative priors or more info / structure in the model. And think generatively while you're at it. When you put down priors, draw from them when you simulate data.
> - what does your posterior predictive check look like? If you simulate fake data and it looks just like the real data, that also signals a non identifiability. If the fake data looks nothing like real data, then something else is wrong.
>
> >
> > I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters.
>
> I missed the other parameters. It sounds like you're describing a non identified model. Check lp__ first and see what you get.
>
> > For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:
> >
> >     a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)
> >     B <- matrix(c(-0.04184048, 0.06290105, 0.01222532, -0.03466200), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
> >     x0 <- c(-0.7, 0.9)
> >     Sigma <- matrix(c(0.01, -0.005, -0.005, 0.03), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
> >     eta <- c(-0.69, -0.40)
> >
> > and we generated 1001 equally-spaced observations, each with n = 1000 in the multinomials.
>
> Hope that helps.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>

we can do by walking over the matrix.  And if it's not
triangular, we'll find out very quickly, so I don't even
think much work would be wasted.

where first is triangular and second is dense or something.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Bob about showing within iteration steps. In my experience trying to explain HMC to people people aren't used to thinking about joint posteriors, particularly in >3 dimensions (they tend to only think of marginals). Thus an illustrative 2d example is much more intuitive to people. That's why I made Figure 3b in my paper (here <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12681/full>), which shows three trajectories: unit diagonal mass matrix, dense mass matrix, and divergence. -Cole

> add the feature.  So it will be able to do it soon.  There's something
> at least in 2D that will plot trajectories, but they quickly become
> very hard to scan without thinning, which kind of defeats the purpose.
>
> The really cool trajectories to visualize (though it's HMC specific)
> is the Hamiltonian simulation within an iteration.  Right now there's
> a problem that we see where a divergent transition started, but not
> where it gets into trouble.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
The good news is, I have found a solution to my problem: Now a key parameter (“week number”) is treated as a truly continuous variable rather than a discrete one.

The bad news is, the program is still really, really slow (as in: three hours to reach reasonable convergence on a fairly simple test problem). I don’t understand why.

Here’s how I made the problem continuous (skip the stuff between the === below if you don’t need the details)

===
I have a coefficient betaTOD[ week, TOD] that quantifies the “time of day (TOD) effect” in a given week. If, in week 4, at 9:00 every day the electric load is 2 kW, then betaTOD[ 4, 9] = 2
I write this coefficient as a sum: betaTOD[ week, TOD] =  betaTODinit [ TOD ] + phiTOD[ week, TOD]
betaTODinit is sampled from a prior
phiTOD is a step function that starts in one week and ends in another. It has a start week defined by weekStartTOD, a magnitude defined by deltaTOD, and a duration defined by tauTOD.

I want to be able to have “impulses” that last for some number of weeks at a given time of day. At 9 am, if the load is 1 kW in weeks 1 and 2 and 3, and then goes up to 2 kW for weeks 4 and 5 and 6, and then drops back to 1 kW, I want to capture this as an impulse that has a height of 1 kW, a duration of 3 weeks, and starts in week 4.

The problem is that, as described, this is a discrete problem even if I make the start time and the duration continuous: whether the “9 am” effect starts when week = 3.001 or 3.999 makes no difference: either way, the impulse doesn’t apply in week 3 but it does in week 4.  (In the full model I want to fit, there’s a reason I don’t start an impulse mid-week; otherwise, it would make sense for week = 3.5 to mean the impulse starts on Wednesday. But for this toy problem, an impulse either applies to the whole week at a given time of day, or it doesn’t apply at all that week).
===

My solution, which I was SURE was going to work, was to change the definition of the model so that a non-integer start time has an effect on the predictions. Suppose the candidate start time is 3.001. Previously, what this meant is that the first week in which the effect occurs is week 4, which the first week after the start of the impulse.  What I did was change this so that now some fraction of the effect shows up _before_ the start time. What fraction?
f =  (integer start week - continuous start week) So, if the candidate start time is week = 3.001, this generates an integer start week of 4, and we get f= 0.999. So even though the “start time” is just AFTER 3.0, we get 99.9% of the effect during week 3. In contrast, if week = 3.999, we only get 0.1% of the effect in the week 3.

The effect of all of this is that the program can converge on the right answer along a continuous path.  If it tries a start time of 3.001 for an impulse that actually started in week 4, it will apply a lot of that impulse to week 3 and thus overestimate that week (assuming the impulse is positive). It can gradually work its way towards a start time of 4.0 by going downhill (towards lower error) all the way. Of course Stan isn’t trying to just run downhill, it’s sampling, but the point is it now has a nicely behaved continuous model for doing this. And it works!

But it works…so…very….slowly.

I’m doing an 11-week test problem, 24 times of day, 5 days per week. I have only one “impulse” for each time of day (e.g. there can be one start time and duration and magnitude for 1:00, and a different start time and duration and magnitude at 2:00, and so on).  So, 24 impulses, each defined by 3 adjustable parameters, plus the 24 parameters that define the initial state…altogether that’s about 100 parameters. How can it take hours?

I’ve taken a look at the “pairs” plot and it looks like the model is spending all of its time in a few regions of parameter space that aren’t near the maximum. See the attached plot. Here I did 800 iterations and as you can see t

. The “right answer” is:
betaTODinit[10] = 1.0,  (This is the magnitude of the “hour 10” effect in week 1)
deltaTOD[1,10] = 1.0,  (This is the magnitude of the impulse)
weekStartTOD[1,10] = 3.0, (This is the start time of the impulse)
sigma[10] = 0.05 (This is the amount of noise added to the signal, which would otherwise be a square wave)

If it finds the right parameters for these and for all of the other parameters in the model — everywhere there’s a 10 in the list above, there can be any number from 1 to 24 — it can have its predictions match the data almost exactly, the only difference is iid normal noise with sd = 0.05.  But unless I cook the books by giving it very tight priors around the right answer, it doesn’t find it.

Basically it looks like its step size is way too small. But I’ve tried increasing adapt_delta to 0.95 (from the default of 0.8) and this doesn’t seem to help.

If I print out some values for debugging, it typically makes really really tiny steps (near some incorrect answer) until suddenly it takes a big jump towards a somewhat better answer and then takes really really tiny steps again. You can see this in the pairs() plot. As I’m writing this, I’m running it while I watch it print out the maximum residual. The model is trying to pull this towards zero: y ~ N( yhat, sigma) and sigma ~ half-normal(0, sigmaMax).  Anyway, it spend hundreds of iterations with a big max residual, around 2.2, changing only the fourth or fifth digit. Then suddenly it ran down to about 1.3 and then stalled there. Then down to 0.9 and stalled there….and that chain just ended at 1000 iterations and now it is doing another one, starting with the max residual around 1.45 again only changing the fourth digit as I write this…whoah, except it just jumped down to 0.76…and now back up to 0.93, where it is changing only in the fourth decimal place.

You’ve said in the past that slow convergence usually means a bug in the model, and of course that’s possible here…but the fact that I can give it tight priors around the right answer and it agrees that yep, that’s the right answer…that makes me think there’s not a bug.

There is inevitably some correlation between parameter estimates — for example,  if it has found the “right” end time but its start time is too early, it needs to both move the start time later and decrease the duration in order to make things better — but even if it were just picking completely at random, half the time it tries a later start time it should try a lower duration. Surely it should not take thousands and thousands of iterations to make progress.

I’m baffled.

Ideas welcome!

P

messages.body_plain:
> > When making such comparisons you have to be very careful with
> > your evaluations.  Different priors choices can affect not only sampling
> > speed and posterior inferences, but also the ability to fit the model
> > accurately at all.  Wishart and Inverse-Wishart not only imply odd
> > distributions for the correlations but they induce nasty posteriors that
> > frustrate accurate fitting, leading to the kinds of problems you see
> > here.
>
> Well most of my problems went away once I managed to reparameterize the multi normal.

Sure, although the utility of that reparameterization will depend on how
much data you have and other specifics of your exact posterior.  Anyways,
the point is that comparisons before the reparameterization are suspect
at best.

> As regards simulations, I understand they are really an important way to check the model is able to estimate what I want it to estimate. I'm not very good at simulation (I'm learning though) and one thing I find problematic is to make sure I simulate the important potential pathologies of the real dataset. Of course, if my model cannot recover the true parameters of a simulated dataset I know it is not a good model. But if it can, I still can't be sure that it can estimate properly the parameters in the model run on real data since there migth be pathologies in there which I haven't been able to simulate.

No test will confirm that everything is working — the best we can do is
try a bunch of tests that will identify problems.

Trying to fit data simulated from your model will not guarantee that your
fit will work well with real data, but if you can’t even recover simulated
values then you have no hope of doing well on the real data.

Once you’ve confirmed that you can recovered simulated values you
can move onto considering the structure of the real data with posterior
predictive checks, sampler diagnostics, and the like.

> But I have run many (5) chains and got good (excellent!) Rhat values, I get generally very similar results when comparing the different priors (IW, SIW etc.) and in cases they differ they do it in ways corresponding to what should be expected considering the characteristics of the priors. The results do also not differ when I compare runs using different numbers of species included (e.g. 15, 10, or 5 species). And for the situation where I've been able to fit the same (as far as I understand...) model in both JAGS and Stan I also get the same result. These things should indicate I'm not totally off in my analyses, shouldn't they?

They are good indications that there are no disastrous pathologies, but
you can never be too careful.

> I will try to perform simulations as well as posterior predictive checks. And I will check the E-BFMI. For the latter, the problem is that I haven't found out how to get it/calculate it... I've googled it (naturaly, since I didn't know what it was) but mostly found links to stan sites (dev mostly) with long discussions on whether it should be included in default warnings/output from stanfits. I also looked for in the manual but didn't find it. Maybe I missed something but it seems it is no longer part of the default output from stanfits. Any hints are greatly appreciated (as are layman explanations of what it is/measures).

This manuscript, https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00695, is it for the moment.
A conceptual treatment is coming soon.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Cole and Stephen, these figures are great!  Thank you for sharing here.

In case it's useful to anyone, allow me to also throw in a simple animation of a sequence of HMC trajectories around a 2D gaussian that I made a few years ago for illustrative purposes in talks.  An mp4 video, still frames, and python/matplotlib code to generate the animation are here -

https://github.com/nesanders/HMC_viz

The final frame shows a marginal view by rotating the Gaussian to a 2D perspective.  Stephen, I really like your marginal views on the side of the box.

~Nathan

On Wednesday, December 14, 2016 at 1:58:51 PM UTC-5, Cole Monnahan wrote:
> I agree with Bob about showing within iteration steps. In my experience trying to explain HMC to people people aren't used to thinking about joint posteriors, particularly in >3 dimensions (they tend to only think of marginals). Thus an illustrative 2d example is much more intuitive to people. That's why I made Figure 3b in my paper (here <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12681/full>), which shows three trajectories: unit diagonal mass matrix, dense mass matrix, and divergence. -Cole
>
> On Wednesday, December 14, 2016 at 7:41:59 AM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > I thought Jonah showed me that ShinyStan could do what you
> > were doing.  But apparently not, because they added an issue to
> > add the feature.  So it will be able to do it soon.  There's something
> > at least in 2D that will plot trajectories, but they quickly become
> > very hard to scan without thinning, which kind of defeats the purpose.
> >
> > The really cool trajectories to visualize (though it's HMC specific)
> > is the Hamiltonian simulation within an iteration.  Right now there's
> > a problem that we see where a divergent transition started, but not
> > where it gets into trouble.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Dec 13, 2016, at 4:41 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Huh, I only now saw the 'trivariate' option in shinystan. Very cool. I may actually use that to look at some wonky areas of the posterior of one of my models.
> > >
> > > However, in my defense, I wanted a plot that showed trajectories and marginals so students can get what I mean by that from an image.
> > > I should use shinystan more often; every time I open it I discover something new.
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, December 13, 2016 at 3:24:55 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > ShinyStan can automatically generate those plots for arbitrary models
> > > and it lets you rotate them with up to three parameters.
> > >
> > > The trick is explaining why you get a bowl in the first place (conserved
> > > Hamiltonian gives you a level set).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Dec 13, 2016, at 4:15 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hey everyone,
> > > >
> > > > I was playing with rgl and thought others might appreciate this figure I generated for explaining what an HMC sampler is more or less doing.
> > > > I actually generated it for a class paper because the prof is not familiar with Bayesian inference, posterior distributions, MCMC, or HMC.
> > > >
> > > > I more or less explain it as "imagine flipping this upside down and rolling a ball around in it and recording the coordinates in space every so many seconds.
> > > > The samples were from stan, of course, using NUTS. Though the image isn't on the log-scale, I still tell the students (or the prof) to flip it upside down and imagine randomly flicking a marble in some direction and recording the positions.
> > > > This made sense to many of my undergraduates, and they better understood what I meant by a marginal distribution too. The inner line is the first 10 non-warmup steps.
> > > >
> > > > The figure is below, but one can view a webGL version of it (that you can rotate and such) in the attached index.html.

Not to be nitpicky but be careful distinguishing 'measurement' noise - which you might attribute to assay error, which will be normally distributed (your $SIGMA) in nonmem. Looks like Stan is not warming up right for those odd looking chains. You may want to control initialization a bit more. messages.subject_clean: stiff ODEs and population PK models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas,

You may want to look at the work we're doing to develop a suite of Stan functions for pharmacometric applications, particularly PKPD models. Here's a couple relevant links:
https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/torstenManual.pdf
https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/README.md
The user manual provides some popPK and popPKPD examples. The code and data for the examples is also available in the repo.

We usually describe inter-individual variation in the model parameters as lognormal, though usually coded in terms of a multivariate normal distribution of log transformed parameters. Of course this is because the parameters typically make sense only if they are positive -- but there are sometimes exceptions.

Cheers,
Bill

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Extremely slow (or no) convergence of model with discrete steps...how to improve?
messages.body_plain:
Hmmm, hard to do this over email . . . my quick thought is the generic recommendation to strip down the model and see if everything's ok on a simpler version.  From the pairs plot it looks like things are multimodal which makes me really tempted to use this as an example for my new adaptive simulated tempering algorithm.  But I wonder whether there's a way to make the model even more continuous in some way.  Also I wonder if there's some real nonidentifiability because of the starting and stopping model.

Just for example--and plz recognize that I'm making it up becuase I'm not trying to follow all your details--suppose you have something that starts at time 1.3 and ends at time 10.2.  Then couldn't it also be something that starts at 1.3 and ends at X, plus another something that starts at X and ends at 10.2?  You get the idea.  If there are lots of these impulses and they can adjoin or overlap, then there could be lots of stories that will legitimately fit the data.  Which suggests maybe some stronger priors are needed about the legnths of these impulses, or the time between them, or something like that.

A

> On Dec 14, 2016, at 2:38 PM, Phillip Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
>
>
> The good news is, I have found a solution to my problem: Now a key parameter (“week number”) is treated as a truly continuous variable rather than a discrete one.
>
> The bad news is, the program is still really, really slow (as in: three hours to reach reasonable convergence on a fairly simple test problem). I don’t understand why.
>
> Here’s how I made the problem continuous (skip the stuff between the === below if you don’t need the details)
>
> ===
> I have a coefficient betaTOD[ week, TOD] that quantifies the “time of day (TOD) effect” in a given week. If, in week 4, at 9:00 every day the electric load is 2 kW, then betaTOD[ 4, 9] = 2
> I write this coefficient as a sum: betaTOD[ week, TOD] =  betaTODinit [ TOD ] + phiTOD[ week, TOD]
> betaTODinit is sampled from a prior
> phiTOD is a step function that starts in one week and ends in another. It has a start week defined by weekStartTOD, a magnitude defined by deltaTOD, and a duration defined by tauTOD.
>
> I want to be able to have “impulses” that last for some number of weeks at a given time of day. At 9 am, if the load is 1 kW in weeks 1 and 2 and 3, and then goes up to 2 kW for weeks 4 and 5 and 6, and then drops back to 1 kW, I want to capture this as an impulse that has a height of 1 kW, a duration of 3 weeks, and starts in week 4.
>
> The problem is that, as described, this is a discrete problem even if I make the start time and the duration continuous: whether the “9 am” effect starts when week = 3.001 or 3.999 makes no difference: either way, the impulse doesn’t apply in week 3 but it does in week 4.  (In the full model I want to fit, there’s a reason I don’t start an impulse mid-week; otherwise, it would make sense for week = 3.5 to mean the impulse starts on Wednesday. But for this toy problem, an impulse either applies to the whole week at a given time of day, or it doesn’t apply at all that week).
> ===
>
> My solution, which I was SURE was going to work, was to change the definition of the model so that a non-integer start time has an effect on the predictions. Suppose the candidate start time is 3.001. Previously, what this meant is that the first week in which the effect occurs is week 4, which the first week after the start of the impulse.  What I did was change this so that now some fraction of the effect shows up _before_ the start time. What fraction?
> f =  (integer start week - continuous start week) So, if the candidate start time is week = 3.001, this generates an integer start week of 4, and we get f= 0.999. So even though the “start time” is just AFTER 3.0, we get 99.9% of the effect during week 3. In contrast, if week = 3.999, we only get 0.1% of the effect in the week 3.
>
> The effect of all of this is that the program can converge on the right answer along a continuous path.  If it tries a start time of 3.001 for an impulse that actually started in week 4, it will apply a lot of that impulse to week 3 and thus overestimate that week (assuming the impulse is positive). It can gradually work its way towards a start time of 4.0 by going downhill (towards lower error) all the way. Of course Stan isn’t trying to just run downhill, it’s sampling, but the point is it now has a nicely behaved continuous model for doing this. And it works!
>
> But it works…so…very….slowly.
>
> I’m doing an 11-week test problem, 24 times of day, 5 days per week. I have only one “impulse” for each time of day (e.g. there can be one start time and duration and magnitude for 1:00, and a different start time and duration and magnitude at 2:00, and so on).  So, 24 impulses, each defined by 3 adjustable parameters, plus the 24 parameters that define the initial state…altogether that’s about 100 parameters. How can it take hours?
>
> I’ve taken a look at the “pairs” plot and it looks like the model is spending all of its time in a few regions of parameter space that aren’t near the maximum. See the attached plot. Here I did 800 iterations and as you can see t
>
>
> . The “right answer” is:
> betaTODinit[10] = 1.0,  (This is the magnitude of the “hour 10” effect in week 1)
> deltaTOD[1,10] = 1.0,  (This is the magnitude of the impulse)
> weekStartTOD[1,10] = 3.0, (This is the start time of the impulse)
> sigma[10] = 0.05 (This is the amount of noise added to the signal, which would otherwise be a square wave)
>
> If it finds the right parameters for these and for all of the other parameters in the model — everywhere there’s a 10 in the list above, there can be any number from 1 to 24 — it can have its predictions match the data almost exactly, the only difference is iid normal noise with sd = 0.05.  But unless I cook the books by giving it very tight priors around the right answer, it doesn’t find it.
>
> Basically it looks like its step size is way too small. But I’ve tried increasing adapt_delta to 0.95 (from the default of 0.8) and this doesn’t seem to help.
>
> If I print out some values for debugging, it typically makes really really tiny steps (near some incorrect answer) until suddenly it takes a big jump towards a somewhat better answer and then takes really really tiny steps again. You can see this in the pairs() plot. As I’m writing this, I’m running it while I watch it print out the maximum residual. The model is trying to pull this towards zero: y ~ N( yhat, sigma) and sigma ~ half-normal(0, sigmaMax).  Anyway, it spend hundreds of iterations with a big max residual, around 2.2, changing only the fourth or fifth digit. Then suddenly it ran down to about 1.3 and then stalled there. Then down to 0.9 and stalled there….and that chain just ended at 1000 iterations and now it is doing another one, starting with the max residual around 1.45 again only changing the fourth digit as I write this…whoah, except it just jumped down to 0.76…and now back up to 0.93, where it is changing only in the fourth decimal place.
>
> You’ve said in the past that slow convergence usually means a bug in the model, and of course that’s possible here…but the fact that I can give it tight priors around the right answer and it agrees that yep, that’s the right answer…that makes me think there’s not a bug.
>
> There is inevitably some correlation between parameter estimates — for example,  if it has found the “right” end time but its start time is too early, it needs to both move the start time later and decrease the duration in order to make things better — but even if it were just picking completely at random, half the time it tries a later start time it should try a lower duration. Surely it should not take thousands and thousands of iterations to make progress.
>
> I’m baffled.
>
> Ideas welcome!
>
> P
>

> <pairsPlot.png>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sub sampling the posterior [rstan]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] sub sampling the posterior [rstan]
messages.body_plain:
We (with Juho and Markus) have also an example were we obtain 4000 draws, check the diagnostics, and then would like to further computation with as few draws as possible. It's better to choose the smaller number of draws determinisitically and not randomly. For example, to pick 40 draws, simple deterministic approach is to pick every 100th draw from each chain (not from the permuted draws!). In our case we might be willing to use even more computationally intensive deterministic method (such as support points https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01811) which would give lower variance for the further estimates than the simple approach mentioned above. An example of slow computation is projection predictive model reduction for some models. For us, rstan support for thinning is low priority as the basic thinning is so easy to do anyway (and the support point method would require additional testing).

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the paper!

I've read it and although it's way above my head I think I got an intuitive idea of E-BFMI.

So, before I close this thread, and since I'm still not sure how to extract E-BFMI:
Is there a simple way to extract E-BFMI from a stanfit? Is it hidden somewhere in the stanfit object or do I have to calculate it myself?
If the latter, would this function (using rstan) do it?
E_BFMI <- function(stanfit){
  nsamp <- dim(stanfit)[1]
  pars <- get_sampler_params(stanfit, inc_warmup=F)
  lapply(pars, function(x){
        deltaE <- x[1:nsamp-1, 'energy__'] - x[2:nsamp, 'energy__']
        margE <- x[,'energy__'] - mean(x[, 'energy__'])
        numer <- sum(deltaE^2)
        denom <- sum(margE^2)
        numer/denom
  })
}

And for visual inspection I could histogram deltaE and margE as calculated above?

Thanks for any help!

/Martin

Den onsdag 14 december 2016 kl. 21:05:55 UTC+1 skrev Michael Betancourt:
>
> > > When making such comparisons you have to be very careful with
> > > your evaluations.  Different priors choices can affect not only sampling
> > > speed and posterior inferences, but also the ability to fit the model
> > > accurately at all.  Wishart and Inverse-Wishart not only imply odd
> > > distributions for the correlations but they induce nasty posteriors that
> > > frustrate accurate fitting, leading to the kinds of problems you see
> > > here.
> >
> > Well most of my problems went away once I managed to reparameterize the multi normal.
>
> Sure, although the utility of that reparameterization will depend on how
> much data you have and other specifics of your exact posterior.  Anyways,
> the point is that comparisons before the reparameterization are suspect
> at best.
>
> > As regards simulations, I understand they are really an important way to check the model is able to estimate what I want it to estimate. I'm not very good at simulation (I'm learning though) and one thing I find problematic is to make sure I simulate the important potential pathologies of the real dataset. Of course, if my model cannot recover the true parameters of a simulated dataset I know it is not a good model. But if it can, I still can't be sure that it can estimate properly the parameters in the model run on real data since there migth be pathologies in there which I haven't been able to simulate.
>
> No test will confirm that everything is working — the best we can do is
> try a bunch of tests that will identify problems.
>
> Trying to fit data simulated from your model will not guarantee that your
> fit will work well with real data, but if you can’t even recover simulated
> values then you have no hope of doing well on the real data.
>
> Once you’ve confirmed that you can recovered simulated values you
> can move onto considering the structure of the real data with posterior
> predictive checks, sampler diagnostics, and the like.
>
> > But I have run many (5) chains and got good (excellent!) Rhat values, I get generally very similar results when comparing the different priors (IW, SIW etc.) and in cases they differ they do it in ways corresponding to what should be expected considering the characteristics of the priors. The results do also not differ when I compare runs using different numbers of species included (e.g. 15, 10, or 5 species). And for the situation where I've been able to fit the same (as far as I understand...) model in both JAGS and Stan I also get the same result. These things should indicate I'm not totally off in my analyses, shouldn't they?
>
> They are good indications that there are no disastrous pathologies, but
> you can never be too careful.
>
> > I will try to perform simulations as well as posterior predictive checks. And I will check the E-BFMI. For the latter, the problem is that I haven't found out how to get it/calculate it... I've googled it (naturaly, since I didn't know what it was) but mostly found links to stan sites (dev mostly) with long discussions on whether it should be included in default warnings/output from stanfits. I also looked for in the manual but didn't find it. Maybe I missed something but it seems it is no longer part of the default output from stanfits. Any hints are greatly appreciated (as are layman explanations of what it is/measures).
>
> This manuscript, https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00695, is it for the moment.
> A conceptual treatment is coming soon.
>

I fully agree that it's difficult to follow the recommendations as they keep changing. I've noticed that big reason why our prior recommendations are changing is that Stan makes it so much easier to use better priors, but also the better inference and diagnostic methods in Stan help reveal problems in the old recommendations! Lot of prior discussions have been collected to wiki https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations and a paper is in progress.

Aki
