Hi!

What Aki describes is roughly my motivation - and I agree that it may be too easy to do myself rather than bloat the rstan R package with it. Sebastian

On Friday, December 16, 2016 at 9:16:15 AM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> We (with Juho and Markus) have also an example were we obtain 4000 draws, check the diagnostics, and then would like to further computation with as few draws as possible. It's better to choose the smaller number of draws determinisitically and not randomly. For example, to pick 40 draws, simple deterministic approach is to pick every 100th draw from each chain (not from the permuted draws!). In our case we might be willing to use even more computationally intensive deterministic method (such as support points https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01811) which would give lower variance for the further estimates than the simple approach mentioned above. An example of slow computation is projection predictive model reduction for some models. For us, rstan support for thinning is low priority as the basic thinning is so easy to do anyway (and the support point method would require additional testing).
>

> On Dec 18, 2016, at 2:52 PM, Weijia You <weij...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Jon,
>
> Thank you very much for your code for I'm working on an unsupervised HMM model estimation now. But I have two questions here:
>
> 1) it seems that only Forwards algorithm is applied. In the model part, only the variable "pred" is called and "prob_grp" is never used, am I right?

That is right.  A Stan program codes up the log posterior
up to an additive constant --- that's usually just the log
joint coded as the log prior plus the log likelihood.
The forward algorithm is an O(N * K^2) algorithm to compute
the log likelihood (N is input length and K is number of
states).  If you look at the meaning of the nodes in
the forward algorithm, you'll see that for the final row if you
do log_sum_exp, you get the log density for the data.  That is,
it marginalizes out all the hidden state choices leaving you
with the density of the input given the parameters.

The backward algorithm lets you also compute all the marginals
on a per-input basis and also all the transition marginals,
which can really accelerate training the log density and
in many cases makes it trivial due to conjugacy.  Then what
you get is what looks like the second step of the EM algorithm.

I'm going to write all this up in a case study when I get
some time unless someone else beats me to it.

> 2) I tried to run the code but the estimation seems to be a bit far away from the true value.
> TP<-matrix(c(0.8,0.2,0.3,0.7),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE);mu = (2,5), but the estimation I got is:

> sigma[2] 1.00    0.02 0.03 0.96 0.98 1.00 1.02  1.04     3  1.95
>
> Also I noticed that Rhat is quite far from the ideal value around 1.

This looks like a label-switching problem.  Look at the traceplots
for mu[1] and mu[2] and see what it looks like --- they're probably mirror
images. You can try just running one chain or including something in the
model that identifies the parameters, like setting mu[1] < mu[2] by
declaring mu as an ordered vector.  Sometimes you can solve the problem
with inits near the posterior mode you want.  In this case (label
switching), the posterior modes are all truly symmetric.

messages.body_plain:
Check out this to develop some intuitions:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

What do you tell people now when they ask you to justify an
(inverse) Wishart?

What the inverse Wishart has going for it is that it's the conjugate
prior for covariance matrices in a multivariate normal model.  As
such, it can be represented as prior multivariate normal data.

The LKJ prior is like a beta prior in some ways.  The
bigger the parameter, the more concentrated the prior is around the
unit correlation matrix.  So it lets you directly parameterize
correlation.

Then you can control the scales any way you want to allow for both long
and short-tailed behavior or zero-avoiding behavior (e.g., Cauchy, normal,
lognormal).

In the 2D case this is like putting a beta prior stretched from (0,1)
to (-1, 1) on the correlation rho, and putting an independent
prior on the scales sigma[1] and sigma[2]:

  Sigma = sigma[1] * sigma[1]         rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2]
          rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2]   sigma[2] * sigma[2]

You see people do this all the time in the 2D case and the LKJ
prior is just a natural generalization to higher dimensions.

To gain some degree of separation between the scale priors and
the correlation priors, Gelman and Hill hacked something similar
in their regression book by scaling a covariance matrix with an
inverse Wishart prior.  It's much easier to get the effect they were
after with a scaled LKJ prior.

- Bob

On Sunday, December 18, 2016 at 12:27:51 PM UTC-5, Ben Ogorek wrote:
> In my Stan code <https://github.com/baogorek/Miscellaneous/blob/master/R_code/stan/ragged_array_cov_est.stan>, I believe I got it to work by creating a "master" covariance matrix in transformed parameters and then putting sub-segments of the data vector into local variable of fixed size in the model block. The only bad thing is having to "repeat myself" for every vector size:

It would probably be better to pass the data as two (or n_clusters) vectors, one for each cluster.

> Also, as an inexperienced bayesian practitioner, there are a few additional points that concern me:
> My priors don't ensure positive definiteness,

Then your priors do not integrate to 1 over admissible region of the parameter space. To be positive definite, you need to declare rho2 as

real<lower=-bound(rho1),upper=bound(rho1)> rho2;

where bound is defined in the functions block as

real bound(real rho1) return sqrt( 1 / ( 1 + (1 - rho1) / (1 + rho1) ) );

> Stan gives a warning message about my "transformation" of the data into the cluster-sized variables,

That is an identity "transformation" and thus the Jacobian matrix is the identity matrix, whose log-determinant is a constant (zero), so no adjustment needs to be made.

> There seems to be some bias in the posterior draws, but perhaps this is expected

from the lack of positive definiteness.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Weijia,

Very happy to hear that someone is making use of my example!

1) "pred" is our prior which we need in to compute the posterior density.  "prob_grp" is calculated because it is a parameter of interest.  "pred" is the probability of the value of the state at time t considering data up to time t-1 (i.e. a 1-step prediction).  "prob_grp" is the probability of the state considering the data from all time points.

2) Label switching is almost certainly your issue.  Try to examine a summary of the samples generated by each chain separately and the issue should become clear.

I hope that this is useful,

Jon.

On one hand the center of the posterior seems to be overfititng to the data,
but on the other hand the breadth of the posterior remains sufficiently wide
so that the entire posterior isn’t overfitting much.  You might want to try
splitting the data in two, fitting on one half and using the other half for the
PPC to see if it’s any different.

There might be more sophisticated correlations between the categories
that you’re not modeling which pulls the measurement variation to larger
values to compensate.  You could also try an explicitly zero-infated model
to see if that allow the model to better capture the lower categories.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow mixing and poor estimation in multivariate state-space model with multinomial observations
messages.body_plain:
Informative priors, I think. We can probably get fairly good prior information about eta. Also, we may be able to get prior information about x at some time points (at the end of the time series, not at the start), which will help. But also, a lot of what we're interested in is differences in x between time points, or derivatives of the expected value of x at time points, which are invariant under translation and so are not affected by the identifiability problem.

Matt

On Wednesday, December 14, 2016 at 6:11:41 PM UTC, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Woohoo! I'm glad my intuition was right. (It's definitely not always that way.)
>
> Let us know how you deal with it. I can think: more structure or stronger priors. But there might be something else. Like different process.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
> On Wed, Dec 14, 2016 at 1:06 PM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you. That was very helpful. We've established that it is an identifiability problem after all (obvious in retrospect). Traceplots of lp__ were indeed roughly the same for chains with very different values for eta. Once we knew where to look, it was easy to show that adding eta makes the model not identifiable (it was working fine before we added that). It's possible to show that for any set of parameters (a, B, x_0, Sigma, eta), there is another set (a + B * eta, B, x_0 - eta, Sigma, 0) with the same likelihood (and it's nothing to do with the nonlinear transformation, just a translation of the latent process).
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, December 13, 2016 at 7:24:56 AM UTC, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > Hi Matthew,
> > >
> > > Thanks for being thorough. There are definitely missing pieces in the description like why the stochastic differential equation looks the way it does. (I don't know these models, so this might be obvious to people that do work on these models, bit definitely not to me.)
> > >
> > > Some simpler questions to start with:
> > > Did you simulate the data from that process?
> > > What was the last version of this model that was fitting reliably?
> > >
> > > Long questions like these are hard to answer. Maybe ask your question more plainly and you'll get more help? I'll try the best I can. More below.
> > >
> > > On Dec 11, 2016, at 10:30 AM, Matthew Spencer <matt.sp...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > I'm working on a multivariate state-space model in which the latent process x is system of linear stochastic differential equations (two-dimensional in this case):
> > > >
> > > > dx = (a + Bx(t)) dt + noise,
> > > >
> > > > where a is an unknown vector and B is an unknown matrix, and the noise term (a multivariate Wiener process) has unknown covariance matrix Sigma.
> > > >
> > > > There are multinomial observations at a series of time points, with parameter vector given by a one-one but nonlinear transformation of x + eta, where eta is an unknown vector. The nonlinear transformation (inverse isometric logratio) is basically the softmax of the result of multiplying x on the left by a known matrix (I didn't actually use softmax to code it, although perhaps I should have done).
> > >
> > > Use softmax and run with identical seeds. Make sure results are identical. (if you're thinking it's a gradient issue, well, you should check that it's not a function value issue first.)
> > >
> > > >
> > > > It's a lot like this:
> > > >
> > > > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/TukPmAw84iE
> > > >
> > > > apart from the nonlinear transformation and multinomial observations.
> > > >
> > > > If eta is fixed, everything works fine, but when we try to estimate eta, for some simulated data sets the chains look as though they are mixing very slowly, effective sample sizes for eta and a are very small, and the R-hat for eta and a are well above 1. The posterior distributions for elements of eta are usually multimodal (because different chains do different things), and often none of the modes coincides with known values for simulated data. We also have similar but less severe problems with a when eta is estimated.
> > >
> > > The traceplots look bad. Can you show the results of fixed eta? Can you make one eta a parameter and see if that works?
> > >
> > > Because chains end up in different places doesn't quite mean that it's multimodal. It could also mean that the posterior is improper and chains aren't actually converging. From the traceplots, it didn't look like chains were actually stuck in modes.
> > >
> > > >
> > > > We're pretty sure that the model is identifiable (and for some simulated data sets it seems to work OK).
> > >
> > > ?
> > > If you've got something to tell you that, could you enlighten me? I have intuition when things aren't identified, but I have a very hard time telling when it will be. The geometry of the unconstrained space isn't just defined by the Stan program. It's actually the joint lpdf, which depends on data. And I stay away from claims like that when it's clear that something is not correct.
> > >
> > > > Furthermore, similar models in which the observation process is (for example) a multivariate t-distribution with location vector given by x + eta (not transformed) work fine (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08363),
> > >
> > > I didn't dig through the paper, but did you implement that model?
> > >
> > > > which suggests to me that it's not an identifiability problem.
> > > > So I think that the problem must be in how the nonlinear transformation of x + eta affects the gradient of the multinomial log-likelihood.
> > >
> > > Or it's a non identifiability through the non linear transformation.
> > >
> > > One thing to check: how are the values of lp__ for the different chains? If they're all roughly the same values, thats clearly a non identifiability: different values of parameters are resulting in the same joint lpdf on the unconstrained space. Quick check: traceplot the lp__.
> > >
> > > Now, if you think it's really the gradients, there is a test gradient mode built in just for this purpose. Check the doc on your interface of choice.
> > >
> > >
> > > > But we don't get any warnings about Jacobian problems, and plotting log probability against the elements of eta didn't immediately suggest a funnel problem to me (although I might not have been looking in the right way).
> > >
> > > Jacobian warnings are a function of the Stan program and don't have anything to do with runtime diagnosis.
> > >
> > > Plotting lp__ against eta and not seeing that... what did you see? Sounds like you spotted non identifiability,but maybe didn't know what it looked like?
> > >
> > > >
> > > > What can I do to diagnose the problem?
> > >
> > > My suggestions:
> > > - always start simpler. Find a model that fits and then build up from there. If you jump to where things aren't working, the space of things that could have gone wrong is too large.
> > > - don't assume anything is right. I wouldn't buy that the whole model is specified correctly. I'd start there. How do you know the function value is right? Have you plugged in values and evaluated the lp__ coming out?
> > > - were there divergences or problems with tree depth? If so, fix those first.
> > > - put more informative priors or more info / structure in the model. And think generatively while you're at it. When you put down priors, draw from them when you simulate data.
> > > - what does your posterior predictive check look like? If you simulate fake data and it looks just like the real data, that also signals a non identifiability. If the fake data looks nothing like real data, then something else is wrong.
> > >
> > > >
> > > > I've attached a description of the model (stanusers.pdf), our current Stan code (pollen.stan), the Bash script we use to run it in cmdstan 2.12.0 (run4chains.sh) with a simulated data set (simdataBrostrom.txt), example trace plots (stansimTrace.pdf), and kernel density plots of the posterior distributions of each parameter, with the true values as red lines (plotpostparms.pdf). Pairs plots of the posterior distributions were too big too post here, but showed obvious problems with eta, and some fairly strong correlations among some other parameters.
> > >
> > > I missed the other parameters. It sounds like you're describing a non identified model. Check lp__ first and see what you get.
> > >
> > > > For this case, the true values used to generate simulated data in R were:
> > > >
> > > >     a <- c(0.10471002, -0.03106714)
> > > >     B <- matrix(c(-0.04184048, 0.06290105, 0.01222532, -0.03466200), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
> > > >     x0 <- c(-0.7, 0.9)
> > > >     Sigma <- matrix(c(0.01, -0.005, -0.005, 0.03), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
> > > >     eta <- c(-0.69, -0.40)
> > > >
> > > > and we generated 1001 equally-spaced observations, each with n = 1000 in the multinomials.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >

messages.body_plain:
This has been solved <https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2016-December/443572.html>. PKI and shinystan now install without problem.

Le lundi 12 décembre 2016 12:19:19 UTC+1, Luciano Moffatt a écrit :
> Hello everyone,
>
> I spend Sunday trying to install rstan following the instuctions listed on the page:
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Installing-RStan-on-Mac-or-Linux
>
> and it failed to compile no rstan but its dependencies. Digging into the problem I found the solution.
> The solution is simple: install not the lastest version of libssl-dev (1.1.0c-2),  but version 1.0 by the usual command
>
> sudo apt-get install libssl1.0
>
> The lastest version of libssl changed the definitions in its headers of some structures and the package PKI, needed by rstan, does not compile under libssl-1.1.0 but it compiles without a problem with libssl-1.0.
>
> I hope that this information can reach other people trying to install rstan in debian testing or any system that install the latest version of libssl.
>
> An advice in the page  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Installing-RStan-on-Mac-or-Linux  would certainly helps.
>
> All my best and thanks for accepting me in the group!!
>
> Luciano
>

messages.body_plain:
awesome. Thanks for taking the time to respond.

To answer your question - people don't ask at this point. Mainly because of the contraints of what NONMEM gives you (basically only inverse wishart unless you want to jump through a lot of hoops).

Also, other than the very small (passionate) minority, the additional hurdles bayesian analysis poses to the status quo of model development makes it so very few people are developing models in that fashion. It's really only under situations where either

a) you a priori know you want to make quantification and handling of uncertainity 'first class'

b) all other options have failed

are people turning to bayesian techniques.

For example, if you look at the ddmore model repository of ~200 models http://repository.ddmore.eu/ as well as my personal interactions with the model bases at Merck, the FDA, and our own group pushing that number to probably 300+ models, I think less than 5% of the models used full bayes, especially for PK models. You see it more when doing like model based meta analysis or some systems biology/PBPK modeling though, and there only metrum and some select individuals seem to make an consistent noise in the space.

Anyway - I don't want to turn this into an exposition, however if you are interested in the why of lack of full bayes (much of which I bet you can guess at) or what stan can (continue) doing to make a dent in that, I'm happy to expand on the state of things.

Thanks again for the pointers!

Devin

On Sunday, December 18, 2016 at 7:07:50 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Check out this to develop some intuitions:
>
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf
>
> What do you tell people now when they ask you to justify an
> (inverse) Wishart?
>
> What the inverse Wishart has going for it is that it's the conjugate
> prior for covariance matrices in a multivariate normal model.  As
> such, it can be represented as prior multivariate normal data.
>
> The LKJ prior is like a beta prior in some ways.  The
> bigger the parameter, the more concentrated the prior is around the
> unit correlation matrix.  So it lets you directly parameterize
> correlation.
>
> Then you can control the scales any way you want to allow for both long
> and short-tailed behavior or zero-avoiding behavior (e.g., Cauchy, normal,
> lognormal).
>
> In the 2D case this is like putting a beta prior stretched from (0,1)
> to (-1, 1) on the correlation rho, and putting an independent
> prior on the scales sigma[1] and sigma[2]:
>
>   Sigma = sigma[1] * sigma[1]         rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2]
>           rho * sigma[1] * sigma[2]   sigma[2] * sigma[2]
>
> You see people do this all the time in the 2D case and the LKJ
> prior is just a natural generalization to higher dimensions.
>
> To gain some degree of separation between the scale priors and
> the correlation priors, Gelman and Hill hacked something similar
> in their regression book by scaling a covariance matrix with an
> inverse Wishart prior.  It's much easier to get the effect they were
> after with a scaled LKJ prior.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Greetings!

I put together a model that has 2 sets of parameters that I want to be similar unless the data suggests otherwise. I implemented this idea by using squared_distance. So I have parameter vector v1 and parameter vector v2. I take similarity = squared_distance(v1,v2) in the transformed parameters block and then sample similarity from exponential(1). When stan builds my model I get a warning:

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal):
Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
    similarity[lev, pa] ~ exponential(...)

I read through chapter 33 of the manual. I understood that I need to adjust the target by the absolute determinant of the jacobian of the transform. However, my jacobian isn't square. It's 1 by the number of parameters times 2. I didn't search exhaustively, but I didn't find this situation addressed in the manual. What is the proper thing to do?

Thank you.

> You mean in publishing?  Because for the most part, Bayesian
modeling is easier because posterior means are so much better
behaved than posterior modes (e.g., we don't have to limit models
like NONMEM [or lme4 does] in order to fit them with max marginal
likelihood).

Hurdles namely in terms of implementation details (eg. I know i want a 2 compartment model with linear absorption with covariates of weight and gender, but how do I code that and then look at model diagnostics), and from an acceptance perspective - 'matching' up to historical comparisons. Eg, its very easy at this point to say, model development was performed using step-wise covariate modeling using a forward inclusion criteria of p < 0.05 and backwards step of p < 0.001. Here are x, y, z diagnostic plots. You can point to 20 other publications with similar diagnostics and interpretations. For example, the 2 primary plots shown to demonstrate model adequacy is conditional weighted residuals  and observed vs individual predicted concentrations, both shown here: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries

These frequentist diagnostics by and large go out the window for bayesian analysis. I don't say this as a good or bad thing, just that the current status quo heavily favors coloring by those numbers to provide historical backing to the modeling strategy used.

> I don't care so much about why people don't do full Bayes, but I am curious about what you think Stan can do.

I believe they are reasonably tightly coupled in a lot of situations, somewhat touched on above.

First, for the remaining discussion we can set aside models that only stan/winbugs/etc can handle, and instead focus on what can be done such that people who would normally have turned to nonmem would instead grab Stan.

1) Push out some more (simple, but holistic) examples.

This is going to be the largest hurdle once the ODE implementation settles. For better or worse, the majority of people will want to 'copy-paste' their way through scenarios they are familiar with to wrap their head around. Many companies have model libraries of 100's of models with 'tricks' on how to implement things.

For example, I'm picking away at an extremely simple example: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries and the associated code for the project: https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes

Such case studies would cover:
- what the data looks like
- model setup with some information
- diagnostic outputs with some minimal interpretation

I know documentation is so low on priorities for the core team, but without some more examples, people such as myself are stuck being unable to directly contribute because it can be difficult to even get off the ground. 2-3 different case-study-based examples would give enough overlapping surface area to provide a feedback loop of being able to generate more community-driven examples off those templates. Similarly, as I mentioned at the beginning, there needs to be at least some guidance in terms of interpretation. This might be comparing a false model to the true model and noting some of the things, or even just a note here or there about what one might look for.

2) Provide some 'expert opinion' or commentary from Andrew or others that can allay some question to approaches to model selection. Namely companies often waste time debating over covariate selection. Giving a nod to reasonable approach(es) would be a huge boon. This is made more tricky by the current gold standard of stepwise covariate modeling via change in objective function values does not have a clear a bayesian equivalent?.  Metrum, and myself personally, are using a full model approach to essentially select for covariates that can be deemed clinically relevant based on their posterior distribution http://metrumrg.com/assets/pubs/GastonguayPAGE2011.pdf

2.1) If accomplishing this requires pre/post-processing, providing some tooling around accomplishing this goal. The #1 way via MLE right now is via step-wise modeling, and much of that is due to it being 'good enough' statistically, and dead simple due to it being implemented as little more than a config file + base model structure http://psn.sourceforge.net/pdfdocs/scm_userguide.pdf I think the above full model approach diagnostics are almost completely implemented from a visually in jonah's bayesplot, but could use some additional helpers for continuous covariates (as shown on slide 27 above).

3) Stay the course with Metrum implementing an events system and general ODE implementation details. I imagine there will also need to be some wrappers/templating around other constructs that might not fall under that initial objective (lag time, bioavailability fractions, transit compartments)?

4) longer term (that I hesitate to even pose at this point due to how many more important fundamental constructs need to be implemented first) an additional abstraction layer to give more nonmem style control-file that removes some constructs like explicitly coding to loop through individuals. For example, you can see here how 1 cmt model with analytical solution is defined for a population. https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes/blob/master/models/one_cmt_iv.cpp vs the current stan implementation https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/TwoCptModelPopulation/TwoCptModelPopulation.stan

By and large, it seems people running models in pharma seem to fall under opposite ends of the spectrum: 1) your formally trained statisticians, and 2) (myself included) have background in biological sciences, some math and have been picking up stats on the way, but virtually no formal training, including 'simple' things like digesting proofs. For those of us in camp #2, there is this huge gap between the baby step of here is bayes rule and why its awesome, to 'introductory' texts where the expectation is still at minimum undergrad courses in inference, probability, and general comfort digesting proofs and formula.   An intermediate ground of applied examples could allow people to more directly connect with the domain while also providing pointers to the theory such that they can digest as they become more comfortable.

Hopefully not too long winded.

And as a bonus, here, for example, might be an excellent case study:

Which dose should we choose to maximize the benefit/risk profile in a target population, given rich data from a small subset of individuals studied in a previous trial? Let's say we've done a trial and have data for ~100 individuals at 4 escalating dose levels, each with 4-6 samples. To answer this we will need to do the following

1) Build and evaluate structural and residual error model(s) - is it one cmt/two cmt, and is the residual error additive, exponential, some combination
    - what are the diagnostic plots/calculated values used to compare such models

2) Determine the effect of covariates on model parameters to determine which to retain, as well as to get a feel for which will need to be most closely monitored for potential dose adjustment in later phases (or to kill the drug all together).
    - how do you address covariate inclusion/exclusion and overall building

3) Simulate from the final model and compare against some criteria (such as % of individuals in a given exposure window).
    - how to simulate under different designs

3.5) perform sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of being 'wrong' on a given parameter - say the population variability on clearance - what if it was 50% greater, lower, etc. This can be relevant when moving to different subpopulation, eg studied in healthy now going to sick patients with additional comorbidities that may effect drug clearance.

4) bonus: use the above model as a prior to fit some new data.

Hope this helps.

Devin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] jacobian adjustment for squared_distance?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] jacobian adjustment for squared_distance?
messages.body_plain:
Our Jacobians are the usual ones from multivariate
calculus change of variables.  They are always N to N.

If you try to do this:

  d(y1, y2) = (y1 - y2)' * (y1 - y2)

and then say

 d(y1, y2) ~ foo(...)

you'll see that you can't properly normalize in the
2N-dimensional space making up y1 and y2 because you
can move y1 and y2 together in any direction to get the
same distance.  This is why you need N to N transforms.
They need to map volumes to volumes or you wind up
with unmeasureable sets (too low a dimension).  And it
needs to be an invertible mapping, which also won't work
with a reduction to distances.

But all is not lost.  We encourage people to think of
models generatively, and it just so happens that least squares
wasn't an accident, and that:

  log multi_normal(y1 | y2, I) = - 0.5 * d(y1, y2) + constant

So what you can do is put a conditional distribution on y1 given
y2 based on distance.  Then you can put whatever distribution you
want on y2 and the result will be a well normalized prior if
the prior on y2 can be normalized.  (Stan doesn't need the normalization
constants, but it does require posteriors to be proper.)

Alternatively, you may be thinking about something like both y1 and y2
coming from some process that generates them starting from some shared latent
z, in which case you can have something like:

  p(y1 | z) = ...
  p(y2 | z) = ...
  p(z) = ...

But without something anchoring the position, you won't get a normalizable
prior.

- Bob

I still didn't follow most of that.  I'm not sure what you mean
by "calculating" when you say calculating a variable leads to
misconvergence.  Do you mean adding a new variable to a model?
Adding new parameters can cause problems if they're not identified.

In general, there's no way to estimate the posterior mean and standard
deviation of a parameter without sampling.  Sometimes you can do it analytically.
For example, you can integrate out the beta a beta-binomial to get the
beta-binomial distribution and integrate out the gamma of a gamma-poisson
to get a negative binomial.  Is that what you're trying to do?  You
say you don't care about log_ex, but then you are asking for its mean
and standard deviation.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The summary for a Stan fit isn't a confidence interval,
it's a posterior interval.

If you have two parameters a and b, you can't provide
a Bayesian answer to "are they different" because unless
one's a function of the other one, the statement Pr[a = f(b) | data]
will be zero.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  That's very much in line with what others have
told us.  We are teaching such classes with such case
studies---Bill Gillespie of Metrum's taught a bunch and
we just taught a class in Paris this Fall and will probably
be doing more.  We just need to make some of the case studies
public.

To think that this is how some pharmacologists choose covariates
is frightening.  We tend to include all the covariates we have
and let the priors and hierarchical modeling sort them out.
Or we'll do that, then select out the ones that aren't doing
predictively after the model is fit (Aki Vehtari has some papers
on this approach).

Those 100 model PK/PD libraries can (and are) being built on
top of Stan.  Our target audience is really the people writing those
libraries rather than the users of those libraries.  That is,
it's another level on top of Stan, like the RStanArm package.
Hopefully this level of user knows more stats.   What we'd like to
do is bring more people up to this level.  That's why doc's so
important.  The whole point of working directly in Stan (or BUGS
or JAGS or NONMEM) is that you can make more reasonable data
and modeling choices for your scientific process and measurement
process.

Just to clear up one misconception:  doc is *not* a low
priority for us!   It is, unfortunately, a very low priority
for most programs in most funding agencies.

- Bob

> On Dec 19, 2016, at 8:02 PM, Devin Pastoor <devin....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > You mean in publishing?  Because for the most part, Bayesian
> modeling is easier because posterior means are so much better
> behaved than posterior modes (e.g., we don't have to limit models
> like NONMEM [or lme4 does] in order to fit them with max marginal
> likelihood).
>
> Hurdles namely in terms of implementation details (eg. I know i want a 2 compartment model with linear absorption with covariates of weight and gender, but how do I code that and then look at model diagnostics), and from an acceptance perspective - 'matching' up to historical comparisons. Eg, its very easy at this point to say, model development was performed using step-wise covariate modeling using a forward inclusion criteria of p < 0.05 and backwards step of p < 0.001. Here are x, y, z diagnostic plots. You can point to 20 other publications with similar diagnostics and interpretations. For example, the 2 primary plots shown to demonstrate model adequacy is conditional weighted residuals  and observed vs individual predicted concentrations, both shown here: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries
>
> These frequentist diagnostics by and large go out the window for bayesian analysis. I don't say this as a good or bad thing, just that the current status quo heavily favors coloring by those numbers to provide historical backing to the modeling strategy used.
>
>
> > I don't care so much about why people don't do full Bayes, but I am curious about what you think Stan can do.
>
> I believe they are reasonably tightly coupled in a lot of situations, somewhat touched on above.
>
> First, for the remaining discussion we can set aside models that only stan/winbugs/etc can handle, and instead focus on what can be done such that people who would normally have turned to nonmem would instead grab Stan.
>
>
> 1) Push out some more (simple, but holistic) examples.
>
> This is going to be the largest hurdle once the ODE implementation settles. For better or worse, the majority of people will want to 'copy-paste' their way through scenarios they are familiar with to wrap their head around. Many companies have model libraries of 100's of models with 'tricks' on how to implement things.
>
> For example, I'm picking away at an extremely simple example: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries and the associated code for the project: https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes
>
> Such case studies would cover:
> - what the data looks like
> - model setup with some information
> - diagnostic outputs with some minimal interpretation
>
> I know documentation is so low on priorities for the core team, but without some more examples, people such as myself are stuck being unable to directly contribute because it can be difficult to even get off the ground. 2-3 different case-study-based examples would give enough overlapping surface area to provide a feedback loop of being able to generate more community-driven examples off those templates. Similarly, as I mentioned at the beginning, there needs to be at least some guidance in terms of interpretation. This might be comparing a false model to the true model and noting some of the things, or even just a note here or there about what one might look for.
>
> 2) Provide some 'expert opinion' or commentary from Andrew or others that can allay some question to approaches to model selection. Namely companies often waste time debating over covariate selection. Giving a nod to reasonable approach(es) would be a huge boon. This is made more tricky by the current gold standard of stepwise covariate modeling via change in objective function values does not have a clear a bayesian equivalent?.  Metrum, and myself personally, are using a full model approach to essentially select for covariates that can be deemed clinically relevant based on their posterior distribution http://metrumrg.com/assets/pubs/GastonguayPAGE2011.pdf
>
> 2.1) If accomplishing this requires pre/post-processing, providing some tooling around accomplishing this goal. The #1 way via MLE right now is via step-wise modeling, and much of that is due to it being 'good enough' statistically, and dead simple due to it being implemented as little more than a config file + base model structure http://psn.sourceforge.net/pdfdocs/scm_userguide.pdf I think the above full model approach diagnostics are almost completely implemented from a visually in jonah's bayesplot, but could use some additional helpers for continuous covariates (as shown on slide 27 above).
>
> 3) Stay the course with Metrum implementing an events system and general ODE implementation details. I imagine there will also need to be some wrappers/templating around other constructs that might not fall under that initial objective (lag time, bioavailability fractions, transit compartments)?
>
> 4) longer term (that I hesitate to even pose at this point due to how many more important fundamental constructs need to be implemented first) an additional abstraction layer to give more nonmem style control-file that removes some constructs like explicitly coding to loop through individuals. For example, you can see here how 1 cmt model with analytical solution is defined for a population. https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes/blob/master/models/one_cmt_iv.cpp vs the current stan implementation https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/TwoCptModelPopulation/TwoCptModelPopulation.stan
>
>
> By and large, it seems people running models in pharma seem to fall under opposite ends of the spectrum: 1) your formally trained statisticians, and 2) (myself included) have background in biological sciences, some math and have been picking up stats on the way, but virtually no formal training, including 'simple' things like digesting proofs. For those of us in camp #2, there is this huge gap between the baby step of here is bayes rule and why its awesome, to 'introductory' texts where the expectation is still at minimum undergrad courses in inference, probability, and general comfort digesting proofs and formula.   An intermediate ground of applied examples could allow people to more directly connect with the domain while also providing pointers to the theory such that they can digest as they become more comfortable.
>
>
> Hopefully not too long winded.
>
>
> And as a bonus, here, for example, might be an excellent case study:
>
> Which dose should we choose to maximize the benefit/risk profile in a target population, given rich data from a small subset of individuals studied in a previous trial? Let's say we've done a trial and have data for ~100 individuals at 4 escalating dose levels, each with 4-6 samples. To answer this we will need to do the following
>
> 1) Build and evaluate structural and residual error model(s) - is it one cmt/two cmt, and is the residual error additive, exponential, some combination
>     - what are the diagnostic plots/calculated values used to compare such models
>
> 2) Determine the effect of covariates on model parameters to determine which to retain, as well as to get a feel for which will need to be most closely monitored for potential dose adjustment in later phases (or to kill the drug all together).
>     - how do you address covariate inclusion/exclusion and overall building
>
>
>
> 3) Simulate from the final model and compare against some criteria (such as % of individuals in a given exposure window).
>     - how to simulate under different designs
>
> 3.5) perform sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of being 'wrong' on a given parameter - say the population variability on clearance - what if it was 50% greater, lower, etc. This can be relevant when moving to different subpopulation, eg studied in healthy now going to sick patients with additional comorbidities that may effect drug clearance.
>
>
> 4) bonus: use the above model as a prior to fit some new data.
>
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> Devin
>
> On Monday, December 19, 2016 at 5:59:00 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Dec 19, 2016, at 5:30 PM, Devin Pastoor <devin....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > awesome. Thanks for taking the time to respond.
> >
> > To answer your question - people don't ask at this point. Mainly because of the contraints of what NONMEM gives you (basically only inverse wishart unless you want to jump through a lot of hoops).
>
> I figured that'd be the answer.
>
> > Also, other than the very small (passionate) minority, the additional hurdles bayesian analysis poses to the status quo of model development
>
> You mean in publishing?  Because for the most part, Bayesian
> modeling is easier because posterior means are so much better
> behaved than posterior modes (e.g., we don't have to limit models
> like NONMEM [or lme4 does] in order to fit them with max marginal
> likelihood).
>
> > makes it so very few people are developing models in that fashion.
>
> We must know them all :-)
>
> > It's really only under situations where either
> >
> > a) you a priori know you want to make quantification and handling of uncertainity 'first class'
> >
> > b) all other options have failed
> >
> > are people turning to bayesian techniques.
>
> I think as people get more sophisticated in thinking about uncertainty,
> (a) will be come a priority, and as they want to build more
> sophisticated models, (b) is critical.  We've come into projects largely
> because of (b) --- people had models to fit that they couldn't fit
> with NONMEM or other off-the-shelf tools.
>
> > For example, if you look at the ddmore model repository of ~200 models http://repository.ddmore.eu/ as well as my personal interactions with the model bases at Merck, the FDA, and our own group pushing that number to probably 300+ models, I think less than 5% of the models used full bayes, especially for PK models. You see it more when doing like model based meta analysis or some systems biology/PBPK modeling though, and there only metrum and some select individuals seem to make an consistent noise in the space.
>
> We have an ONR grant to make PK/PD easier with Metrum. They're
> working on NONMEM-style interfaces for "events" (dosing and measurement)
> and on better solvers (just added a matrix exponential).
>
> > Anyway - I don't want to turn this into an exposition, however if you are interested in the why of lack of full bayes (much of which I bet you can guess at) or what stan can (continue) doing to make a dent in that, I'm happy to expand on the state of things.
>
> I don't care so much about why people don't do full Bayes, but
> I am curious about what you think Stan can do.
>
> - Bob
>

> On Dec 19, 2016, at 10:43 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> 2016-12-20 13:29 GMT+11:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> I still didn't follow most of that.  I'm not sure what you mean
> by "calculating" when you say calculating a variable leads to
> misconvergence.  Do you mean adding a new variable to a model?
> Adding new parameters can cause problems if they're not identified.
>
> Calculating is probably the wrong word. Yes I add a new parameter to the model. Such parameters is the ex standard deviation ex_sd

This is already getting confused.  You're not calculating the
standard deviation of ex when you do this:

  ex ~ normal(mu, ex_sd)

All it does is add a term to the log density.  Then the prior
on ex_sd (including improper uniform if you don't include one)
will have an effect, as well.  And you'll get uncertainty around
ex_sd, not just a calculation based on whatever ex is, even if
ex is fixed as data.

> For example if I want to tell to the user whether ex_mean[1] is different from ex_mean[2]
>
> Can I just use this formulation?
>
> 1)
>
> data y (0-Inf), a (0-1, simplex)
> parameters ex_mean (0-Inf)
>
> y[n] ~ density( a[1] * ex_mean[1] + a[2] * ex_mean[2], error);

Yes.  But I don't know what "error" is.  We tend to use
Greek letters for parameters (alpha, beta, sigma, etc.)
and Roman letters (x, y, m, n, M, N) for data.

> I would think not, because I also need to know what is the variability around
> ex_mean.

You mean give them a prior?

> My answer was, let's try to get standard deviation for each ex_mean.

This is where you're really losing me.  I'm going to stop here
and hope you can regroup.  Are you talking about in the
posterior?  You get that automatically.

- Bob

> On Mon, Dec 19, 2016 at 09:15:36PM -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> you'll see that you can't properly normalize in the
>> 2N-dimensional space making up y1 and y2 because you
>> can move y1 and y2 together in any direction to get the
>> same distance.
>
> Sure
>
>> But all is not lost.  We encourage people to think of
>> models generatively, and it just so happens that least squares
>> wasn't an accident, and that:
>>
>>  log multi_normal(y1 | y2, I) = - 0.5 * d(y1, y2) + constant
>>
>> So what you can do is put a conditional distribution on y1 given
>> y2 based on distance.
>
> Ah, that works!

Oh, and it's more efficient to code in Stan as

  y1 ~ normal(y2, sigma);

assuming the length scale's the same in every dimension.  Or even just
fix a value for sigma (I did that implicitly with I, which I should've
included as sigma * I, where I is the identity matrix).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
So mu is a parameter 3-vector, sigma is a scalar, y[n] is a known scalar,
and the a[n, ] is a known simplex?

And you want to ask a question about the marginal posterior

  p(mu | y, a)

such as do the mu[1], mu[2] and mu[3] components have the same
posterior distribution?

How do you want to measure difference?  You can look at one-sided
event probabilities like

  Pr[mu[1] > mu[2] | y, a]

Presumably if that's a very high value, you know they're different.

But I don't think that's the question you really want to ask.

Usually, what people do is compare whole models, like a simple model,
two-component mixture and three-component mixture.  Just because
a three component mixture has very distinct mu[1], mu[2] and mu[3]
posteriors, it doesn't mean it's giving you any added value over a two-component
mixture.  But you have to decide what it is you value---some
prediction, perhaps?

- Bob

multiple comparisons so techniques like scm + some reduction are in place. The other, historically, difficult part
about letting things sort, is convergence issues with more complex models, especially to get standard errors.
Thankfully, this is extremely natural in the bayesian context.

I've pinged Charles and by proxy Bill to help out with the case study generation, so hopefully I can alleviate some
of the time for them on that end and let them focus on implementations.

Thanks again for the pointers.

> be doing more.  We just need to make some of the case studies
> public.
>
> To think that this is how some pharmacologists choose covariates
> is frightening.  We tend to include all the covariates we have
> and let the priors and hierarchical modeling sort them out.
> Or we'll do that, then select out the ones that aren't doing
> predictively after the model is fit (Aki Vehtari has some papers
> on this approach).
>
> Those 100 model PK/PD libraries can (and are) being built on
> top of Stan.  Our target audience is really the people writing those
> libraries rather than the users of those libraries.  That is,
> it's another level on top of Stan, like the RStanArm package.
> Hopefully this level of user knows more stats.   What we'd like to
> do is bring more people up to this level.  That's why doc's so
> important.  The whole point of working directly in Stan (or BUGS
> or JAGS or NONMEM) is that you can make more reasonable data
> and modeling choices for your scientific process and measurement
> process.
>
> Just to clear up one misconception:  doc is *not* a low
> priority for us!   It is, unfortunately, a very low priority
> for most programs in most funding agencies.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Dec 19, 2016, at 8:02 PM, Devin Pastoor <devin....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > You mean in publishing?  Because for the most part, Bayesian
> > modeling is easier because posterior means are so much better
> > behaved than posterior modes (e.g., we don't have to limit models
> > like NONMEM [or lme4 does] in order to fit them with max marginal
> > likelihood).
> >
> > Hurdles namely in terms of implementation details (eg. I know i want a 2 compartment model with linear absorption with covariates of weight and gender, but how do I code that and then look at model diagnostics), and from an acceptance perspective - 'matching' up to historical comparisons. Eg, its very easy at this point to say, model development was performed using step-wise covariate modeling using a forward inclusion criteria of p < 0.05 and backwards step of p < 0.001. Here are x, y, z diagnostic plots. You can point to 20 other publications with similar diagnostics and interpretations. For example, the 2 primary plots shown to demonstrate model adequacy is conditional weighted residuals  and observed vs individual predicted concentrations, both shown here: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries
> >
> > These frequentist diagnostics by and large go out the window for bayesian analysis. I don't say this as a good or bad thing, just that the current status quo heavily favors coloring by those numbers to provide historical backing to the modeling strategy used.
> >
> >
> > > I don't care so much about why people don't do full Bayes, but I am curious about what you think Stan can do.
> >
> > I believe they are reasonably tightly coupled in a lot of situations, somewhat touched on above.
> >
> > First, for the remaining discussion we can set aside models that only stan/winbugs/etc can handle, and instead focus on what can be done such that people who would normally have turned to nonmem would instead grab Stan.
> >
> >
> > 1) Push out some more (simple, but holistic) examples.
> >
> > This is going to be the largest hurdle once the ODE implementation settles. For better or worse, the majority of people will want to 'copy-paste' their way through scenarios they are familiar with to wrap their head around. Many companies have model libraries of 100's of models with 'tricks' on how to implement things.
> >
> > For example, I'm picking away at an extremely simple example: http://devinpastoor.com/simplest_bayes/foce-analysis.html#visual-summaries and the associated code for the project: https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes
> >
> > Such case studies would cover:
> > - what the data looks like
> > - model setup with some information
> > - diagnostic outputs with some minimal interpretation
> >
> > I know documentation is so low on priorities for the core team, but without some more examples, people such as myself are stuck being unable to directly contribute because it can be difficult to even get off the ground. 2-3 different case-study-based examples would give enough overlapping surface area to provide a feedback loop of being able to generate more community-driven examples off those templates. Similarly, as I mentioned at the beginning, there needs to be at least some guidance in terms of interpretation. This might be comparing a false model to the true model and noting some of the things, or even just a note here or there about what one might look for.
> >
> > 2) Provide some 'expert opinion' or commentary from Andrew or others that can allay some question to approaches to model selection. Namely companies often waste time debating over covariate selection. Giving a nod to reasonable approach(es) would be a huge boon. This is made more tricky by the current gold standard of stepwise covariate modeling via change in objective function values does not have a clear a bayesian equivalent?.  Metrum, and myself personally, are using a full model approach to essentially select for covariates that can be deemed clinically relevant based on their posterior distribution http://metrumrg.com/assets/pubs/GastonguayPAGE2011.pdf
> >
> > 2.1) If accomplishing this requires pre/post-processing, providing some tooling around accomplishing this goal. The #1 way via MLE right now is via step-wise modeling, and much of that is due to it being 'good enough' statistically, and dead simple due to it being implemented as little more than a config file + base model structure http://psn.sourceforge.net/pdfdocs/scm_userguide.pdf I think the above full model approach diagnostics are almost completely implemented from a visually in jonah's bayesplot, but could use some additional helpers for continuous covariates (as shown on slide 27 above).
> >
> > 3) Stay the course with Metrum implementing an events system and general ODE implementation details. I imagine there will also need to be some wrappers/templating around other constructs that might not fall under that initial objective (lag time, bioavailability fractions, transit compartments)?
> >
> > 4) longer term (that I hesitate to even pose at this point due to how many more important fundamental constructs need to be implemented first) an additional abstraction layer to give more nonmem style control-file that removes some constructs like explicitly coding to loop through individuals. For example, you can see here how 1 cmt model with analytical solution is defined for a population. https://github.com/dpastoor/simplest_bayes/blob/master/models/one_cmt_iv.cpp vs the current stan implementation https://github.com/charlesm93/example-models/blob/feature/issue-70-PKPDexamples-torsten/PKPD/torsten/TwoCptModelPopulation/TwoCptModelPopulation.stan
> >
> >
> > By and large, it seems people running models in pharma seem to fall under opposite ends of the spectrum: 1) your formally trained statisticians, and 2) (myself included) have background in biological sciences, some math and have been picking up stats on the way, but virtually no formal training, including 'simple' things like digesting proofs. For those of us in camp #2, there is this huge gap between the baby step of here is bayes rule and why its awesome, to 'introductory' texts where the expectation is still at minimum undergrad courses in inference, probability, and general comfort digesting proofs and formula.   An intermediate ground of applied examples could allow people to more directly connect with the domain while also providing pointers to the theory such that they can digest as they become more comfortable.
> >
> >
> > Hopefully not too long winded.
> >
> >
> > And as a bonus, here, for example, might be an excellent case study:
> >
> > Which dose should we choose to maximize the benefit/risk profile in a target population, given rich data from a small subset of individuals studied in a previous trial? Let's say we've done a trial and have data for ~100 individuals at 4 escalating dose levels, each with 4-6 samples. To answer this we will need to do the following
> >
> > 1) Build and evaluate structural and residual error model(s) - is it one cmt/two cmt, and is the residual error additive, exponential, some combination
> >     - what are the diagnostic plots/calculated values used to compare such models
> >
> > 2) Determine the effect of covariates on model parameters to determine which to retain, as well as to get a feel for which will need to be most closely monitored for potential dose adjustment in later phases (or to kill the drug all together).
> >     - how do you address covariate inclusion/exclusion and overall building
> >
> >
> >
> > 3) Simulate from the final model and compare against some criteria (such as % of individuals in a given exposure window).
> >     - how to simulate under different designs
> >
> > 3.5) perform sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of being 'wrong' on a given parameter - say the population variability on clearance - what if it was 50% greater, lower, etc. This can be relevant when moving to different subpopulation, eg studied in healthy now going to sick patients with additional comorbidities that may effect drug clearance.
> >
> >
> > 4) bonus: use the above model as a prior to fit some new data.
> >
> >
> > Hope this helps.
> >
> > Devin
> >
> > On Monday, December 19, 2016 at 5:59:00 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Dec 19, 2016, at 5:30 PM, Devin Pastoor <devin....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > awesome. Thanks for taking the time to respond.
> > >
> > > To answer your question - people don't ask at this point. Mainly because of the contraints of what NONMEM gives you (basically only inverse wishart unless you want to jump through a lot of hoops).
> >
> > I figured that'd be the answer.
> >
> > > Also, other than the very small (passionate) minority, the additional hurdles bayesian analysis poses to the status quo of model development
> >
> > You mean in publishing?  Because for the most part, Bayesian
> > modeling is easier because posterior means are so much better
> > behaved than posterior modes (e.g., we don't have to limit models
> > like NONMEM [or lme4 does] in order to fit them with max marginal
> > likelihood).
> >
> > > makes it so very few people are developing models in that fashion.
> >
> > We must know them all :-)
> >
> > > It's really only under situations where either
> > >
> > > a) you a priori know you want to make quantification and handling of uncertainity 'first class'
> > >
> > > b) all other options have failed
> > >
> > > are people turning to bayesian techniques.
> >
> > I think as people get more sophisticated in thinking about uncertainty,
> > (a) will be come a priority, and as they want to build more
> > sophisticated models, (b) is critical.  We've come into projects largely
> > because of (b) --- people had models to fit that they couldn't fit
> > with NONMEM or other off-the-shelf tools.
> >
> > > For example, if you look at the ddmore model repository of ~200 models http://repository.ddmore.eu/ as well as my personal interactions with the model bases at Merck, the FDA, and our own group pushing that number to probably 300+ models, I think less than 5% of the models used full bayes, especially for PK models. You see it more when doing like model based meta analysis or some systems biology/PBPK modeling though, and there only metrum and some select individuals seem to make an consistent noise in the space.
> >
> > We have an ONR grant to make PK/PD easier with Metrum. They're
> > working on NONMEM-style interfaces for "events" (dosing and measurement)
> > and on better solvers (just added a matrix exponential).
> >
> > > Anyway - I don't want to turn this into an exposition, however if you are interested in the why of lack of full bayes (much of which I bet you can guess at) or what stan can (continue) doing to make a dent in that, I'm happy to expand on the state of things.

> >
> > - Bob

> On Dec 17, 2016, at 9:21 AM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Right, but when I try doing real * vector it gives me the vector / vector error

If you have (real * vector), the result is vector.  Same with (vector * real).
You can do (row_vector * vector) and get a real, or (vector * row_vector)
and get a matrix. But you can't do (vector * vector) because the dimensions
don't conform to matrix multiplication.

> (which cannot really be corrected by pointwise division because the vectors' sizes are different),

Do you have a simple example of the types you want
to define and operations you want to perform?  We can help
with specifics of error messages.

> and there's also the problem where scale[country] doesn't work because country is a vector (even though what I really mean is scale[country[i]] for every i, as defined in the for loop).

country is going to be an array if it's an index.  and if
it's an array of K elements, then scale[country] will also
have K elements, (scale[country[1]], ..., scale[country[K]])

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
No.  The sampling statements only increment the log
density, so all the terms used in them must be defined
before they are used.

You can use RNGs in the generated quantities block if
that's what you're trying to accomplish.  Otherwise, you
just need to declare the unknowns as parameters.  You can
just forget about them during inference and focus on
the marginal of the other paramters.

- Bob

> country is going to be an array if it's an index.  and if

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for this helpful information. I did not realize I was incurring bias by putting prior mass on impossible outcomes.

In reviewing my matrix algebra, I see that for this simple 3x3 case, it's possible to derive simple algebraic relationships between rho1 and rho2 that ensure positive definiteness. One way seems to be to ensure the determinant of the entire 3x3 correlation matrix is itself positive.

Of course, when I scale up to a larger matrix for my real life situation (a sports problem), I'm probably not going to be able to derive simple bounds like this with, say, 5 different correlations in a 12x12 matrix. It looks like there's some literature out there discussing similar issues (like this paper <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4217169/>), but I'd be interested in hearing if there are other tricks Stan users have in the face of complex constraints.

On Sun, Dec 18, 2016 at 8:49 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sunday, December 18, 2016 at 12:27:51 PM UTC-5, Ben Ogorek wrote:
> > In my Stan code <https://github.com/baogorek/Miscellaneous/blob/master/R_code/stan/ragged_array_cov_est.stan>, I believe I got it to work by creating a "master" covariance matrix in transformed parameters and then putting sub-segments of the data vector into local variable of fixed size in the model block. The only bad thing is having to "repeat myself" for every vector size:
>
> It would probably be better to pass the data as two (or n_clusters) vectors, one for each cluster.
>
> > Also, as an inexperienced bayesian practitioner, there are a few additional points that concern me:
> > My priors don't ensure positive definiteness,
> Then your priors do not integrate to 1 over admissible region of the parameter space. To be positive definite, you need to declare rho2 as
>
> real<lower=-bound(rho1),upper=bound(rho1)> rho2;
>
> where bound is defined in the functions block as
>
> real bound(real rho1) return sqrt( 1 / ( 1 + (1 - rho1) / (1 + rho1) ) );
> > Stan gives a warning message about my "transformation" of the data into the cluster-sized variables,
> That is an identity "transformation" and thus the Jacobian matrix is the identity matrix, whose log-determinant is a constant (zero), so no adjustment needs to be made.
>
> > There seems to be some bias in the posterior draws, but perhaps this is expected
> from the lack of positive definiteness.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm helping a friend with a fantasy football game where players choose a "lineup" of 1 Quarterback (QB), 3 Wide Recievers (WR), 2 Running Backs (RB), a Tight End (TE), a "Flex player" (WR, RB, or TE), and a defense. Points are awarded at the player level based on performance in a single game, and thus these picks can be from the same team or different teams. But within-team player correlations are part of the strategy; if a QB has a high "scoring" game, then the WRs from the same team are also more likely to have high scoring games.

My approach seeks to incorporate these player correlations by modeling the weekly match-up vectors between teams. These will be of variable dimension, but one match-up vector might look like:

(QB, WR1, WR2, WR3, WR4, RB1, RB2, RB3, TE1, TE2, Def)

I'd like to structure the correlation matrix such that:
  * Corr(QB,  WRj) = rho_qb_wr
  * Corr(QB,  RBj) = rho_qb_rb
  * Corr(QB,  TEj) = rho_qb_te
  * Corr(QB,  Def) = rho_qb_def
  * Corr(WRi, WRj) = rho_wr, i /= j
  * Corr(RBi, WRj) = rho_rb_wr
  * Corr(WRi, TEj) = rho_wr_te
  * Corr(WRi, Def) = rho_wr_def
  * Corr(RBi, RBj) = rho_rb, i /= j
  * Corr(RBi, TEj) = rho_rb_te
  * Corr(RBi, Def) = rho_rb_def
  * Corr(TEi, TEj) = rho_te, i /= j
  * Corr(TEi, Def) = rho_te_def

If my math is right, that's 110 possible correlations down to 13. But will the problem of getting reasonable priors for the rho's be tractable?

Additionally, since this is a covariance matrix modeling problem, I also considered the structural equation model:

QB_points ~ sum(WR_points) + sum(RB_points) + ... + Def_points,
WR1_points ~ sum(WR_not_WR1_points) + sum(RB_points) + ... + Def_points,
...

This would induce a player correlation matrix, but I dropped it when I considered what a pain it would be to simulate from.

We should put a huge warning on diag_matrix as it's hugely inefficient
in that it fills up a square matrix with zeroes, all of which go on
the autodiff stack.  For efficiency, you can use this:

  diag_pre_multiply(cf_sigma, cf_raw)

instead of diag_matrix(cf_sigma) * cf_raw.  We introduced the more
efficient specialized functions later, but didn't want to remove the
natural ones.  When we get a lint mode going, we'll be able to warn people
to rethink uses of diag_matrix automatically.

- Bob

I did comparison with stan cmd 2.13.1 between the performance when jacobian of ODE is not supplied and when jacobian is supplied. Sebastian taught me the trick by using dMod and cOde. My ODE is 34 state and quite stiff. I have lot of parameters but just estimate few of them.

TEST GRADIENT MODE

 Log probability=-17.7607

 param idx           value           model     finite diff           error
         0               0        -40.7104        -40.7104   -1.58568e-008

This is the general challenge with sparse storage/computation — there’s
an overhead for filling in the matrix randomly instead of sequentially and
you have to enough enough sparsity/redundancy before the speed up
overcomes that overhead.

The only potential intermediate scenario is if you had a very structured
matrix in which case you would have to exploit the particular structure
to build up the full matrix, for example with low-rank approximations.

> On Dec 21, 2016, at 4:01 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Ah, my bad for over-simplifying the situation. While the example I provided filled the second matrix in the transformed data section, in my models I'd actually be building the second matrix in the transformed parameters block.
>
> I'm actually looking to speed up computation of the covariance matrix in a Gaussian Process by computing only the unique entries (there's usually lots of redundancy in these matrices) then populating the matrix by reference to the unique entries.

If these are parameters, copying is OK, but you don't want to recreate
them.

So if you've done this:

  alpha[1] = beta * gamma;

then you don't want to do this:

  alpha[2] = beta * gamma;  // BAD --- high overhead

It'll allocate memory in our arena, call constructors, copy
pointers, do arithmetic, and that's just going forward; it'll
also cause extra virtual function calls during and more arithmetic
during derivative calculation.

Instead, you just want to reuse the old entry

  alpha[2] = alpha[1];  // GOOD

This just copies a pointer and doesn't add new elements to
the expression graph.  And it automatically carries out a kind
of dynamic programming during derivative calculations.

> Here's a gist containing an example of fitting a standard GP versus this faster approach: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/2e3988449f1790873223cd4e7a499e3f
>
> With the covariance matrix filled with a loop it's about 30% faster than the standard GP (at least, for the scenario of maximum redundancy in the covariance matrix, which occurs when the observations occur on a grid). I was hoping there might be a trick to push it even further, but presumably your prior conclusion (that the loop is as fast as this gets) persists, correct?

Yes, loops are fast in Stan.  Computation time is
proportional to the size of the expression graph and
the form of functions in it (lgamma is more expensive
than exp is more expensive than multiplication).  All
the copying and everything else isn't even usually
measurable.  Loops are just compiled to C++ and most
of the vectorization, like in arrays, is just for convenience.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You want to use a Cholesky factor parameterization of
a covariance matrix.  Then it'll require some footwork to
do the modifications you do:

    GaussLogLike[k] = log (pi_z[k]) + multi_normal_lpdf(X[n]|
                                   ((alpha[n]*sum_alpha)*mu[k])/sum(alpha),
                                        ((beta[n]*sum_beta)*Sigma[k])/sum(beta));

The more I read these messages, the more I think our users
must have defective space keys on their keyboards!  I'd write this as:

    gauss_ll[k] = log(pi_z[k])
                + multi_normal_lpdf(X[n] | alpha[n] * sum_alpha /sum(alpha) * mu[k],
                                           beta[n] * sum_beta / sum(beta) * Sigma[k]);

The reason I reordered is that it's better to do all the scalar
arithmetic together to reduce the number of scalar * matrix multiplies.
Arithmetic operators are all left associative
(i.e., (a * b / c) == ((a * b) / c)).

Presumably, contrary to the naming, sum_alpha != sum(alpha) --- otherwise
just drop them all.  You'll have to figure out how to calculate the Cholesky
factor of of beta[n] * sum_beta * Sigma[k] / sum(beta) from the Cholesky factor
 of Sigma.

I don't understand why you'd want to overparameterize like this, but the
above is what you'll need to do to make it efficient.

We generally use a scaled correlation matrix with an LKJ prior on the correlation
matrix.

- Bob

messages.subject: Fix for NUTS bug from R
messages.subject_clean: Fix for NUTS bug from R
messages.body_plain:
If you are using rstan 2.13.x, you can now fix the NUTS bug that has been present in Stan since 2.10.0 by executing once

download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/stan/develop/src/stan/mcmc/hmc/nuts/base_nuts.hpp",
              destfile = system.file("include", "src", "stan", "mcmc", "hmc", "nuts", "base_nuts.hpp",
                                     package = "StanHeaders"))

If your version of R still cannot download from https URLs, you can go to the above URL in a webbrowser and Save As to the path returned by

system.file("include", "src", "stan", "mcmc", "hmc", "nuts", "base_nuts.hpp", package = "StanHeaders")

This may not work if you have rstan 2.12.x or earlier, so in that case, first upgrade to rstan 2.13.x via

update.packages("rstan")

While this will fix (the (co)variances in) models that you write yourself and estimate with rstan or brms, it will not help with models estimated by packages like rstanarm because the sampler was compiled in. I will try to get fixed packages onto CRAN as soon as I can.

Ben

I currently use the mcmc procedure in SAS and am interested in switching to Stan for GLM modeling. One of the features in sas which helped immensely with chain convergence was the ability to assign groups of parameters to individual parameter blocks, each block in its own Markov chain. I could not find any Stan documentation on blocking of parameters.

Here's a description of the process currently implemented in sas:http://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/66859/HTML/default/viewer.htm#statug_mcmc_details05.htm

The Julia language has a similar implementation, below is an excerpt from their support site:

"Mamba holds other distinct advantages over existing offerings. In particular, it provides arbitrary blocking of model parameters and designation of block-specific samplers; samplers that can be used with the included simulation engine or apart from it"

http://mambajl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/intro.html

messages.body_plain:
The blocking algorithms provide a single Markov chain
that alternates sampling subsets of the parameters.
BUGS and JAGS, for example, block all of their multivariate
parameters.

As Ben says, we update all in one block.

To compare samplers, write the same model in each and
measure the effective sample sizes divided by time it
took to fit.  And use our n_eff measure to keep a level
playing field---it's more conservative than other estimators
people use for n_eff.

NIMBLE is the closest tool in R to something like
Mamba.jl and PyMC3 lets you block HMC and NUTS in Python.
We're probably not going to add blocking to Stan any time
soon because with HMC, it tends to reduce mixing rather than
enhancing it (though see Radford Neal's overview of HMC where
he blocked hierarchical parameters---the best approach we've
found is to reparameterize).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan+R users,

Version 1.1.0 of the bayesplot R package is now available on CRAN <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bayesplot>.
There are a few fixes and a decent number of new features. Release  <https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/releases/tag/v1.1.0>
notes <https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/releases/tag/v1.1.0> are copied below. The package can be installed in the standard
way from CRAN using

install.packages("bayesplot")

 - Stan Development Team

-----

bayesplot 1.1.0 Release Notes

(GitHub issue/PR numbers in parentheses)

Fixes:

* Images in vignettes should now render properly using `png` device. Thanks to
TJ Mahr. (#51)

* xaxis_title(FALSE) and yaxis_title(FALSE) now set axis titles to NULL
rather than changing theme elements to element_blank(). This makes it easier
to add axis titles to plots for which they are turned off by default. Thanks to Bill
Harris. (#53)

New Features:

* Introduce ppc_error_hist_grouped function for plotting predictive errors
by level of a grouping variable. (#40)

* Add argument divergences to the mcmc_trace function. For models fit using
HMC/NUTS this can be used to display divergences as a rug at the bottom of the
trace plot. (#42)

* Introduce bayesplot_grid function for juxtaposing plots and enforcing shared
axis limits. (#59)

* Introduce mcmc_recover_intervals function for comparing MCMC estimates to "true"
parameter values used to simulate the data. (#56)

* The stat argument for all ppc_stat_* functions now accepts a function
instead of only the name of a function. (#31)

messages.body_plain:
There may be other issues, but if you want to implement a zero-inflation model then
you need to implement a _mixture_ between the mass at zero and the rest of your
distribution.  See the "Zero-Inflated and Hurdle Models” section of the manual.  That
said, when you mix a discrete and continuous distribution you have to be careful to
not evaluate the continuous density at bad points.

But I may be misunderstanding the model that you’re trying to build — it’ll probably
be easiest if you can write out the model you’re trying to implement in math.

> n_in_gr <- N/N_re
>
> # Covariate

>
> # Random effects
> Groups <- rep(1:N_re, each = n_in_gr)
> a <- rnorm(N_re, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
>
> # Binary part
> g1  <- 1           # Intercept
> eta_bin <- g1      # Intercept only model, just for start
> Pi <- exp(eta_bin) / (1 + exp(eta_bin))
> W <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = Pi)
>
> # Gamma part
> b1 <- 1            # Intercept
> b2 <- 2            # Slope
> eta_cont <- b1 + b2 * X1 + a[Groups]
> shape <- 10
> Yg <- rgamma(n = N, shape = shape, rate = shape/exp(eta_cont))
>
> # ZI data
> Y <- W * Yg
>
> # Data

>   Y = Y,           # ZAG data
>   X1 = X1,         # Covariate
>   Groups = Groups) # Random factor
>

>

>
> X_cont <- model.matrix(~ X1, data = dat)
> X_bin <- model.matrix(~ 1, data = dat)
>

>   X_cont = X_cont, # model matrix for continuous part

>

> data {
>   int<lower=1> N;      // total number of observations

>   matrix[N, K_cont] X_cont;// model matrix for continuous part
>   int N_re; // number of random effects
>   int<lower=1,upper=N_re> Groups[N]; // map observations to groups

>   vector[N] eta_bin;
>   vector[N] A;
>   for(n in 1:N){

>   }
>   if (K_bin > 1) {
>       for(i in 2:K_bin){
>       g ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>     }
>   }
>   // for random effects
>   sigma ~ cauchy(0, 25);
>   a ~ normal(0, sigma);
>   // for gamma params
>   shape ~ gamma(0.01, 0.01);
>   // likelihood contribution
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     if ( Y[n] == 0 )
>       1 ~ bernoulli_logit(eta_bin[n]);
>     else
>       0 ~ bernoulli_logit(eta_bin[n]);
>       Y[n] ~ gamma(shape, shape / exp(eta_cont[n]));
>   }
> }
> "
>
> sM1 <- stan(model_code = cM1, model_name="ZAG",
